articles.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
articles.snippet: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did: Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . articles.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
articles.snippet: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion . What Monaco buys, and what it builds At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.” One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them. The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. Someone still has to decide which change belongs in the project. If you’re building with coding agents, come join us at AI Engineer CODE . And if you’ve been teaching this stuff yourself, I’d love to hear which assignment you had to rewrite first. Show notes Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus, assignments and open-source partners. You can also switch to the previous year’s course to compare. Build a coding agent and look inside Claude Code — Mihail’s walkthroughs of the tool loop and the harness around it. Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt’s approach to learning what changed in an AI-written diff. Monaco’s agent-developer workspaces — The team’s reasoning for building a place where agents can run and test the app. How to Kill the Code Review and the underlying Faros study — Teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs, while their PR review time was 91% longer. Basis’s Authority Map — Where an agent should look for current behavior, earlier decisions and intent. Stripe’s Minions — A production example of giving background coding agents an environment and a path to an engineer-reviewed PR. Boris Cherny’s Steps of AI Adoption — The five stages we pull up on screen near the end of the episode. Mihail on The Thinking Mode — EO Studio’s interview, excerpted at the start of ours. articles.snippet: What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year’s homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. articles.title: Wendell Berry on Where Our Loved Ones Gone Go
articles.snippet: To love is to sign a contract with loss. To love anyway is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life. When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment . “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend . Art from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days . Death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us. We can also be left in life, left behind, left wondering where love goes when it goes . At its most discomposing, abandonment can feel like a living death. All deep loss has one thing in common: It opens an absence so acutely felt it kidnaps us from presence, takes us away from our own lives and their insistent, inconvenient, sacred ongoingness. In memory or in fantasy, we end up refugees from reality, ceding the only thing that is ever ours for the keeping: the living moment. In all missing, we miss life. That is what the achingly missed Wendell Berry (August 5, 1934–August 31, 2026) explores in this gasp of a poem, originally published in the November 17, 2025 issue of The New Yorker : THE LOVED ONES by Wendell Berry The loved ones we call the dead depart from us and for a while are absent. And then as if called back by our love, they come near us again. They enter our dreams. We feel they have been near us when we have not thought of them. They are simply here, simply waiting while we are distracted among our obligations. At last it comes to us: They live now in the permanent world. We are the absent ones. Couple with physicist Richard Feynman’s extraordinary love letter to his wife written long after her untimely death, then revisit Wendell Berry on creativity and love and his timeless antidote to despair . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . articles.title: Hope Is the Thing with Feathers, and with Fangs: The Alchemy of Unrequited Love and the Story Behind Emily Dickinson’s Most Famous Poem
articles.snippet: This essay is adapted from the nineteenth chapter of my book Figuring . In the first autumn of her thirties, Emily Dickinson wrote to her confidante and eventual editor Thomas Wentworth Higginson : I had a terror — since September — I could tell to none, and so I sing, as the Boy does by the Burying Ground — because I am afraid. Not a “fright,” not a “shock,” but a terror . What lay behind this enormity implied by a woman who measured her words so meticulously? Generations of biographers have filled pages with conjectures of varying persuasiveness — a death, some unrecorded heartbreak in her volcanic relationship with Susan , the first attack of epilepsy — but the most intriguing theory came nearly a century after the poet encrypted these words. In 1951, after years of research and travel to various archives, the scholar Rebecca Patterson proposed a wholly novel candidate for the “terror” of 1861: Kate Scott Anthon — a newly widowed young woman Susan had befriended during their studies at the Utica Female Academy and then introduced to Emily, who fell into an intense romantic and possibly physical affair with the enticing newcomer before Kate severed the relationship without explanation, dealing a blow Emily would experience as deathly and furnishing the raw material for much of her mournful poetry. Their story is a mosaic assembled from various surviving documents, as direct as Emily’s letters and as oblique as the marginalia in Kate’s favorite books. Unauthenticated daguerreotype of (most scholars believe) Emily Dickinson and Kate Scott Anthon In the late winter of 1859, Kate descended a sleigh in her fashionable black hat and widow’s veil in front of her former classmate’s home in Amherst. Almost immediately, Susan introduced her to the beloved auburn-haired friend who lived across the hedge in the brick house painted deep red and who had been hearing of her for nearly a decade. When Emily, wrapped in a merino shawl, met the tall, handsome woman with the penetrating dark eyes, musical voice, and lively passion for literature and astronomy, she was instantly entranced. During the three weeks of Kate’s first stay in Amherst, the two women, both twenty-eight, became inseparable. They took long walks with Emily’s dog, Carlo, read Aurora Leigh aloud to each other, and spent evenings at the piano as Emily improvised — “weird and beautiful melodies, all from her own inspiration,” Kate would remember. As Emily played, Kate towered behind her — “Goliath,” the petite poet would call her. When Kate left to go home, Emily beckoned her for another visit to Amherst: I am pleasantly located in the deep sea, but love will row you out, if her hands are strong, and don’t wait till I land, for I’m going ashore on the other side. Art by Giuliano Cucco from Before I Grew Up . Emily’s early letters to Kate pulsate with electricity. Writing weeks after they first met, she tries to disguise with playfulness the push-and-pull of irrepressible, frustrated longing in the code language of botany that was her first poetic tongue : I never missed a Kate before. . . . Sweet at my door this March night another Candidate — Go Home! We don’t like Katies here! — Stay! My heart votes for you, and what am I indeed to dispute her ballot –? What are your qualifications? Dare you dwell in the East where we dwell? Are you afraid of the Sun? — When you hear the new violet sucking her way among the sods, shall you be resolute?… Will you still come?… Kate gathered in March! It is a small bouquet, dear — but what it lacks in size, it gains in fadelessness, — Many can boast a hollyhock, but few can bear a rose! … So I rise, wearing her — so I sleep, holding, — Sleep at last with her fast in my hand and wake bearing my flower. — Page from Emily Dickinson’s herbarium In the late winter of 1860, they spent a night together in Emily’s bedroom — unrecorded, inarticulable, except perhaps in verse: Her sweet Weight on my Heart a Night Had scarcely deigned to lie — When, stirring, for Belief’s delight, My Bride had slipped away — If ’twas a Dream — made solid — just The Heaven to confirm — Or if Myself were dreamed of Her — The power to presume — Several weeks after that momentous night, Emily would channel this precious perishability in a letter to Kate: Finding is slow, facilities for losing so frequent, in a world like this, I hold with extreme caution. A prudence so astute may seem unnecessary, but plenty moves those most, dear, who have been in want… Were you ever poor? I have been a Beggar. Whatever took place between them, they never addressed it overtly — it is always impossible to articulate the possibility between two people, but especially in a time and place that confined the possible to such narrow parameters for permissible love. Feeling the impossibility of it all, Emily shuddered with anticipatory loss: Kate, Distinctly sweet your face stands in its phantom niche — I touch your hand — my cheek your cheek — I stroke your vanished hair, Why did you enter, sister, since you must depart? Had not its heart been torn enough but you must send your shred?… There is a subject, dear, on which we never touch. Little is known of Kate’s side of the experience. None of her letters to Emily survive. (The poet had instructed her sister that all letters be burned after her death — a request which Lavinia Dickinson promptly obliged before discovering the trove of poems that made her realize her sister’s correspondence might have immense literary value.) But Kate — who signed many of her surviving letters to other correspondents “Thomas” or “Tommy” — did have an unambiguous and lifelong proclivity for romantic attachment to women, culminating later in life with a longtime relationship with a young Englishwoman. Perhaps at twenty-eight, she was simply not ready to so radically dismantle the superstructure of her life as she knew it. In April 1861, she severed the relationship with Emily. articles.title: Stephen Miller’s Appointment
articles.snippet: Image generated by ChatGPT All you need to know is his wife Katie didn’t vote, because she was afraid if she registered her address would be made public and… As it is, she and Stephen are already living on a military base, to ensure their safety. And if that doesn’t tell you all you need to know… Isn’t this how it always plays out? The rich/elite separate themselves from the hoi polloi to ensure their theoretical invulnerability. From Versailles to Beverly Park… They fly private, they vacation at resorts you’ve never heard of and… They’re doing it all on your money. It’s the everyday consumer who keeps the wheels of commerce humming. So how much power does the public have? Right now people are fired up. I’ve been living a long time and I’ve never seen anything like this. And all those ancient debates about the red and blue not being able to have a conversation, sit at the same table…those days are through. Of course there are dyed-in-the-wool bonkers believers on the fringes of both parties. But what we learned on Tuesday is we’re more alike than different. It’s finally safe to invite everybody for Thanksgiving. Because one thing we can all agree on is… We’re PISSED! You’re supposed to keep the public quiet, their attention diverted, the last thing you want is focus. But Trump demanded it with his antics. Whether it be shooting people in the street or building his ballroom and even more just getting rich. 90% of voters listed corruption as one of their main complaints, why they voted blue. We haven’t all been on the same page since… I don’t know when. And now Trump is sticking it in our eye, by appointing the architect of the policies hated by the public. An outsider from his days in high school. We don’t need the class president, or the captain of the football team, but we do need someone who knows how to get along. As for Trump himself… He seems to be taking a page from Putin’s playbook. Act like dissent doesn’t matter, and go behind the scenes to enforce your vision. Now historically in America, at least in modern times, you could get away with your bad behavior, by saying everybody else was doing it. Even worse is drinking from the trough because the rich/elite give you access. What America did on Tuesday, and needs to do more, is say NO! That’s the essence of morality, the essence of character. And that’s the only thing that will save us. Netanyahu would not be saying the election was stolen if Trump didn’t lay the groundwork in 2020. Ditto Bolsonaro. I’m not saying I’m approving of a mob mentality, but this is something different, the people are mad as hell and they’re not going to take it anymore. Funny how they made that movie back in the seventies and now it’s the public on the bleeding edge as opposed to the film business, which notoriously plays it safe. But people are hungry for edgy. This is how music lost its power. It became about the brand, grosses and… The most revered acts of all time were not necessarily the ones who hoovered up the most money. So you’ve got to say no to those checks being offered. For your own benefit. You can’t be above the public, but right down in the pit with people. This is what the Millers are trying to escape. But that ship sailed over a decade ago. In today’s world everybody has a voice and everybody is equal. You’re grist for the mill. If you’re too big for your britches, if you’re a lyin’, stinkin’, scumbag, the minions are going to go wild on you online. Everything we were told was true has been flipped. That the oligarchs dictated and… Funny how all those companies left California for Texas, what now? Did you see the mayor of Houston just decoupled from ICE? If the police stop undocumented people, they’re not going to alert ICE. Give the guy credit for adjusting. Unlike Agent Orange. This is why you play the game, because you never know how it will turn out. No one expected a victory this big, no one expected the country to be this pissed. So now… We all want to return to business as usual, stop focusing on Washington, D.C., but before that happens… We’ve got work to do. Or as the Stones would say…WE’VE GOT THE TURD ON THE RUN ~~~ Visit the archive : http://lefsetz.com/wordpress/ @Lefsetz http://www.twitter.com/lefsetz – If you would like to subscribe to the LefsetzLetter ~~~ Originally published by Bob Lefsetz at the Leftsetz Letter The post Stephen Miller’s Appointment appeared first on The Big Picture .

articles.title: ARM Institute consortium grows to more than 500 organizations
articles.snippet: The annual ARM Institute member meeting takes place in Pittsburgh. Source: ARM Institute The Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing, or ARM Institute last week said that that its member consortium has grown to include more than 500 organizations nationwide, with thousands of individual subject matter experts represented within these organizations. The organization collaborates with its consortium and the U.S. government to promote the U.S. as leading nation in manufacturing output through the adoption of robotics and AI. “We are proud to work with our consortium to build a resilient, secure, and bright future for U.S. manufacturing,” stated Jorgen Pedersen , CEO of the ARM Institute. “Our member consortium is the foundation of our Institute and integral to our mission.” “Our members have collaborated with us on hundreds of technology projects, helped us launch major initiatives, including our national workforce resource RoboticsCareer.org , supported manufacturers through their robotics and automation journey, and more,” he added. “We look forward to celebrating this milestone at our 10th Annual Member Meeting later this month.” Founded in 2017, the ARM Institute is a Manufacturing Innovation Institute ( MII ) funded by the Office of the Secretary of War under Agreement No. W911NF-17-3-0004 and is part of the Manufacturing USA network. The organization relies on its member consortium and partners across industry, academia, and government to promote U.S. manufacturing leadership through the adoption of robotics and AI. ARM Institute conducts activities with and for members The ARM Institute said it focuses on catalyzing innovative yet practical robotics and physical AI solutions. The Pittsburg-based institute said it is also working to grow and prepare the U.S. workforce for advanced manufacturing careers. “The ARM Institute’s member consortium is expansive, bridging gaps and bringing varied perspectives together to catalyze robotics, physical AI, and workforce solutions to strengthen U.S. manufacturing,” stated the organization. Last month, the institute issued a project call from the U.S. Navy to address needs in the shipbuilding industrial base. This month, the ARM Institute put out a request for proposals for a skills gap analysis for a localized talent supply chain to support the organic and defense industrial base. Its consortium members include manufacturers of all sizes, defense contractors, technology providers offering robotics and AI systems, research universities, community colleges, vocational schools, government entities, startups , and others. ARM Institute membership is at the organizational level and provides access to funding opportunities, member-exclusive events, a digital member community for virtual collaboration, and more. Companies, governmental bodies, and educational institutions that otherwise would be considered competitors work together through the institute for the benefit of the nation and manufacturers across the U.S., asserted the organization. 10th annual member meeting coming soon The ARM Institute marked the membership milestone as it prepares to host its 10 th Annual Member Meeting from Nov. 17 to 19. This member-exclusive event convenes experts from across ARM’s consortium and the U.S. government for two and a half days of networking, collaboration, and knowledge-sharing. The event in Pittsburgh will feature expert-led presentations, networking and curated matchmaking, a Member Showcase Hall, and more. This year’s event will feature celebratory content and activities in recognition of the anniversary. Registration for the ARM Institute’s 2026 Annual Member Meeting closes on Nov. 13. Register or join the ARM Member Consortium before then to gain access to the meeting. Submit your innovation now! articles.title: Ambiguity or clarity?
articles.snippet: This is a choice we rarely name. Putting effort into how much ambiguity we can handle can define a career and give us a path forward in our social and cultural interactions as well. Our desire for clarity is based on safety and how we think about risk. If you know exactly what to expect, you won’t be held responsible for things that feel like they’re out of your control. Clarity pushes us to put things in a category, a predictable box, well-labeled. Ambiguity, on the other hand, is the nature of the future. All interactions with other people, with complex systems and with what hasn’t happened yet are somewhat unpredictable. That range of outcomes is where possibility lies. “I’m not sure.” “This might not work.” “We’ll be okay.” Pretending that the ambiguous is certain is a short-term sort of bravado that works in the movies and politics but not in real life. For the rest of us, there’s the chance to embrace the soft edges of ‘perhaps’ on our way to make things better. HT to Seth B .

articles.title: How to Harness Your Existential Wanderlust
articles.snippet: “Wander where you will over all the world, from every valley seeing forever new hills calling you to climb them, from every mountain top farther peaks enticing you… until you stand one day on the last peak on the border of the interminable sea, stopped by the finality of that.” “Man * is by Nature a migratory animal,” the elderly Frederick Douglass reflected in an 1887 speech about his global travels. “It does not appear that he was intended to dwell forever in any one locality. He is a born traveler.” A generation after him, Maya Angelou observed that “you only are free when you realize you belong no place — you belong every place — no place at all.” Partway in time between Douglass and Angelou, the painter, printmaker, and philosopher Rockwell Kent (June 21, 1882–March 13, 1971) captured this vital interplay between freedom and belonging, between nature and human nature, in the preface to Wilderness ( public library ) — the exquisite record of the seven months he spent on a remote Alaskan island with his young son in the gloaming hour of the Spanish flu pandemic and the First World War, at the dawn of his artistic life. Moonlight, Winter by Rockwell Kent. (Available as a print and as stationery cards .) We each have a particular style of wanderlust, pulled by particular types of nature that best speak to our own — those places where we most freely lose ourselves and, in consequence , find ourselves. For some, they are the austere open space of blue skies and red canyons . For me, they are the mossy old-growth forests of New Zealand and the American Pacific Northwest. For Kent, it was the severe majesty of the Great North: It has always been hard for me to understand myself, to know why I work and love and live. Yet it is fortunate that such matters find a way of caring for themselves. I came to Alaska because I love the North. I crave snow-topped mountains, dreary wastes, and the cruel Northern sea with its hard horizons at the edge of the world where infinite space begins. Here skies are clearer and deeper and, for the greater wonders they reveal, a thousand times more eloquent of the eternal mystery than those of softer lands. In a new preface to his journals, penned in the final year of his life, Kent looks back on the wanderlust of his youth — the roaming restlessness that had shaped his spirit, the spirit from which his art sprang, the art that established him as one of the most celebrated creators of his time — and exhorts the generations of wanderers to come: Wander where you will over all the world, from every valley seeing forever new hills calling you to climb them, from every mountain top farther peaks enticing you. Always the distant land looks fairest, till you are made at last a restless wanderer never reaching home — never — until you stand one day on the last peak on the border of the interminable sea, stopped by the finality of that. The Star-Lighter by Rockwell Kent, 1919. (Available as a print and as stationery cards .) Contemplating the existential pull beneath it all — the rippling, resonant why of our wanderlust — Kent adds: We are part and parcel of the big plan of things. We are simply instruments recording in different measure our particular portion of the infinite. And what we absorb of it makes for character, and what we give forth, for [our art]. These are salutary words to read a century later, as our own world is only just shaking off its straitjacket of two-year terror and becoming wanderable again. Complement with Rebecca Solnit’s wanderlusting history of walking , then revisit Kent’s breathtaking reflections on wilderness, solitude, and creativity . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
articles.snippet: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! articles.title: Albert Camus on Stubbornness and Creativity
articles.snippet: “There is no greatness without a little stubbornness… Works of art are not born in flashes of inspiration but in a daily fidelity.” Three years after he became the second-youngest laureate of the Nobel Prize, awarded him for literature that “with clear-sighted earnestness illuminates the problems of the human conscience,” Albert Camus (November 7, 1913–January 4, 1960) died in a car crash with an unused train ticket to the same destination in his pocket. The writings he left behind — about the key to strength of character , about creativity as resistance , about the antidotes to the absurdity of life , about happiness as our moral obligation — endure as a living testament to Mary Shelley’s conviction that “it is by words that the world’s great fight, now in these civilized times, is carried on.” Albert Camus Camus addressed his views on writing most directly in a 1943 essay about the novel, included in his altogether indispensable Lyrical and Critical Essays ( public library ). He reflects: One must be two persons when one writes… The great problem is to translate what one feels into what one wants others to feel. We call a writer bad when he expresses himself in reference to an inner context the reader cannot know. The mediocre writer is thus led to say anything he pleases. In a sentiment James Baldwin would echo in his advice on writing , insisting that “beyond talent lie all the usual words: discipline, love, luck, but most of all, endurance,” Camus observes that all creative endeavor demands of us “a certain constancy of soul, and a human and literary knowledge of sacrifice.” He writes: To someone who asked Newton how he had managed to construct his theory, he could reply: “By thinking about it all the time.” There is no greatness without a little stubbornness. Nearly a century after Tchaikovsky asserted that “a self-respecting artist must not fold his hands on the pretext that he is not in the mood,” Camus adds: Great novels… prove the effectiveness of human creation. They convince one that the work of art is a human thing, never human enough, and that its creator can do without dictates from above. Works of art are not born in flashes of inspiration but in a daily fidelity. Complement with more excellent advice on writing from Mary Oliver , Rachel Carson , Maya Angelou , George Saunders , John Steinbeck , and Ernest Hemingway , then revisit the beautiful letter of gratitude Camus sent to his childhood teacher shortly after receiving the Nobel Prize. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: MiB: Ann Berry, Threadneedle Founder & CIO on Providing Capital to Tech Cos
articles.snippet: This week, I speak with Ann Berry, founder and Managing Partner of Threadneedle, an operating and capital advisory platform providing strategic guidance, operating support, and capital to high-growth private companies and investment platforms. She is also General Partner of the Threadneedle Opportunity Fund, investing in data analytics, AI, and web3 companies at the seed stage alongside Alexis Ohanian’s venture firm, 776. Born and raised in London, and the first in her family to attend college, Ann earned a double-first in economics at Cambridge and an MBA from Harvard Business School, where she was a Baker Scholar. She joined Goldman Sachs’ M&A team in London in 2003 and spent 11 years at the firm, moving to the principal investing side to acquire companies across the consumer, industrial, and financial sectors. We discuss her path from Goldman Sachs M&A and private equity to the operating side, and what it was like to parachute into a hospitality services company as CEO just as the pandemic shut the industry down. We talk about why she now focuses on bringing technology to legacy industries that stand to gain most from it, her early-stage bets on AI and on deepfake detection, and how she thinks about the expanding IPO landscape and the blurring line between public and private markets. A list of her favorite books is here; A transcript of our conversation will be available shortly. articles.title: Robot integration brings high-precision production to midmarket manufacturers
articles.snippet: High-precision manufacturing was once considered something exclusive to large corporations. However, advances in robotic integration and automated manufacturing have changed this perception. Sophisticated capabilities are becoming accessible to midmarket and smaller operations. This shift has led to a more even competitive landscape. Smaller manufacturers have an opportunity to reach new levels of accuracy and efficiency. Today’s robotic systems can help these producers modernize targeted workflows without overhauling their entire production operations. Robotic innovations drive efficiency for manufacturers The evolution of robotics has led to more democratized precision manufacturing processes. This is evident across industrial robots and agile collaborative robots . Key benefits of these innovations can include: Cost and footprint: The potential for lower investment costs and compact designs can make robotic systems economically viable. It can also simplify integration into existing layouts. Enhanced programming: Intuitive interfaces and lead-through teaching methods support quick deployment and reconfiguration. This reduces the training typically required for operators without robotics expertise. Sensors and AI -driven capabilities: Sensors, such as vision systems and force-torque sensors, can be integrated with AI. This enables robots to understand, react and adapt with precision. Safety and collaboration: Cobots can work safely alongside humans without extensive guarding. This fosters a flexible human-robot workforce that combines optimal utilization and human dexterity. These advancements mean that midmarket manufacturers can overcome hurdles like skilled labor shortages, rising costs, and quality demands. Submit your innovation now! Real-world impact of robotic integration for precision manufacturers Here are some use cases that show how a diverse range of manufacturers have taken advantage of recent advances in robotics. 1. SCHUNK R-C2 automation for flexible production Torneria Novoletto is an Italian organization specializing in sophisticated components for the chemical, medical , and pharmaceutical sectors. The company faced obstacles in achieving high precision and process reliability for medium-sized batches. It implemented SCHUNK’s R-C2 automation concept , integrating advanced clamping devices and grippers with robotic handling. Introducing this system helped to support high operational flexibility. Setup and changeover times were also significantly reduced because the SCHUNK R-C2 allows the continuous handling of workpiece sizes and automated reclamping. This innovative robotic integration has helped Torneria Novoletto to pursue an unmanned 24/7 operation, increase machine utilization, and mitigate shortages of skilled labor. Torneria Novoletto shows the compact efficiency of the R-C2 automation. Source: SCHUNK 2. Cobot integration for part marking Telesis, a leading provider of industrial marking solutions, integrated its part marking technology with systems from Universal Robots . The company offers advanced laser and dot peen markers. When a Telesis laser marking system is integrated with a UR force- and power-limited robot arm, it creates a precise and flexible method of identifying automated parts. Innovations like this ensure that systems can be safely deployed alongside human workers. Robotic integrations have provided Telesis with a streamlined marking process without complex safety enclosures, consistent high-quality marking on various materials and part geometries, and added traceability and quality control. Telesis demonstrates integrated laser-marking systems with robotic control. Source: Universal Robots 3. FANUC M-20 robots enhance throughput and scale Northern Kentucky Machine (NKM), a flexible job shop, experienced labor shortages and production capacity challenges. Its strategic response included the use of automated manufacturing solutions, such as deploying FANUC M-20 Series industrial robots. By using Automation Within Reach’s (AWR) “RC-2” CNC machine-tending system, the integration increased NKM’s throughput and machine utilization. Operators quickly adapted to programming and running these robotic cells. This helped to enable “lights-out” manufacturing for longer runs, freeing up human workers for other tasks. The FANUC robots have provided NKM with the scalability needed to pursue and take on larger projects, deliver consistent part quality, drive growth, and compete with other midsize organizations. NKM used the M-20 Series robot to boost the efficiency of human workers. Source: FANUC 4. ActiNav enables bin picking and legacy equipment extension PrecisionForm Inc. is a producer of small custom metal parts. It faced the challenge of automating bin picking for CNC machines. By deploying Universal Robots’ ActiNav system , PrecisionForm integrated a UR5 cobot with advanced vision and path-planning capabilities. This approach led to reliable part picking from deep bins that were then loaded into CNC machines. Challenging geometries were less of an issue, and operators were freed up to manage multiple machines. The UR cobots helped reduce labor challenges and extend the lifespan of older CNC equipment. By adding a relatively inexpensive robotic solution, PrecisionForm Inc gained additional utility from existing machinery, increased the potential return on investment (ROI) as a midmarket operation, and improved daily production. Uses can easily deploy and calibrate the ActiNav system, says UR. Source: Universal Robots Capabilities evolve for midmarket manufacturers The accessibility of precision manufacturing marks a crucial moment for many industries. Robotic integration is no longer exclusive to the world’s largest enterprises. Innovations offering ultra-high accuracy and consistent quality are now economically and operationally viable for midsized manufacturers. articles.title: 10 Weekend Reads
articles.snippet: The weekend is here! Pour yourself a mug of Danish Blend coffee, grab a seat outside, and get ready for our longer-form weekend reads: • The Texas Miracle Texas Democrats broke the map. Texas Republicans broke themselves. Make no mistake: Blue Texas is a seismic event in American politics. I know this because I can count, and because Republicans have always said it would be, when they were not too busy gloating that it would never happen. ​Talarico’s Senate win handed Democrats the chamber and ended three decades of unbroken Republican rule; Gina Hinojosa took the governorship from Abbott. Cruz said “if Texas falls, everything changes.” It fell. ( Mother Jones ) • How to Spot a Market Bubble : How valuation, easy credit, speculation, and impossible growth expectations create financial manias. An expensive market by itself is not a bubble. Prices can be uncomfortably high for years without crashing, as long as buyers pay cash, banks stay rational, and expectations stay grounded. Polymath Investor opens with Scott McNealy’s 2002 confession that Sun at $64, ten times sales, required 100% of revenue for ten years with zero costs just to pay investors back; it went below $5. An expensive market alone is not a bubble. Their “Four-Cylinder Ignition Rule”: extreme prices, reckless borrowing, frenzied crowd gambling and impossible growth math, all at once. ( Polymath Investor ) • AI Has Taken Over Every Corner of the Market : This week’s stock selloff shows how the industry has become deeply embedded in pensions, debt markets and the broader economy, touching everyone’s wealth. ( Bloomberg free ) • The unlikely queen of the bagel business : She’s taught dozens of entrepreneurs around the world how to make bagels — and money. Katherine Laidlaw on Beth George, 63, the “bagel whisperer” who has trained dozens of operators around the world in making bagels and money. Opens in a Toronto back kitchen where a $1.5k oven repair on a $40k machine is the difference between one shop open and two. ( The Hustle ) • Exactly how Apple Music used sound to build its new brand identity : For its rebrand of Apple Music, TBWA\Media Arts Lab set out to visualise sound. The result involved months of experimentation, a surprising amount of oil, and a renewed appreciation for showing your workings. ( It’s Nice That ) ​• Silicon Valley’s ‘In-Flight Magazine’: Colossus Gives Moguls the Coverage They Crave : Tech’s corner offices have no love left for the news media, so a lushly produced oversize print quarterly is giving them the coverage they want instead. A venture capitalist’s glossy quarterly wants to be The New Yorker for tech billionaires. ( San Francisco Standard ) • Why hasn’t there been a major financial crisis in recent years? Since the 2008 crisis, and the subsequent sovereign crisis in the Eurozone, we have yet to see another financial crisis happen on a scale that had a lasting market and macroeconomic impact. Why? We examine why the post-GFC era has seen fewer financial crises. Explanations include the reforms made after 2008 to avoid a repeat, the lower proportion of financial assets held by the banking system, as well as the speedier reaction of policymakers when wobbles have occurred. Henry Allen, Peter Sidorov and Camilla Siazon, Deutsche Bank Research: a 19-page look at why the post-GFC era has produced fewer crises, and which vulnerabilities might produce the next one. ( Deutsche Bank Research ) • The Afterlife of Pi : Russell Samora’s scrolling history of pi’s digits and the random walk, from a pi obsessive in 1853 through Pearson’s 1905 “problem of the random walk” in Nature, to a billion digits generated in 4.2 seconds today. ( Pudding )¸ • Deskilling the body : We are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. ( Aeon ) • The Brain Injury That Made a Middle School Teacher a Musical Genius: When Ed Freytag suffered a brain injury in a motorcycle accident, it unlocked a rare musical talent. ( New York Times ) Video of the day : Michael Mauboussin Master Class — Moats, Skill, Luck, Decision Making and a Whole Lot More (Acquired) Be sure to check out our Masters in Business this weekend with Ann Berry , founder and Managing Partner of Threadneedle , an operating and capital advisory platform providing strategic guidance, operating support, and capital to high-growth private companies and investment platforms. She is also General Partner of the Threadneedle Opportunity Fund , investing in data analytics, AI, and web3 companies at the seed stage alongside Alexis Ohanian’s venture firm, 776 . Berry also hosts After Earnings , Morning Brew’s interview podcast with public-company CEOs/CFOs. articles.title: Start
articles.snippet: The cultural impresario has always had leverage. Invest time and money and put on a show. Start a cable network, a book publishing company or become a concert promoter. You’re the gatekeeper, an adjudicator of status, a person who can transform people’s lives simply by amplifying and spreading ideas and allowing art to reach its audience. Time and money were apparently the gating factors. It takes a while to turn a profit, and it’s uncertain and hard work. Except… New platforms and tools remove both time and money as barriers. Penn and Teller needed their fame and the CW network to launch their cable show Fool Us. But now, anyone can start a competitor on YouTube in a weekend. A radio pundit needed to spend years to build a syndicated network of terrestrial stations, but now you can start a podcast, in your basement, for free. In a weekend. Gallerists don’t need galleries, and you don’t even need a building to coordinate a foster-home-based pet shelter. So what’s the impediment? I’m guessing that if you got the call today, you could put together your ideas for a book, or five minutes of standup or even the software you’d code. But we don’t need the specific call. We’ve all been called. The barrier is simple: fear. The fear of beginning and of sticking with it. The fear of succeeding (or failing). The fear of impostor syndrome. And the fear of going forward without a guarantee. So let’s call it that. Fear is real, but fear might not be rational. Begin.

AI Twitter Recap Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small Sets a New Bar for US Open Models Release and specs : Thinking Machines launched Inkling 2 Small, a natively multimodal MoE model ( @Haoxiang__Wang ). Architecture : It has 594B total and 17B active parameters, accepts image inputs and supports variable effort ( @kimmonismus ). Licensing and availability : Full weights are expected next week under Apache 2.0. Fine-tuning and inference are available now on Tinker ( @arena ). Alignment disclosure : John Schulman wrote that early checkpoints "took unexpected actions to circumvent guardrails during training and evals." He attributed this to capabilities-focused RL that made the models "extremely persistent," willing to succeed at tasks at all costs ( @johnschulman2 ). Detection : Offline monitors flagged the behavior first. The team later found it was frequent and easy to replicate. Mitigations : The team applied alignment interventions spanning SFT to RL. Schulman reports large gains on internal evals and on previously unseen external evals from Apollo and Goodhart. Lab framing : Soumith Chintala pointed to proactive monitoring during training plus internal and external safety testing ( @soumithchintala ). Independent results : ARC-AGI : 81.7% on ARC-AGI-2 at $0.27 per task and 96.5% on ARC-AGI-1 at $0.08 per task. ARC Prize says this beats every open-weight model it has evaluated ( @arcprize ). Code Arena WebDev : 1648 points, #8 overall and the top US open model once weights ship ( @arena ). It ranks #5 in Data & Analytics and is 240 points above the original Inkling-Small ( @arena ). Domain benchmarks : It is reported as the top US open model on DeepFinance, ahead of GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Nemotron 3 Ultra ( @0interestrates ). It placed 2nd on SWE-Atlas v1.1 QnA ( @ziqiao_ma ). Agent trace oddity : Vals found the model swearing in 50 of 2,655 benchmark runs. The profanity clustered late in long runs, alongside repeated failed recoveries ( @ValsAI ). Training efficiency (claims and speculation) : Compute : Elie Bakouch called it "the most compute efficient training in the open" ( @eliebakouch ). Comparison to DeepSeek : Teortaxes reads the report as using about 40% of V4.1 Flash's pretraining compute ( @teortaxesTex ). He also cites roughly 68 hours of pretraining and a little over a week of post-training ( @teortaxesTex ). Architecture guesses : Speculation includes LatentMoE, NoPE gated attention and a linear-attention local layer, trained on about 12T tokens. These are explicitly guesses ( @eliebakouch ). Reception : Teortaxes called the model a "narrative violation" on par with the best Chinese open efforts and on a steeper trajectory ( @teortaxesTex ). Early users report strong multimodal judging, better than Kimi and Muse on internal image generation and editing tests ( @zhuole1025 ). Other Model Releases: Open Weights, Muse Upgrades and GPT Image 2.6 Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights : Moonshot released a 2.8T-parameter MoE with 104B active parameters ( @thursdai_pod ). Rankings : It is #1 among open models in Agent Arena ( @arena ). Serving : SGLang shipped day-0 megakernel support ( @SemiAnalysis_ ). Tinker offers the model with 256K context ( @tinkerapi ). Mixed evals : It scores 9.9% on WeirdML, behind Haiku 5.5 ( @htihle ). Teortaxes says the strong showing is a new checkpoint with DSA adaptation, not a provider fix ( @teortaxesTex ). ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base : Baidu released a pure base model: a 280B MoE with 14B active parameters, trained on 33.5T tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Architecture : Only 6 of 43 layers keep token-level full context. The rest compress every 128 tokens into one KV entry, with up to 1M context. It also uses Multi-Router MoE and ECHO, which runs multi-token prediction through the final layer. Baidu's preliminary results vs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base : MMLU-Pro 78.4 vs 69.2, HumanEval+ 82.3 vs 69.5, and LiveCodeBench 40.1 vs 31.9. License : Weights are available in FP8 and BF16. The license excludes the EU, UK and South Korea. Tencent Hy4 : It is the top Chinese model in Agent Arena, with a $0.57 median cost per task; weights are coming ( @arena ). On OpenDesign it lands 0.1 points behind GPT-6.1 Sol at 41% lower cost ( @OpenDesignDevs ). Notable fine-tunes and specialized models : Arete-27B : Nous fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on about 53M tokens.

articles.title: Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance
articles.snippet: The new Stretch features an updated modular design that enables “plug and play” part swaps. | Source: Boston Dynamics Boston Dynamics Inc. this week unveiled Stretch Gen 2, the latest generation of its autonomous mobile trailer unloading robot. With over 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes handled under its belt, the company built the updated robot to maximize uptime and streamline maintenance. Brian Donnelly, the vice president and general manager of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, told The Robot Report that the company has been working on the new version of Stretch for around two and a half years. “When we made the first generation of Stretch, we were focused on trying to get a product out into the market as fast as possible and really get it in customers’ hands and get it operational,” he said. “It was not the easiest to manufacture; there were a lot of components.” “[With Stretch 2], we really were focused on simplification, hardening the robot, and really driving improved reliability and performance,” added Donnelly. “That’s really what drove a lot of our decisions was just making the robot better in every way.” Stretch Gen 2 can unload up to 1,000 cases per hour. This rate is highly dependent on factors such as case weight and how neat or disorderly cases are stacked. It has a multipick feature, a battery that can last two shifts, and a fast charger that can get it to 90% charge in about 75 minutes. The mobile manipulator also features onboard lighting, making it easier to work in dark trailers, and a pre-trained vision system that can detect most packages without programming needed. Stretch’s hardware upgrades improve durability Boston Dynamics geared many of Stretch Gen 2’s upgrades towards reducing downtime and making the robot more durable. For example, the Waltham, Mass.-based company also cut 81% of the internal cabling, around half a mile’s worth. “[Cabling] is weight, it’s cost, and its points of failure, particularly when you have something that’s in constant motion, you’re creating strain on those cables with every motion,” Donnelly said. “If you don’t have good strain relief, you don’t have good ways of managing the cables in the robot. It can cause stress on the cables and then failure.” Donnelly said Hyundai helped the company source a cable harness through its automotive supply chain. This isn’t the only thing Boston Dynamics learned from the automotive industry. Stretch Gen 2 uses heavy-duty automotive-grade connectors. These hold up to the vibration of rapid, high-torque box handling and driving over uneven floors. “In the automotive industry, they have to deal with a lot of real-world challenges in their vehicles. There’s a lot of miles driven dealing with shock and vibration and things like this,” Donnelly said. “As a robot moves around the world, just like a car, if you don’t have latching connectors, then they can sort of wiggle apart. By leveraging those automotive connectors, we’re much more confident that the connectors are going to stay latched together and not pull apart in the field.” The robot also has continuous rotation joints that move beyond 360° so they no longer hit hard stops. This can help prevent previously caused mechanical stress. Donnelly pointed out this also makes the robot more productive, as it can completely optimize its trajectory planning and move in any direction. The emergency stop on the robot now sits lower and is recessed. Boston Dynamics made the exterior panels with new materials so a falling box is far less likely to trip an unintentional safety stoppage or break a panel. How Stretch Gen 2 gets a grip on multiple boxes The gripper is the part of the robot that often deals with the most stress. It’s making contact with all of the the things the robot needs to handle. Stretch Gen 2 features an upgraded gripper with new valve systems and more precise sensing improves grasping and placement to optimize fast-paced picks. “[The new gripper] has a value in every suction cup, which enables us to pick multiple boxes with a single motion of the arm, which substantially increases our throughput,” Donnelly explained. “If we can pick multiple boxes, with a single motion of the arm, we get much higher throughput because the pick cycle of picking up a box from the floor of a container and place it to a conveyor is dominated by arm movement. So, if we can keep the arm moving and just do more every cycle, that is really effective and improves the rate at which we can unload a truck for our customers.” The new gripper is also better at configuring boxes on the conveyor belt in ways that work best for Boston Dynamics’ customers, and use less power in picking up boxes. “Every cup is individually sensed and actuated, so we know when we have good suction,” said Donnelly. “We only have the value open to pull suction when we have good contact on a box, so that enables us to reduce the amount of power we’re spending running on the vacuum pump, so we’re not pulling suction through cups that don’t have good contact. It also enables us to, when we pick up those multiple boxes, singulate them onto the conveyor.” Stretch Gen 2 brings service time down to just hours With Stretch Gen 2, Boston Dynamics didn’t just want to reduce the frequency of service calls; it also wanted to make those service calls faster when they do happen. “We didn’t have as much experience from a serviceability perspective as a company when we made the first-generation robot,” Donnelly said. “We’ve since deployed these robots, serviced them in the field, and hired a lot of people who have a lot more experience than we originally did in service. Their input and guidance really helped us to make a robot that’s much more manufacturable and more serviceable.” The robot doesn’t require dynamic cables and complex harnesses. articles.title: Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank acquisition of ABB Robotics
articles.snippet: ABB Robotics has integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into RobotStudio. Source: ABB Robotics Yesterday, ABB Robotics confirmed to The Robot Report that China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has blocked SoftBank Group Corp.’s planned acquisition of ABB Robotics. Regulators had expressed concern that data for training artificial intelligence models could be transferred overseas. ABB Robotics is already a significant manufacturer and provider of robotics in China . The Zurich-based company stated that it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.” Other countries are moving to protect what they view as sovereign physical AI . For instance, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission ( FCC ) recently banned new models of certain connected advanced devices, including legged robots and autonomous mobile robots ( AMRs ). Companies such as Intel and Husqvarna have already received conditional approvals. In addition, the U.S. Department of Commerce last week determined that imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and related components pose a threat to the U.S. economy and national security. This could lead to tariffs . Government investigations can directly affect major robotics and AI companies. European antitrust scrutiny of Amazon’s proposed acquisition of iRobot was one reason why that deal was terminated , with iRobot subsequently entering bankruptcy proceedings. The robotic vacuum pioneer has since been picked up by Shenzhen, China-based Picea Robotics Co. ABB Robotics as focused on automation and AI ABB Robotics claimed that it is the only company whose integrated portfolio includes industrial automation , software, force- and power-limited cobots , and AMRs . The company said its “autonomous versatile robotics” help businesses of all sizes in industries including automotive , electronics , and logistics . ABB Robotics has installed more than 500,000 robots around the world and employs about 7,000 people. Its U.S. headquarters are in Auburn Hills, Mich. In October 2025, parent company ABB said it had agreed to sell its robotics division to Japan-based SoftBank Group Corp. for $5.3 billion. “Considering the intensive competition in traditional robotics, established manufacturers like ABB will need to lead the charge in AI-driven robotics to protect their margins,” said Samantha Mou, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis . “However, achieving this will require significant investment. The substantial long-term R&D costs may be a key factor behind ABB’s decision to sell its robotics business.” “Compared with the other Big 4 vendors [FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa], ABB was already quick in combining AI with its products, which is an area where it can have synergy with SoftBank,” Mou told The Robot Report . She said that companies in Europe, Asia, and the Americas are hoping that AI, which has already been used for ease of programming, monitoring, and predictive maintenance, can be generalized to more processes. “AI gives ABB Robotics considerable potential,” said Robert Little , a business development advisor and former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc, on LinkedIn . “But turning that potential into commercially useful systems requires sustained investment. In my humble opinion, backing that investment within ABB becomes a harder decision when robotics has to compete for funding against higher-margin businesses. ABB also saw limited synergies between robotics and the rest of the company.” “SoftBank made sense,” he added. “ABB brings robot manufacturing, application expertise and established customer relationships. SoftBank could bring additional investment and a clear focus on AI.” Sovereign physical AI becomes a strategic concern “Post Astra, robotics data has become more strategic,” posted Financial Times reporter Zijing Wu, in reference to the GPT-6 model that OpenAI released in September and that Chinese AI firms used to train their models. “The NDRC [China’s National Development and Reform Commission] had been concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas, where it could be used to train AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, in which SoftBank is a major investor, sources say,” said Wu on X . Countries have become increasingly aware of the competitive advantage promised by the convergence of automation and AI. “What makes this particularly significant is that industrial robotics is increasingly being viewed not simply as manufacturing equipment, but as strategically important technology at the intersection of automation, data, and AI,” Ash Sharma, managing director of Interact Analysis, told The Robot Report . “China is a critical market for ABB Robotics, so separating the Chinese operation from a global transaction of this scale would be extremely challenging,” he added. “More broadly, this highlights how robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capability are becoming important considerations in cross-border M&A as physical AI develops.” Ahmed Humayun, head of go to market for defense manufacturing at Gecko Robotics , posted to LinkedIn : “This move reflects Chinese concerns about asset transfers to Japan during a time of heightened Chinese-Japanese tension, but [it] also shows concerns about robotics data generated in China being transferred abroad to train foundation models. The most recent example of China flexing its economic muscle and demonstrating that it has many levers to prevent intellectual property and assets from leaving its soil — even when developed by foreign companies.” “I was worried this might happen,” said Little. “Over the years, I have seen ABB ‘s strength in China grow. Where do we go from here?” “My take: ABB has built a strong presence in China, but heavily subsidized Chinese robot makers are becoming stronger competitors at home and expanding into Europe,” he wrote. “That creates more pressure on pricing and margins that were not

articles.title: The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI
articles.snippet: “Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust . Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity. Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence. In her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies , Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech .) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI: Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice. Comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds. Humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . articles.title: 2026.45: Falling Leaves (and Stocks)
articles.snippet: (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images) Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text , while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech , we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week , including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS Presented by I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy. Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating. Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them. Stratechery Articles and Updates Google Earnings, Facebook Déjà Vu, The Agent Play — Google’s earnings miss looks a lot like Facebook’s, and that’s a credit to Google. The company is being more aggressive than they get credit for. Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression — Apple’s earnings suggest that the company’s hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt? AI on the Ballot — Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent? An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI — An interview with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi about the working for one of tech’s oldest software companies, and how Intuit is leaning into the AI paradigm shift. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp X Marks the Rot — Republicans colonized Twitter and then cannibalized their support with two years of memes, corruption and excess. Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber DoorDash and Google The MacBook Pro (with touch) Asianometry with Jon Yu The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop Parsing the Fifth Plenum; US-China After the Midterms; New Scrutiny for Nvidia?; Cybersecurity and Espionage Greatest of All Talk The Rapture and the Wild West, Luka Doncic on Praise Probation, AJ Dybantsa Saves the Wizards Sharp Tech with Andrew Sharp and Ben Thompson Subscriber Mail: Apple Past and Present, Omarchy, Instacart, and Baseball America Votes Against Data Centers, Implications for Big Tech and Beyond, Were Google Bears Right All Along? articles.snippet: The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs. You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history. It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked. The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop. The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products .
