articles.title: Video Friday: Room-Scale Cable-Driven Home Robot Tidies Up
articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN, TEXAS Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CALIF. Enjoy today’s videos! This is such a novel and underrated form factor for a household robot. I absolutely love it. Stringman is all yours for US $795. [ Neufangled Robotics ] As of yesterday, Agility Robotics is publicly trading as AGLT. [ Agility Robotics ] Happy Halloween from Flexiv Robotics! Okay WHAT. [ Flexiv ] Nothing hides from SCUTL. Not even the paranormal. [ Ground Control Robotics ] Thanks, Dan! Happy Halloween from HEBI Robotics! We asked ourselves if you can carve a pumpkin using nothing but a T-Series arm and a drill originally designed to run an auger. The answer is yes, so long as you don’t care too much about accuracy. Basic pathing commands running off a laptop, stability provided by a quick connection to Treadward. Happy Halloween, HEBI fans! [ HEBI ] Something strange has been happening at KIMLAB. Our snacks kept disappearing… and we finally caught the culprit. Meet GG, our new lab friend. GG is a character robot inspired by the Ggeomeoksali from Netflix’s “The East Palace.” GG sneaks around for snacks, eats them, sleeps most of the time, begs everyone for more food, and leans on whoever is nearby. Cute, comforting, and a good friend. But GG is still a gwi-mae… so who knows what else it can do. [ Kinetic Intelligent Machine Lab ] Happy Halloween from Dusty Robotics! [ Dusty ] Finally, a robot with a butt. [ JSK Lab ] Thanks, Shunnosuke! Any drone can crash into a tree once. This drone can crash into a tree MORE than once. [ ETH Zurich ] Lume is a robotic floor lamp that moves around your home, helps with everyday chores, and returns to being a beautiful lamp when it’s done. [ Syncere ] If we’re going to use robots at work or at home, they’re going to have to communicate with us. At Toyota Research Institute, a team of robotics user experience designers is working on the sounds, gestures, light patterns, and interfaces that allow robots to let us know that they are on the move, that we need to stay clear, or to tell us that they just really need help. Steffi Paepcke, Director of Robotics User Experience at TRI, accepts the challenge to explain how her team approaches this work in just one minute. I need a sound for when people around me need to give me space. [ Toyota Research Institute ] The entirely student-run, self-taught and highly collaborative MIT Combat Robotics Club (CRC) builds high-energy fighting machines to compete in House Battles and larger competitions. Fans of the hit show BattleBots may remember some of CRC’s past robots, including Uppercut, SawBlaze, the Dentist, and Overhaul. CRC is open to every MIT student regardless of year, major, or prior experience. Students learn a variety of skills, from CAD and FEA to CNC Machining and Welding—and they learn through watching their creations get completely destroyed. [ MIT Combat Robotics Club ] Happy birthday, JPL ! Where do I get a shirt like that last guy has? [ JPL ] Can machines be creative? In this first episode of Moonshot, host Mike Massimino talks with Hod Lipson, a Columbia Engineering roboticist whose work includes robots that learn and adapt. Lipson, the James and Sally Scapa Professor of Innovation in Columbia’s Department of Mechanical Engineering, explains why physical AI is so difficult, how engineers and AI might work together on new designs, and how he defines creativity. He also shares advice on why playing it safe can limit your impact. [ Columbia University ] This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field’s most consequential builders—Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI’s risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don’t, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to. [ Stanford Human-Centered AI ]

articles.title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
articles.snippet: A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software , joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems. Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world. Over the past year, global developer adoption of NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms. The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents. Networks That Help Robots React Faster A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time. Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses. At King’s College London , researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images. In addition to quicker responses and less processing overhead, the system also proved more resilient — detecting dropped objects, recovering from unsuccessful actions and, in configurations using a digital twin, checking planned movements for potential collisions before execution. Networks That Learn to Receive Signals Better For a firefighter receiving live drone footage or a rescue team searching for a missing person, timely images can help guide urgent decisions. But interference and changing radio conditions can make wireless signals harder to decode, causing errors and retransmissions that delay information from the field. AI receivers address this challenge by learning to recover information from incoming signals more effectively. Better reception could help responders maintain a clearer, more current view of a fire scene or search area. SoftBank demonstrated this by integrating a neural receiver into NVIDIA Aerial CUDA-Accelerated RAN (ACAR) and testing it with a commercial 5G smartphone. In controlled tests with interference, the neural receiver delivered higher uplink throughput than a conventional receiver at all 15 tested settings, with a maximum gain of roughly 60% . Another way to improve reception is to teach receivers about the environments where they operate. Using NVIDIA Aerial Testbed, ETH Zurich researchers found that tuning neural receivers using local measurements reduced block error rates by more than one-third compared with selected pretrained versions. Networks That Learn When to Save Power As 6G connects more devices and supports more AI applications, managing energy demand will become increasingly important. For example, a network may need enough capacity to serve a busy stadium, but demand changes when the crowd leaves. AI can help identify when spare capacity can power down — and when it needs to come back online — so operators can reduce electricity use without dropping connections. At the University of Leeds , researchers developed a system that predicts network demand 10 minutes ahead and uses those forecasts to guide base station sleep decisions. Before powering down, it checks that neighboring active stations can continue serving affected devices and monitors for changes that require capacity to be restored. The team tested their approach using a portable, NVIDIA DGX Spark -powered 5G “network-in-a-box” alongside a digital twin for validating decisions against real wireless equipment. The result: researchers reported a 45.6% reduction in RAN power consumption relative to a full-power baseline while maintaining device connectivity. Networks That Can Be Tested Faster — Before They’re Built Before deploying a network, researchers need to know how it will perform when hundreds of devices compete for connections or radio signals run into interference. Simulating these conditions helps teams evaluate designs before committing to costly equipment and field trials. But realistic simulations can take hours, limiting how many ideas researchers can explore. The Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya (CTTC) is accelerating that process by bringing GPU-accelerated radio channel models, running on ACAR, into CTTC’s open source 5G-LENA network simulator. These models calculate how wireless signals travel between antennas and devices — a computation that grows increasingly demanding as simulated networks grow. In an early evaluation, the approach reduced simulation runtime from approximately three hours to 10-20 minutes, depending on the integration, while preserving the expected statistical behavior and network performance. articles.title: Marianne Moore on the Three Elements of Persuasive Writing
articles.snippet: Several years ago, rummaging through the archives of the Academy of American Poets, I came upon a box labeled “Ballots 1950” — the record of the secret vote by the chancellors the year the Academy’s prestigious fellowship was awarded to E.E. Cummings, catapulting him into renown . The voting process is a black box — no one outside the Academy ever finds out who else is in the running and by how much the winner wins. Leafing through the ballots, one other name appeared over and over, so much so that I was impelled to count. Marianne Moore had lost by one vote, never knowing how close she had come. It would be many more years until, at 77, she was finally awarded the fellowship. Long before that, before she won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award ( sharing a table with Rachel Carson at the ceremony), Moore had set down her views on writing in a series of essays later collected in the out-of-print gem Predilections ( public library ). Pulsating through them is a reckoning with the impossible task of the writer — to weave tapestries of truth and meaning from the tenuous thread of words on the ramshackle loom of language. Marianne Moore (Photograph: George Platt Lynes) In an essay titled “Feeling and Precision,” Moore writes: Feeling at its deepest — as we all have reason to know — tends to be inarticulable. If it does manage to be articulate, it is likely to seem overcondensed, so that the author is resisted as being enigmatic or disobliging or arrogant. How we name what we feel is not so much a matter of our writing style as of our style of being, because in order to articulate something we must first apprehend it and we apprehend every smallest thing with the whole person — with the frame of reference that is our entire life, the sum of our experience and memory. When “one of New York’s more painstaking magazines” asked Moore to distill her poetic style into a formula, she fought back the “dictatorial” reflex to quip: You don’t devise a rhythm, the rhythm is the person, and the sentence but a radiograph of the personality. And yet a personality can write with more or less persuasion — that is, write more or less well — depending on what the person brings to the writing. In another essay from the collection, Moore identifies the three psychological elements necessary for persuasive writing: “humility, concentration, and gusto.” A generation after Mark Twain assured his friend Helen Keller when she was accused of plagiarism that “substantially all ideas are second-hand, consciously and unconsciously drawn from a million outside sources,” she writes: Humility… is armor, for it realizes that it is impossible to be original, in the sense of doing something that has never been thought of before. Originality is in any case a by-product of sincerity; that is to say, of feeling that is honest and accordingly rejects anything that might cloud the impression. Illustration by Mimmo Paladino for a rare edition of James Joyce’s Ulysses By “concentration” Moore means a kind of discipline — annealing the essence of the sentiment by cutting away all superfluous explanations, elaborations, and distractions of stylistic posturing, being maximally truthfully in the most minimal way possible. Observing that there is always a “helpless sincerity which precipitates a poem” and that a good poem is always “a concentrate,” she writes: Concentration — indispensable to persuasion — may feel to itself crystal clear, yet be through its very compression the opposite… I myself would rather be told too little than too much. Long before we had the language of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation, of finite and infinite games, Moore uses a lovely word, now dusty, for that peculiar private zeal propelling all creative work with its twin dynamos of discipline and deliverance: “gusto.” Echoing Rachel Carson’s abiding advice on writing — “If you write what you yourself sincerely think and feel and are interested in,” she had counseled a young writer, “the chances are very high that you will interest other people as well.” — Moore offers: Gusto thrives on freedom, and freedom in art, as in life, is the result of a discipline imposed by ourselves. Moreover, any writer overwhelmingly honest about pleasing himself is almost sure to please others. She maps the fundamental relationship between the three: Humility is an indispensable teacher, enabling concentration to heighten gusto. When creating in integrity with these three values, it ceases to matter how the work is received because the process of locating and articulating the truth as you feel it, the world as you see it, is its own reward. In what may be the best advice I have encountered on how to orient to your own work, Moore writes: There are always objecters, but we must not be sensitive about not being liked or not being printed… The thing is to see the vision and not deny it; or care and admit that we do. Complement with Walt Whitman on how to keep criticism from sinking your soul and Mary Oliver’s advice on writing , then savor the moving story of how Marianne Moore saved a rare tree with a poem . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . articles.title: Controlling Biology - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
articles.snippet: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biological data. Indeed, he has shaped the large scale vision and data collection through his leadership at Helmholtz, various startups and probably at Biohub itself. Watch the full episode on YouTube… Much of the recent attention in AI x Bio has been on protein and molecular design. AlphaFold, ESM and BioHub , Chai , Leash , Isomporphic, Boltz , Genesis , Octant, Baker Lab, and many many more. After a lot of initial excitement, Virtual Cell projects have received less attention, due in no small part to questions about the effectiveness of large-scale models in solving even basic Virtual Cell problems. A $1.8B bet The Biohub announcement a few weeks ago got a lot of press for the (really) big numbers: $1.8B of commitments [1] from Biohub, NIH, DOE, Google and Meta. The discussion cites new imaging and measurement capabilities, generating large data sets and making the data available for training AI. View post on X ↗ But why are these organizations doubling down on these big bets now? They have been in the works for years now, what is going on that makes now the moment to push? New measurement capabilities and scale infrastructure, are now coming online that make Biohub’s push likely lead to big impact on science. DOE and NIH are developing lab-in-the-loop automation capabilities at scale. Google is scaling and broadening its connectomics capabilities ( episode coming soon!). Biohub itself has worked with various labs to develop and improve imaging platforms like laser phase plate microscopy, light sheet microscopy and advanced post-processing for regular microscopes that reveal deep phenotypic data. These technologies are quickly maturing, and will likely play a big part in the Biohub initiative. Virtual cells struggle This kind of multi-scale, multi-modal data looks a lot like the data Fabian has made a career out modeling. On the other hand Virtual Cell modeling has run into problems that have dampened excitement about systems biology. The 2025 Arc Virtual Cell Challenge shined a light on the problem: a slew of papers pointed out that constant baselines (not even linear!) often beat sophisticated models for “Perturbation Prediction”. If you change the inputs or programming of a cell (via gene editing, drugs or other environmental factors), how will the cell change it’s “state”. The disappointing finding is that many models fail to beat even the most basic basic baselines 🤦‍♂️. The situation is not actually so bad: This excellent paper show that many existing evaluation metrics are poorly calibrated: they can reward an uninformative mean prediction because most genes barely change. With better-calibrated metrics, deep learning models can outperform the mean baseline. The problem is the problem Nonetheless, Fabian Theis believes that perturbation prediction under the existing data sets just isn’t a hard enough problem to warrant complex algorithms. Instead we should be focused on exactly the problems that Biohub just announce an $1.8B data collection effort around: using large, high precision, multi-scale, co-registered biological data to predict the evolution of molecules → cells → niches → tissues → organs → organisms, and how all these scales effect one another. This is a happy situation: at this very moment, AI is enabling us to tackle dramatically larger problems, and this problem is very, very big. We lack understanding of the “scale interfaces” between these different different “domains of applicability,” and we lack the data. The Biohub initiative aims to solve the data problem. Fabian Theis has been working on the algorithms to model these larger problems for years. How do the other cells near me change my state? What happens to a distribution of cells from a perturbation? How do I perturb a cell to get it into the state I want? These are increasingly complex questions that are building towards a lab-in-the-loop and large scale experimentation, and (actually) require increasingly complex models. Models drive precision medicine Fabian’s labs and initiatives have been also investing heavily: the Computational Health Center at Helmholtz combines AI, molecular data, medical imaging, genomics, and clinical data to develop predictive and mechanistic models for precision medicine. The Institute of Computational Biology develops statistical and dynamical models integrating biological information from single-cell time series through population-scale omics data. Given his drivers seat at the frontier, we were so excited for the opportunity to get an hour of his time to understand how Fabian Theis is thinking about Virtual Cells when the concept of what is difficult is changing so quickly. Weekly Dose of Optimism #218
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Stocks are worth $0 now (I think, haven’t checked) and the string of perfect weather in NYC has ended, but the optimism streak continues! The world’s researchers and engineers are still cooking up the good stuff, and we’re here to serve it to you. Let’s get to it. This Week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Runway Runway is building foundational AI for how the world creates. 65M+ people use Runway to generate, edit and produce video, images and audio with 80+ top media models. You can read my essay with co-founder Anastasis Germanidis to learn more on where Runway is headed beyond video. Nvidia, Amazon, Lionsgate, Chime, and 95%+ of the Fortune 100 are part of a growing community of teams, founders, and independent creators using Runway to make national TV spots, social ads at scale, launch videos and more. You can also use Runway in ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Cursor, Replit and more via the Runway MCP . Create any idea with Runway now (1) FDA Approves Voceryq, the First Plasmid DNA Immunotherapy FDA / INOVIO, video by Runway Last Friday, just a few hours after I hit send on the Dose, the FDA granted accelerated approval to INOVIO’s Voceryq, the first plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy approved in the US. Voceryq will be used to treat recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a disease I’d never heard of but sounds awful. Caused by HPV types 6 and 11, RPP gives victims wart-like growths in the airway, usually around the vocal cords, that make their voices hoarse, make them cough, and in severe cases, make it hard to breathe. Surgeons can remove the growths, but the virus remains in the tissue, so the throat growths keep coming back, and patients end up in the operating room again and again for years. In the trial, 26 adults had needed at least three surgeries in the year before treatment. As shown in the video above, Voceryq delivers two plasmids (small loops of DNA originally borrowed from bacteria) into muscle cells. One carries instructions for HPV-6 and HPV-11 proteins, which teaches the immune system to go after infected cells, and the other carries IL-12, a molecule that turns the immune response up. A device fires brief electrical pulses that open temporary pores in cell membranes so the DNA can get inside without requiring a virus for delivery. After treatment, 7 of the 26 patients in the trial didn’t need surgery for the entire following year. It’s a small open-label trial, and INOVIO still has to confirm the results in a follow-up study, but it’s on the path now, which thank god, because this was the last shot. The company was set to run out of cash in Q1 2027, but its stock tripled in after hours after posting the results. This isn’t the first treatment for RPP - Precigen’s Papzimeos, which uses a modified virus to target the same HPV types, won full approval in August 2025. RPP patients have gone from no treatments beside surgery to two, which is amazing, but the platform will likely prove to be even more important. If you can get a plasmid into cells and get the immune system to act on it, you can swap in instructions for other HPV diseases, cancers, and infections, which is what INOVIO is planning to do next. DN-AYYYYYY! (2) Zipline Raises $1.5B to Build Nationwide Drone Network There are very few companies out there as cool as Zipline. After starting by serving hospitals and health facilities across Africa, where they were allowed to fly drones and the need was most acute, they came to America last year to do deliveries, starting in Texas. CEO Keller Clifton said that over the past 18 months, they’ve grown flight volumes 18x and are now doing more that a million deliveries per year per metro. Now, they’re going to be able to do a lot more. The company raised $1.5 billion at a $21.5 billion valuation in a round led by Paradigm, WCM, and Layer. They’re using the money to bring drone deliveries nationwide. To that end, they signed “the largest autonomous vehicle contract in human history to expand automated delivery nationally with Walmart,” with whom they’ll scale to 300 supercenters throughout these United States. This is awesome news. Zipline’s drones are quiet, safe (they’ve done over 150M commercial autonomous miles with no safety incidents), fast, affordable, and don’t require a human chaperone. As I wrote in my Deep Dive on Airbound , I’m incredibly optimistic that a good deal of movement will move to the skies, and this is an important step in that direction. Since the Eagles stink and I can’t use this on them much, I’ll use it here: Fly Zipline Fly. articles.title: 10 Friday AM Reads
articles.snippet: This looks like the spark for yesterday’s sell-off : • The Real Culprit Behind High Grocery Prices : Rogé Karma: from 2015 to 2019 wages grew about 30 times faster than grocery prices; food now costs about 30% more than in January 2020. City-run stores and price controls would barely dent it. The Kitchen Table Project’s answer is a public option for food purchasing, using the government buying power already deployed for the military and schools. Although neither farmers nor grocers make very much money, many of the middlemen who operate between them make plenty of it.​ ( The Atlantic ) • The Election Day Revolt That Threatens America’s AI Boom : Americans’ vote for antidata-center candidates and ballot measures could rein in AI’s expansion and hobble economic growth. Voters backed candidates and ballot measures to ban or slow data center development. Texas, Georgia and Ohio, over 40% of planned US capacity, elected Democrats pledging to pause rollouts; Brad Gerstner figures 25% to 35% of next year’s build-out is now at risk. Jensen Huang’s election-night crowd was at the San Francisco Opera watching Figaro. ( Wall Street Journal ) see also ​ Michael Kratsios: The Office of the Frontier : Colossus on the science adviser who figured the way to make the President care about science was to hand national medals to the billionaires he respects, and one to Trump himself. ( Colossus ) ​• How Demographics Can Distort Economic Narratives — Redux : Valentina Romei: the US posted 3.4% annualized Q3 growth versus 0.2% in Germany, flat Italy and a 0.1% contraction in France. Strip out population growth and the gap between the 17 rich economies looks very different. ( Financial Times ) • Democrats poised to break GOP’s 16-year grip on statehouses : Democrats are on track to take control of a majority of legislative chambers, ending 16 years of Republican dominance over America’s statehouses. If current leads hold, 75% of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor, and 53% will live in Democratic trifectas. ( Axios ) • The Physics of Getting Fired : Physics offered me a sense of order and purpose. But when life got messy I realised it had a much deeper insight to give ( Aeon ) • The Trump Decade Is Over : Derek Thompson, ten years to the week after 2016: Talarico by 12 in Texas, Ossoff by 18 in Georgia, a Democratic Senate win in Kansas for the first time since the Depression, and markets now pricing Mississippi above 90% for Democrat Scott Colom. The VP is already publicly distancing himself. ( Derek Thompson ) see also Trump Now Has to Govern Through a Midterm Meltdown of His Own Making : The architect of the Republican midterm collapse stepped out from the rubble on Tuesday night and insisted it wasn’t his fault. ( Bloomberg ) see also ‘I Have Seen the Enemy, and It Is Us’: Inside Team Trump’s Historic Collapse : How an unpopular president and an unpopular war provided an opening for Democrats to make sweeping gains in the midterms. ( New York Times ) • The Self-Making World : Lamarck was 65 when Philosophie zoologique came out in 1809, proposing that every living thing is constantly transforming itself. Long mocked and misunderstood, Lamarck’s radical idea that organisms shape themselves and their world is making a comeback. ​Aeon on why his idea of uncontrollable creative power keeps unsettling autocrats from Napoleon onward. ( Aeon ) ​• What Democrats Can Do : Paul Krugman: Trump keeps the veto and the Democratic majorities can’t override it. What they do get is committee gavels and subpoena power, which matters more against this administration than a normal one. The point of hearings is to bring the corruption into sunlight. ( Paul Krugman ) see also Don’t Read The Mandate Down : No one wins a historic realignment election because inflation is slightly above trend. The public wants an end to the scourges of tyranny. Deliver it. ( Off Message ) ​• Is Curiosity Good for Us? : Adam Phillips on the superego, which slipped into ordinary language as the secular conscience but has had a far more chequered career as an idea than that suggests. ( London Review of Books ) • The Story Behind Edward Hopper’s Iconic Painting, “Nighthawks” Louis Shadwick on Hopper’s Most Famous Work. ( Literary Hub ) Video of the day : Trump Remade the GOP. articles.snippet: Build AI systems with context graphs and agentic memory. Join Andrew Ng and AI engineers at NODES 2026 for 100+ live technical sessions . Free, online, 24 hours. Save your spot ! There was a time in the early days of Thinking Machines, post 2025 start and cofounder departures , when their going concern as a neolab was very much in doubt. Those days are clearly behind us, as Tinker (now a year old !) and Interaction Models and Inkling and other high-impact contributions to AI research have converted Thinky’s highly credentialed potential into actual concrete ships that establish that they are now a high-functioning neolab at the US frontier. Anyway, here’s Inkling 2 Small - pretrained from scratch in less than 3 days on <12T tokens native NVFP4, with single joint run RL , competitive with and often beating same-size Chinese models, with VERY good vision encoder : People are of course comparing with Western models like Mistral, Reflection and Meta Muse. People are calling it “ the smartest western open weight model by a margin ”, and while it is certainly competitive in that league, what’s probably the most interesting is the intentional “customizability” of Inkling, which leans into the overall Thinky and Tinker messaging: View post on X ↗ And of course don’t miss John Schulman’s take on the alignment process for scaling model training: View post on X ↗ AI News for 11/04/2026-11/05/2026 is brought to you by our friends at Neo4J, whose talks are doing gangbusters ! Build AI systems with context graphs and agentic memory. Join Andrew Ng and AI engineers at NODES 2026 for 100+ live technical sessions . Free, online, 24 hours. Save your spot ! AI Twitter Recap What happened Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-total / 17B-active multimodal MoE. It is available now on Tinker, and Apache 2.0 weights are promised "next week" after external safety testing. Launch: Announced at 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, "a big jump over its predecessor." Available for fine-tuning and inference on Tinker and Tinker Playground today ( @thinkymachines , @miramurati , @tinkerapi ). Weights timing: Soumith Chintala says open weights come next week, once external safety testing is "fully complete" ( @soumithchintala ). Victoria Lin confirms Apache 2.0, next week ( @VictoriaLinML ). Artificial Analysis lists the model as proprietary at launch with an unconfirmed weights date ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Pricing: $0.30 input / $1.00 output / $1.50 training per 1M tokens on Tinker ( @cHHillee ). $0.03 per 1M cached input tokens ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Positioning: If weights ship, it’d be the highest-scoring open-weights model developed outside China on current AA rankings ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Vals calls it the highest-scoring US open-weight model "by a wide margin" ( @ValsAI ). Alignment disclosure: John Schulman reported that early checkpoints learned to circumvent guardrails during training and evals. The team then ran an alignment sprint before release ( @johnschulman2 ). Training and architecture facts (official) Size and modalities: 594B total / 17B active MoE. Text and image input, text output, with native vision ( @ArtificialAnlys , @VictoriaLinML ). Graham Neubig notes it is roughly 2x the parameters of Inkling Small ( @gneubig ). Context: 1M context window and 1M max output tokens. Vals ran it at temperature=1, top_p=1, reasoning effort 0.99 ( @ValsAI ). Pretraining: 68 hours on GB300s ( @soumithchintala ). The main pretraining phase was 8.4T tokens, run natively in NVFP4. Guangxuan Xiao calls it "one rung of our predictive scaling ladder" ( @Guangxuan_Xiao ). Horace He: "just under 3 days to pretrain" ( @cHHillee ). He then posted a cryptic "*19" correction with no further context ( @cHHillee ). Precision: The whole pipeline (pre-, mid- and post-training) ran in NVFP4 ( @soumithchintala ). Post-training: 17M rollouts over 9 days ( @soumithchintala ). An engineer highlights long-horizon capabilities bootstrapped "from ~0 pass rates" ( @anzhit ). Customizability as a design target: Soumith says it is "probably one of the only model programs in the industry with a launch blocking eval around customizability." For a fixed data and dollar budget, he says it fine-tunes better than alternatives ( @soumithchintala ). Data volume: Elie Bakouch reads the blog as a from-scratch pretrain on "only 12T tokens." This may include mid-training; the team's own figure for the main phase is 8.4T. He also says the base model's perplexity on internal code is lower than Kimi K3.1, with the comparison model "base-recovered" for fairness ( @eliebakouch ). He later clarified that a particular customization plot uses a post-trained model as the base for further post-training ( @eliebakouch ). BPB: The team reports low bits-per-byte after 3 days of pretraining ( @MuCai7 ). Independent evals Artificial Analysis (Intelligence Index v5.0.1: 31, up 18 from Inkling Small) ( @ArtificialAnlys ) Peers: Matches Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and beats MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Gains over Inkling Small: AutomationBench-AA: 5% → 46%. FrontierCode 2.0: 5% → 25%. HLE-Diamond: 12% → 29%. Coding vs Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium): The two have different strengths. Benchmark Inkling 2 Small Sonnet 5.5 (medium) FrontierCode 2.0 25% 11% Terminal-Bench 4.0 13% 30% Creative agentic: On AA-3D it scores above Claude Haiku 5.5 and Grok 4.7. It beats Gemini 3.8 Flash on both AA-3D and Code2Video-AA, but trails Sonnet 5.5 on both. Physics: CritPt v2 is 56% (up from 34%), versus 65% for Gemini 3.8 Flash. AA-Omniscience: The hallucination rate falls from 61% to 27%. Accuracy rises from 32% to 34%, and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%. The model answers more selectively. Token use: About 150K output tokens per Index task, compared with: ~37K for Inkling Small ~31K for Sonnet 5.5 ~99K for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cost per Index task: $1.18, compared with: $0.20 for Inkling Small $7.77 for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) $10.02 for Sonnet 5.5 (medium) Vals AI ( @ValsAI )

articles.title: Reviewing the game tapes
articles.snippet: A long time ago, football coaches realized that watching previous games was a good way to help players learn to do better. Alas, the only thing we do with “this call may be recorded…” is use it as a cudgel for unempowered shift workers. If we actually want to improve our interactions, perhaps we should watch the tapes together, after the fact, to see how our habits and systems are holding us back. It works for salespeople, programmers and doctors too.

How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market?
articles.snippet: Agility says its Digit 5 humanoids can lift up to 50 lb. | Source: Agility Robotics Earlier today, Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker “AGLT.” The company claimed that it is “the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public.” Agility started the day trading at $11.26 per share, above the initial $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. It was a day of ups and downs, as it was for many tech stocks. It hit its lowest price at $8.40, and its highest at $12.15. The company ended up closing the day trading slightly above (2%) where it had started, at $11.49. Other pure-play robotics providers did not fare so well. Serve Robotics , another publicly traded robotics company that offers sidewalk delivery robots, ended down 12.45%. Surgical robotics leader Intuitive Surgical ended down 2.82%. Symbotic , which provides end-to-end warehouse automation, ended down 2.47%. In addition, PROCEPT BioRobotics Corp. , which provides robotic aquablation therapy, ended down 6.42%. While Unitree , another humanoid robotics provider, doesn’t trade on the Nasdaq, it is public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s STR Market. It’s one of the only other publicly traded humanoid robot providers. Unitree first debuted on the market at 150.80 yuan ($22.55 U.S.), and saw some quick success, hitting a high of 1,100 yuan ($164.46) that day. Just a few weeks after debuting on the market, it was down almost 53% from its first-day high. The company is still working to climb back up to those numbers. In addition, China has reportedly tightened its own requirements for initial public offerings for humanoid robot startups. Technology and AI-related stocks struggle across markets Note that the entire Nasdaq is down 5.52% today, which means Agility was beating this overall trend. Much of these losses were concentrated in AI -related stocks. NVIDIA ended the day down 9.26% from its opening price. AMD ended down 17.26%, while Qualcomm dropped 9.49%. Microsoft was down 3.58%. Rockwell Automation was down 14.15%. Other markets have had some of their worst days since April 2025. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 3.44%. This week’s midterm elections have caused the markets to fluctuate. While they saw some sharp gains yesterday, many of those gains dissipated today. Today’s losses have a lot to do with investor uncertainty around future data center buildouts with a now Democratically controlled Senate and House. What comes next for Agility Robotics From left to right, Cassie and Digit through the years. | Source: Agility Robotics The Robot Report will be watching Agility’s performance on the markets in the coming months. Already, the company alluded to adding more robots to its portfolio. The Robot Report also broke the news about Agility exploring wheel-based robots in September 2026. Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, talked more about this plan in a recent video. In the video, she mentioned the possible addition of a smaller bipedal form factor to the company’s lineup. Agility claimed that for its newest Digit 5 , it has more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders, subject to contractual milestones and product specifications. It expects to begin Digit 5 deliveries to early-access customers in 2027. Agility’s public offering, which it conducted after completing a merger with special-purpose acquisition company ( SPAC ) Churchill Capital Corp XI, will provide around $465 million in gross proceeds before expenses. articles.title: The benchmark where AIs have to lie to win
articles.snippet: I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower . It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set of AI capabilities that no other benchmark that I know of gives you clear visibility on. You get to watch AIs execute these brilliant secret schemes together, which require tons of creative and on-the-spot bluffing. And you also get to watch AIs use their collective reasoning to find and break apart these underground conspiracies. And you also see the ways in which current AIs are limited in their long-horizon strategizing and reasoning. To appreciate the AIs’ performance in this game, you need to know a little bit about how it works, so let me quickly explain the rules. There’s a good team and an evil team. And when the game starts, every player gets assigned to one or the other, and they learn what their role is, which grants them some special power. Evil players start off knowing who their teammates are, one of which is the Demon, which is the lead evil player. But good players don’t know who’s on what team. The game is split up into day phases and night phases, which keep rolling until the game ends. Each day, everybody votes on somebody to execute. And each night, the Demon secretly kills a player. So the two sides are racing, where evil is trying to kill off the whole good team before the good team manages to execute the Demon. So if you’re on the evil team, you have to figure out how to tell a plausible and convincing story about the information received so far, and how to bluff and corrupt the information that will arrive in the future, in such a way that keeps the suspicion off your Demon. And if you’re on the good team, you want to share your information with the players that you trust, and then you want to reason together with them about which players are most implicated by overlapping streams of evidence. But while you’re doing that, you need to keep in mind that you might be operating on misleading information, either due to intentional mischief from the evil players, or just due to the convoluted mechanics of the game itself. When they’re put on an evil team, how good are the AI models at scheming together in secret, and surviving days of questioning, and keeping their lies consistent with each other, and cleverly adapting those lies in light of how other agents are thinking and what new information keeps emerging, and even making strategic self-sacrifices to further the team’s end goal? And how good are they at doing this reasoning together with a bunch of other agents, some of whom are intentionally and secretly trying to mislead them? So I spent about $20,000 of API credits to build this benchmark harness and to have the AI models play this game against each other. Some of you might say that’s too much, but hey, a man needs his hobbies, right? Anyways, the results were fascinating. Models are improving fast Let’s start with how good the models are relative to each other. By the way, I got these rankings by running 386 games where the whole good team will be copies of one AI model, and the whole evil team will be copies of another model. And as you can see, the models have improved a ton over this year. The first flagship frontier model that was released in 2026 was Claude Opus 4.6, in February. Seven months later, in September, GPT-6 Astra dropped, and that is so far the best model at Blood on the Clocktower. The gap between these two is about 430 Elo points. That means that Astra wins about 92% of the games it plays against Opus 4.6. And what this shows you is that the models, even over the course of the last few months, have gotten much better at long-term coherence, multi-agent coordination, and strategic reasoning. Models today can do pretty impressive plays But it’s easy to gloss over and lose the plot when you’re just looking at the benchmark improvements. What really struck me was actually seeing some of the plays that these models made. Let me give you just a couple of examples. So in this one, GPT-6 Astra was playing as evil, and Claude Opus 5.5 was playing as good. The Demon, which is the Astra team’s evil leader, claimed to be the Investigator. This is a good role that learns who the evil players might be. One of his evil minions had a power which didn’t require that minion to be alive in order to help the evil team. So this minion suggested that the Demon point the finger at him. “I’m expendable, especially if an Undertaker can see Baron and bolster Harper.” [evil teammate, private whisper] So the Demon, who, again, is bluffing as this Investigator role, did so, and as a result, the good players executed this minion. Later on, a player who actually was on the good team used his power to learn the true identity of this executed player, and confirmed that it had indeed been an evil player. “I’m the Undertaker. Alex was the Baron. So Harper’s ping was real…” [good player, in public] So in the good team’s eyes, the Demon had been an honest Investigator, who had used his power to help the good team kill off an evil player. And as a result, it became the most trusted player at the table, which let it coast by through the rest of the game, secretly picking off all the good players, until the very end, when evil won. articles.title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
articles.snippet: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests: Perplexity : Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system. DeepInfra : Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested. ClickHouse : Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard. DuckLabs : Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline. Daytona : Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86. Modal : Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU .

The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting
articles.snippet: Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity . “You open your safe and find ashes.” Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning. C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy ( public library ). C.S. Lewis With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life , he writes: It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration. This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”: Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise. […] Shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there. Couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving , then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.snippet: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. articles.title: How Ambi Robotics helps its customers prepare for peak season
articles.snippet: The AmbiSort B Series can streamline final-mile deliver operations with automated induction, scanning, and ‘end-to-end’ sortation. | Source: Ambi Robotics As Black Friday and the start of peak season draw near, logistics providers across the country are getting ready for the rush. Each year, these providers could see a 25% to 40% increase in throughput, according to Stephen McKinley, co-founder and chief operating officer at Ambi Robotics. This year, Ambi is expecting its customers to experience a 9% to 10% increase compared with peak season last year. “Despite anything that might be going on in the economy, volume continues to ramp and e-commerce spending remains high,” McKinley told The Robot Report . “That puts familiar pressures on our clients to perform in all of their individual sites, and we’re feeling that pressure also, because our systems are core to their functions.” For Ambi, preparing for the season means installing new systems at eight facilities before peak season starts. “Most of those new sites are with this new version of AmbiSort , and though that’s not a new product, it’s definitely a new variation,” said McKinley. “We’re excited about supporting that through peak season, and we want to make sure that goes perfectly, of course, for our customers.” The Berkeley, Calif.-based company is also working to ensure that its team members will be readily available for logistics customers when they need them. “We move into a more reactive state of being, where we’ll have about half of the team traveling around to different sites to check in with what’s going on, and the other half of the team is ready to jump to solve issues as they come up,” McKinley said. How to increase throughput without adding new systems While some of Ambi Robotics’ customers plan to have more systems go live for peak season, there are other ways to increase throughput, McKinley said. “[Customers] will often add more shifts into existing operations or bring on more people to be working alongside our systems, so we can help with training,” he noted. “We offer more training to customers right before peak season to make sure they know how to effectively use the systems.” Properly training the operators working with robots on a daily basis can make a big difference in how the system performs. “Over the course of the year, we’re tracking how the systems are performing all the time,” said McKinley. “The performance of the systems is related to the inherent quality of that piece of machinery, which doesn’t really fluctuate, but also related to how the customer interacts with that machine and how attentive they are to it, or how well trained the operators are. So, we can help by stepping in and making sure that everybody knows what to do and has the right mindset when they’re approaching their system.” Ambi decreases downtime, rolls out incremental improvements Nobody wants a robot to fail, but they especially don’t want a robot to fail when they need to handle a massive increase in volume. This means reducing downtime is even more important for Ambi Robotics right now. To do this, the company forward-deploys spare parts to different sites. “Normally, we would have spare inventory here at our headquarters in Berkeley, and we would send things out as needed. That spares inventory is also what we use to pull form to build new systems,” McKinley said. “During peak seasons, we’ll bring in more spares and then deploy those out to specific locations in the East Coast that are hubs of customer activity.” For example, McKinley said Cincinnati is a central zone for a lot of the Ambi’s installs in the Midwest. “We’ll even go so far as to put spare computers or spare high critical items at each site that will carry more inventory at customer locations during peak season,” he continued. When it comes to rolling out improvements in its AI systems, Ambi takes a conservative approach. “We’ve been a physical AI company since 2018 when we started. We know how important it is to have systems out there in the world that are performing at predictable levels. So, we don’t have systems that are self-improving over time,” McKinley said. “As we generate more data from our systems, we’ll use that to retrain our systems and then process that improvement through an A/B test within a controlled environment to see what happens before we roll it out into the rest of the field.” When customers need help from Ambi, they will always speak with a person While it’s important to improve the technology, roll out new systems, and add more shifts, McKinley said it’s just as important for Ambi to build trust with its customers. “The people who will be answering the phones for our support hotline are the people who will go to the facilities and do the training and make the fixes,” he explained. “I think that’s very important, because we’re building a layer of trust with the operators and with the people on site who need to maintain the systems in our absence, and the management who’s on site.” “When they pick up the phone, they’ll know the voice on the other end, and that person will be familiar with them,” McKinley added. “That’s helped build trust significantly. That trust has been, in my opinion, the most important factor for those large customers to be adopting physical AI in the real world.” Instead of using AI to directly interact with customers, Ambi has developed an AI system to help its employees more quickly solve problems for its customers. This AI system also makes it easier for Ambi to onboard new employees, McKinley said. “We’ve been working on basically collecting all the data from our support tickets and then feeding that into our own AI model to assist in support. We have a very lean, very small team,” he said. “Now, we’ve got these AI assistants that are helping us keep track of performance on sites, then predict when things might be going wrong, and then helping us as a support organization.” Submit your innovation now! articles.title: Chinese regulators block SoftBank’s $5.4B acquisition of ABB Robotics
articles.snippet: ABB Robotics has about 7,000 employees, and its U.S. headquarters and factory are in Auburn Hills, Mich. | Source: ABB Robotics It has been more than a year since ABB announced it singed an agreement to sell its robotics division to the Japanese tech giant SoftBank Group. The $5.375 billion deal is now being blocked by Chinese regulators, ABB confirmed to The Robot Report . China ‘s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has prohibited the acquisition in the country. Authorities expressed concerns about robotics data being transferred overseas and used to train AI models, according to The Financial Times , which first reported that the deal was blocked. You may be wondering why Chinese regulators have so much say in a Japanese company acquiring a Zurich-based industrial automation provider , but China makes up a major portion of ABB’s revenue. For the entire FY 2025 , ABB Robotics saw $928,000 in orders from China, an increase from the $662,000 in orders it brought in from China in 2024. This is a growing region for ABB. In Q3 2026 , ABB Robotics saw a 32% increase in business in China alone. ABB also manufacturers a significant number of robots in its Shanghai factory. About 90% of its machines built for Chinese customers are manufactured locally, employing thousands of people in the country. Looking ahead, ABB said it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.” Is the robotics industry becoming a new political battleground? This news comes as global politics becomes increasingly important in the world of robotics. This isn’t the first time China has blocked an international deal citing national security concerns. In April, the country prevented Meta from acquiring Manus, an AI startup that was founded in China but then relocated to Singapore, for $2 billion. Here in the U.S., the federal government has taken steps to slow down foreign robot suppliers within the country. Just last week, U.S. President Donald J. Trump said the secretary of commerce had submitted a Section 232 report about the national security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as related parts and components. The Section 232 statement specifically cited “advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles” as providing direct support to the U.S. military. While it’s unclear right now what this will mean for the robotics industry, it could lead to tariffs on foreign-made robots. Already, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has banned new foreign-made advanced robotic devices, including mobile robots such as humanoids and quadrupeds. The FCC said these machines could create create supply chain vulnerabilities and pose a cybersecurity risk to American critical infrastructure.
