articles.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
articles.snippet: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.” https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ChrisAlexiuk_captions_9MB.mp4 It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand. It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains. “You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.” In non-wizard terms? “There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks. NVIDIAN Chris Alexiuk (left) engages with developers during the Build-a-Claw event at GTC Berlin. “I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.” From Birding to Model-Building Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada. “After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions. “Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.” Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community. “To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.” And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan? “It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.” Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

articles.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
articles.snippet: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain. During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM. Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move. Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power. That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed. An AI factory faces the same limit. More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall. Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy. Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency: Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain. The NVFP4 format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including FLUX.2 [klein] from Black Forest Labs , Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab, Beam 1.0 from Reflection , Meta Muse Spark from Meta , Step 5 Preview from StepFun and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference. Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be distributed across up to 72 GPUs , so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users. Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers. Applying NVFP4 to the KV cache reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM. NVIDIA Vera CPU helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly. When context isn’t actively in use, NVIDIA Dynamo inference software moves it to NVIDIA CMX context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian , DDN , Dell Technologies , Everpure (previously Pure Storage), HPE , IBM , NetApp , VAST and WEKA . Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system. Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM. RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever mod

articles.title: At The Money: How Do Financial Professionals Invest Their Own Money?
articles.snippet: At The Money: How Do Financial Professionals Invest Their Own Money? (November 4, 2026) Most investment authors tell you what to do with your money – but they never tell you what they do with their money. Brian Portnoy holds a PhD from the University of Chicago. His latest book is “ How I Invest My Money ,” foreworded by my partner, Josh Brown (CEO of Ritholtz Wealth). Full transcript below . ~~~ About this week’s guest: Brian Portnoy is founder and CEO of Shaping Wealth , which helps advisors and their clients to achieve “funded contentment,” and operates as an outsourced Chief Behavioral Officer. Portnoy has held senior investment roles throughout the hedge fund and mutual fund industries. For more info, see: Shaping Wealth Bio LinkedIn Twitter At the Money: How Much Money Is Too Much? ~~~ Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here , and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts , YouTube , Spotify , and Bloomberg . And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify TRANSCRIPT: Bloomberg · Barry Ritholtz with Brian Portnoy, CEO of Shaping Wealth · Transcript BARRY RITHOLTZ: Most investment authors tell you what to do with your money, but they never reveal what they do with their own money. That bothered Brian Portnoy. He spent more than 20 years in the mutual fund and hedge fund industries. He holds a PhD from the University of Chicago, and he is the CEO of Shaping Wealth. His 2018 book, The Geometry of Wealth, was really a fascinating exploration of behavioral finance and emotional intelligence. He has co-edited two editions of How I Invest My Money with my partner Josh Brown—full disclosure, Josh is at Ritholtz Wealth Management. So let’s talk a little bit about both of these books. They’re really very different from the usual investment tomes. Tell me a little bit about their genesis. BRIAN PORTNOY: Thanks, Barry. Appreciate it. The genesis is a fun little story. It was 2019, and Josh, who you know and I know is a very sharp and good writer, published a blog with the title “How I Invest My Money,” and he made the simple observation that in all the years that he’s been in the market, no one’s really ever asked him for investment advice or financial planning advice. So he decided to write a blog that walked through how he builds his portfolio, venture investments in friends’ companies, a variety of things. And it got great feedback. It was very well done. I read it, I texted him, I said, “This was great, and hey, what do you think about getting a bunch of our friends together to write similar short blogs or chapters, and we could put it together as a volume?” And he loved the idea. I called our friend Craig Pierce at Harriman House and said, “Craig, what do you think?” I’ll say, from me texting Josh to us having a book contract was about 72 hours. Harriman House was very into it. Josh and I proceeded to build a volume of 25 contributors, and that volume was published in 2020 and really received wonderful reviews. And as you indicated, we’ve followed up with a second volume very recently. BARRY RITHOLTZ: So the really interesting thing about this is, with some people who are free to share their advice, the question comes up: Hey, might they be a little reluctant to open the kimono about how they run their own books, their own portfolios, their own household finances? Did you get any pushback from people who were a little reluctant to drop their professional personas and speak honestly about what they do with their own money? BRIAN PORTNOY: The short answer is no. For the first volume, 25 phone calls, 25 chapters. BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really? BRIAN PORTNOY: Yeah, 25 for 25. BARRY RITHOLTZ: That’s amazing. Second one, no hesitation? Nobody tapped out? Nobody said, “Not for me”? BRIAN PORTNOY: Second volume, 25 for 25. But your word—hesitation. So here’s the thing, and a word that has surfaced with the publishing of these two volumes that I think is so important to being successful financially, which is permission. Effectively, we gave permission to people. They happen to be financial experts, financial advisors, portfolio managers, economists, and the like. But we gave permission to, quote unquote, go there—talk about how you invest your money. Because think about an equity fund manager. Well, they might run a large-cap equity sleeve and be very good at that, but when they think about running their money, well, they’re going to have lots of equities, lots of bonds, they’re going to have real estate, they’re going to be doing a lot of different things with their money beyond the portfolio. Charitable giving and insuring and risk management, on and on. And so the stories ended up being this unbelievable kaleidoscope of different journeys. And Barry, it’s the part that I’m proudest of in this ongoing project. Now 50 chapters, 50 completely distinct life stories from people who all know, quote unquote, the right answer. But then when invited to—and again, given their permission—to really talk about how they invest, how they allocate to the things that are important to them, they went in their own direction and expressed it in a very unique way. BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m really curious about both the first 25 people in the first book and the second 25 people—or I should say the other 24 people, because I’m one of them in the second book. BRIAN PORTNOY: Yep. BARRY RITHOLTZ: How did you put that list together? Did you just go through the contacts on your phone, or was there a “Hey, let’s have a few of these and a few of those”? What did that look like? BRIAN PORTNOY: It was important for me to have a diverse set of voices. One of the outcomes that I want from this ongoing project is for readers—just regular folks, friends and neighbors—to pick up the volume. You’ve now got 50 four-page chapters, very easy bite-size insights. I want people to find voices that resonate with them. And so it was important for me that we have people further along in their career, w

articles.title: Agility Robotics begins trading on Nasdaq
articles.snippet: Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market this morning under the ticker “AGLT,” after the company completed its merger with special-purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, Churchill Capital Corp XI. Agility’s stock opened at $11.26 per share, which was above the $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. The Salem, Ore.-based company ‘s stock was at $10.30 as of press time. “Today marks an important milestone for Agility, but the bigger story is what it means for the future of work,” stated Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics. “AI is moving beyond the digital world and into the physical world, creating new possibilities for how people and machines work together. At Agility, that future is already taking shape.” “Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” she added. “Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together.” Churchill XI shareholders approved the deal on Nov. 2, with more than 84% of votes cast in favor . The transaction closed on Nov. 4. Shares held by existing Agility shareholders and by the Churchill sponsor will be subject to a lock-up restriction on sales for 180 days after the 6ransaction closes, subject to early release based on certain stock price performance measures. The deal provides with about $465 million in gross proceeds before expenses. That includes about $164 million from Churchill XI’s trust account after redemptions, $201 million from a private investment in public equity (PIPE) led by Foxconn , and a $100 million funding round closed after the SPAC announcement. Agility had previously projected more than $620 million in proceeds if no shareholders redeemed. Digit logs operating time, earns revenue Agility Robotics, which spun out of Oregon State University in 2015, makes the Digit humanoid , which has been moving totes in warehouses. The company claimed that Digit has already logged more than 65,000 hours of operation across nine customer facilities. Customers include AGCO , GXO Logistics , Schaeffler , Mercado Libre , and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada . Agility reported $1.78 million in revenue in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, with a net loss of $138.1 million. About 64% of that revenue came from related parties. The company ended 2025 with $103 million in cash. The legged robot developer said it has more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders for its next-generation Digit 5 , subject to contractual milestones and product specifications. It expects to begin Digit 5 deliveries to early-access customers in 2027. “Congratulations to the entire Agility Robotics team on this incredible milestone,” said Nicolaus Radford, co-founder and CEO of humanoid startup Persona AI . “At a time when robotics headlines are too often dominated by hype and flashy demonstrations, Agility has focused on the hard work of putting robots to work. Built on a decade of engineering breakthroughs, relentless persistence and real-world deployments, Jonathan and his team have helped turn the promise of humanoid robotics into a commercial reality, and the entire industry should be celebrating.” Agility said it the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public. But it’s not clear how long that designation will last. The Robot Report broke the news about Agility exploring wheel-based robots in September 2026, and Johnson talked more about it in the company overview (see video above). “We’re exploring other form factors better suited to work in more consumer-facing domains,” she said. “And whether that means a wheeled base or smaller bipedal form factor, our engineers build the best solutions for wherever hard work is done.” Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility, recently said during a social media “Ask Me Anything” that Digit likely won’t get wheels. However, the company is exploring wheeled robots as part of a broader family of multipurpose, human-centric robots. “Digit likely won’t get wheels. But wheeled robots are absolutely in our exploratory roadmap for a family of robots that focus on being human-centric and multi-purpose,” Hurst said. From left to right, Cassie, and Digit through the years. | Source: Agility Robotics Agility Robotics explores licensing its IP Johnson also suggested that Agility Robotics could license its intellectual property to other humanoid developers, positioning the company as a potential technology supplier to the broader industry. New robots and a licensing strategy potentially open up new revenue paths for the company. “We envision Agility becoming the backbone of the humanoid industry as the category begins to scale into new markets and use cases,” said Johnson. “Humanoids of all types and builds could benefit from our extensive research and innovation.” “To build a billion-dollar robotics industry, you need robots that people trust enough to work alongside,” said FORT Robotics founder and CEO Samuel Reeves. “Agility understood early that safety isn’t just a box to check. It’s foundational. Their IPO is a win for Agility and a powerful signal that safety and commercial success go hand in hand.” The post Agility Robotics begins trading on Nasdaq appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: Umberto Eco’s Antilibrary: Why Unread Books Are More Valuable to Our Lives than Read Ones
articles.snippet: How to become an “antischolar” in a culture that treats knowledge as “an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order.” “It is our knowledge — the things we are sure of — that makes the world go wrong and keeps us from seeing and learning,” Lincoln Steffens wrote in his beautiful 1925 essay . Piercingly true as this may be, we’ve known at least since Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave that “most people are not just comfortable in their ignorance, but hostile to anyone who points it out.” . Although science is driven by “thoroughly conscious ignorance” and the spiritual path paved with admonitions against the illusion of thorough understanding , we cling to our knowledge — our incomplete, imperfect, infinitesimal-in-absolute-terms knowledge — like we cling to life itself. And yet the contour of what we know is a mere silhouette cast by the infinite light of the unknown against the screen of the knowable. The great E.F. Schumacher captured this strange dynamic in the concept of adaequatio — the notion that “the understanding of the knower must be adequate to the thing to be known.” But how do we face our inadequacy with grace and negotiate wisely this eternal tension between the known, the unknown, the knowable, and the unknowable? That’s what Lebanese-American scholar, statistician, and essayist Nassim Nicholas Taleb explores in a section of his modern classic The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable ( public library ) — an illuminating inquiry into the unknowable and unpredictable outlier-events that precipitate profound change, and our tendency to manufacture facile post-factum explanations for them based on our limited knowledge. Taleb uses legendary Italian writer Umberto Eco ’s uncommon relationship with books and reading as a parable of the most fruitful relationship with knowledge: The writer Umberto Eco belongs to that small class of scholars who are encyclopedic, insightful, and nondull. He is the owner of a large personal library (containing thirty thousand books), and separates visitors into two categories: those who react with “Wow! Signore professore dottore Eco, what a library you have! How many of these books have you read?” and the others — a very small minority — who get the point that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. Read books are far less valuable than unread ones. The library should contain as much of what you do not know as your financial means, mortgage rates, and the currently tight real-estate market allows you to put there. You will accumulate more knowledge and more books as you grow older, and the growing number of unread books on the shelves will look at you menacingly. Indeed, the more you know, the larger the rows of unread books. Let us call this collection of unread books an antilibrary . Tsudonku: Japanese for leaving a book unread after buying it, typically piled up together with other unread books. Illustration by Ella Frances Sanders from Lost in Translation: An Illustrated Compendium of Untranslatable Words from Around the World . Eco himself has since touched on humanity’s curious relationship with the known and the unknown in his encyclopedia of imaginary lands , the very existence of which is another symptom of our compulsive tendency to fill in the gaps of our understanding with concrete objects of “knowledge,” even if we have to invent them by the force of our imagination. Taleb adds: We tend to treat our knowledge as personal property to be protected and defended. It is an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order. So this tendency to offend Eco’s library sensibility by focusing on the known is a human bias that extends to our mental operations. People don’t walk around with anti-résumés telling you what they have not studied or experienced (it’s the job of their competitors to do that), but it would be nice if they did. Just as we need to stand library logic on its head, we will work on standing knowledge itself on its head. Illustration from The Three Astronauts — Umberto Eco’s little-known vintage semiotic children’s book. Noting that his Black Swan theory centers on “our misunderstanding of the likelihood of surprises” because we underestimate the value of what we don’t know and take what we do know “a little too seriously,” Taleb envisions the perfect dancer in the tango with knowledge: Let us call this an antischolar — someone who focuses on the unread books, and makes an attempt not to treat his knowledge as a treasure, or even a possession, or even a self-esteem enhancement device — a skeptical empiricist. Complement The Black Swan , which is fascinating it its totality, with astrophysicist Marcelo Gleiser on how to live with mystery in a culture obsessed with certitude , philosopher Hannah Arendt on how unanswerable questions give shape to the human experience , and novelist Marilynne Robinson on the beauty of the unknown . HT Bobulate donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation . articles.title: Welcoming Jason Spinell to Collaborative Fund
articles.snippet: We are incredibly excited to announce that Jason Spinell is joining Collaborative Fund as a Partner. Jason and I go back well over a decade to the early-stage venture ecosystem in New York circa 2010. Back then, Jason was the Ventures Director at Undercurrent (a premier design strategy and venture shop), where we spent countless hours trading investment ideas and playing soccer together. Over the last decade, he has been the driving force behind the Slack Fund, which he helped launch in 2016 in San Francisco. Under his leadership, the Slack Fund backed nearly 100 early-stage companies across North America and Europe, including Lattice, Loom, Glean, Hightouch, 1Password, and Fundamental. When Salesforce acquired Slack for $27.7 billion, his mandate expanded significantly. This gave him a front-row seat to Salesforce’s rapid transformation into an AI-first organization, and allowed him the freedom to continue investing across the entire AI stack, from foundational infrastructure and frontier tech to end-user applications. But beyond the resume, Jason is just an exceptional human being. He’s a former freeskier who has appeared in multiple ski films (and Freeskier Magazine!). His favorite book is Yvon Chouinard’s Let My People Go Surfing , he’s deeply thoughtful about the future of work, and he is fundamentally driven by a belief that founders should build what they truly love. Most importantly, he’s someone we deeply trust and respect, and we are thrilled to be learning from him. Please join us in welcoming him to the team!

articles.title: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI
articles.snippet: Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi . Goodarzi took a very non-traditional path to Silicon Valley, joining Intuit in 2004 after working at Siemens and Honeywell. After managing business units across the company he became CEO in 2019, and is taking on the challenge of figuring out how one of tech’s oldest software companies manages the AI paradigm shift. In this interview we discuss Goodarzi’s background and the what it takes to be an effective generalist, and get his take on how Intuit has thrived for 44 years. We discuss the shift from Quicken to Quickbooks, the TurboTax business, and how Goodarzi thinks about the consumer space today. Then we talk about accountants, Intuit’s most important customer acquisition channel, and how the company wants to change the profession from partners to customers via AI. I present the case to Goodarzi that Intuit seems like its being disrupted, and he makes the case why they are well positioned to actual grow their market. We also touch on acquisitions like Credit Karma and Mailchimp, and how Intuit has managed business model changes in the past, and what needs to change in the future. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Being a Generalist | Intuit History | TurboTax and Credit Karma | The Future of Accountants | Disruption | Mailchimp | Intuit’s AI Future Being a Generalist Sasan Goodarzi, welcome to Stratechery. Sasan Goodarzi: Thank you for having me, I’m a big fan of all the work that you do. It’s great to be a part of it. Well, we’ll get to my relationship with Intuit, which I’ve had for many years. Big fan? I’m going to have to think about that one. We are here to talk about Intuit, a company that you have been at, with a brief break, for over 20 years. Before we get to that, however, tell me about your background, which is a very interesting one. Let’s start with where you were born. SG: Yes, I was born in Tehran, in Iran, and I am the youngest of three — 13 years younger than the other two brothers. I was told I was special, I think I was an accident, so there you go. And back then, you’d ship your kids to the U.S. because everybody wanted to come to the U.S. to study and so my brothers were in the U.S. already studying, and my parents decided to do an experiment with me and shipped me to the U.S. at the age of nine and I was very fortunate, because the revolution actually happened. Got it. So you had already left before then, I wasn’t quite sure on that timing. SG: Yeah, yeah. I was very fortunate, I left before the revolution, about eight to nine months before the revolution, and have been in the U.S. ever since. Where did you end up in the U.S.? SG: I came to Orlando, Florida of all places, because my brothers were going to the University of Central Florida. And, by the way, back then we used to say, “U Can’t Finish”, that’s what we called it, but it’s a great university. But anyways, for that reason, I was in Orlando until my early 20s, until I started being moved by Honeywell. Every couple of years, I was going to a different state, which was a lot of fun, and eventually ended up in California. You studied electrical engineering, right? articles.title: George Washington’s error
articles.snippet: In his farewell address, he said, “Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course.” It’s easy to fall in love with the idea that we live in a detached and distant situation. To imagine that culture and society and events out there have no impact on the lives we live. The coal plant across the country, the goings on in the CEO’s office, the impact of tech on our culture… none of them are very far away. We have more leverage and connection than we want to admit. Insulation is scarce. Technology, the competition and the shifts in media come for us, whether we seek them out or not. It doesn’t pay to fret about things we can’t influence, but we might be able to influence more than we realize. Perhaps isolation was useful for George. It’s clearly not true now.

AI Twitter Recap OpenAI's Autonomous Cyber Pipeline Patches 948 Linux Kernel Privilege-Escalation Bugs Pipeline result : OpenAI says its security researchers built an autonomous pipeline for vulnerability discovery, exploitation and patching. In a single run with an upcoming cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, at a total API cost of $1.2M ( announcement ). Novel techniques : OpenAI says the agents discovered and used at least 10 Linux exploitation techniques that its team and consulted experts consider novel. It argues this shows models going beyond applying known methods ( thread ). Disclosure path : OpenAI says it is working with Linux maintainers and Patch the Planet partners on reports and patches ( details ). Scale framing : Eric Wallace says researchers typically find about 20 Linux LPEs a year. He says the model found about 1,000 in one week using about $1M of tokens, and that OpenAI is now putting "a significant amount" of frontier compute toward pro bono open-source patching ( post ). Greg Brockman cites about $1,000 per vulnerability ( post ). Cost trajectory : One comparison puts GPT‑5.6 Sol at 166 vulnerabilities for about $500k in July 2026, against 948 for about $1.2M with the new model ( comparison ). One commenter estimates the real internal cost is far below the API list price; this is an unverified estimate ( estimate ). Context : The run used an unreleased model, separate from the rumored GPT‑6.2 Sol and Astra models covered below ( note ). Open-Weight Model Wave: Kimi K3.1 Pro, Ripple-65B, SWE-2 Flash, Hy4 Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights : Moonshot released weights for its flagship ( release ). Modal describes it as a post-training update to K3, with expanded RL for coding, financial research and long-horizon agentic work. It accepts text and images and has 1M context ( Modal ). Specs : The model has 2.8T total parameters with 104B active ( Ollama ). One commenter credits gated sparse attention for gains in intelligence and efficiency over K3 ( comment ). Independent signal : On Agent Arena it ranks #1 among open models and #13 overall, with +5.1% net improvement across more than 17.5K agentic sessions. That is +4.2pp over K3, and it is #1 open in Bash reliability and steerability ( Arena ). One user reports that on an internal SRE-agent eval it uses more tokens but delivers "shockingly good" quality ( report ). Availability : vLLM and SGLang shipped Day-0 support across AMD, NVIDIA, Rubin and TPU, and SGLang also supports Trainium 2/3 ( SemiAnalysis ). Hosted access is also live on Ollama Cloud with zero data retention, Databricks and SkyPilot ( Databricks ). Ripple-65B Preview (Ricursive) : This is a 65B dense model pretrained from scratch. Ricursive claims it is the best US open-weight model on agentic coding, ahead of larger MoEs including Muse Spark Open-816B, Beam-501B, Inkling-975B and Nemotron 3 Ultra-550B ( launch ). Claimed results : It scores 80.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 against Beam-501B's 80.1%; Beam activates 23B parameters per token. Ricursive reports 12T training tokens, 1M context and an Apache 2.0 license ( summary ). Cost claims : Ricursive cites a $32M budget, which it says covers full R&D including the scaling ladder, data work and the final runs ( footnote ). Prime Intellect ran the pretraining clusters and cites 16x pretraining compute efficiency ( Prime Intellect ). Architecture/ablations : The model uses value residuals and sliding window attention ( notes ). On the scaling ladder, a new architecture on the same data as Olmo3 gave about a 3x gain, and a new dataset on the same architecture gave about 4x ( analysis ). Skepticism : Critics note it still loses to the 284B V4 Flash ( critique ). Others say the "US-only SOTA" framing hides the gap with Chinese models ( comment ), and that the release omits comparisons with Qwen ( critique ). Cognition SWE-2 Flash : Cognition says this coding model outperforms all American open-weight models, including ones 3x larger ( launch ). Base and cost : The model is post-trained on Thinking Machines' Inkling-Small. It costs 20% of SWE-2 and runs about 3x faster ( Jeff Wang ). It is Cognition's first model with a mid-training stage and was built in 6 weeks ( Silas Alberti ). Weights policy : Weights are not public. Cognition plans a secure weight-sharing program for partners and researchers and cites cyber-misuse risk ( details ). Availability : It is free through November for Devin Pro, Max and Teams users ( pricing ). Tencent Hy4 : Tencent reports 75.2 on APEX-Agents against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's 72.1/72.9. API pricing is $0.834/$2.501 per million input

The Souls of Animals
articles.snippet: “They do not sweat and whine about their condition,” Walt Whitman wrote of the other animals, “they do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins, they do not make me sick discussing their duty to God, not one is dissatisfied, not one is demented with the mania of owning things.” Here was “the poet of the body and the poet of the soul” holding up a mirror to us creatures inhabiting an animal body complicated by a soul — that organ of want and worry which we ourselves invented to explain why we make art, why we fall in love, why we yearn to converse with reality in prayers and postulates. It is daring enough to ask what a soul actually is. Carl Jung knew that it defies the substance we are made of : “The soul is partly in eternity and partly in time.” Virginia Woolf knew that it defies our best technology of thought: “One can’t write directly about the soul. Looked at, it vanishes.” It is doubly daring to question the age-old dogma that the soul is the province of the human animal alone. Even as we have incrementally and reluctantly admitted other creatures into the temple of consciousness, we have denied them souls — denied them, because our tools of communication and computation have failed to probe it, an inner life capable of imagination and play, of love and grief, of dreams and wonder. And yet our very language defies our denial: the word animal comes from the Latin for soul . Art by Jackie Morris from The Lost Words by Robert Macfarlane In 1991, long before we came to consider the soul of an octopus , long before fMRI and EEG studies revealed not only that birds dream but what they dream about , Gary Kowalski took up this daring question in The Souls of Animals ( public library ) — an inquiry into the “spiritual lives” (and into what that means) of whooping cranes, elephants, jackdaws, gorillas, songbirds, horses, dogs, and cats. At its center is the idea that spirituality — which he defines as “the development of a moral sense, the appreciation of beauty, the capacity for creativity, and the awareness of one’s self within a larger universe as well as a sense of mystery and wonder about it all” — is a natural byproduct of “the biological order and in the ecology shared by all life.” (There are in this view echoes of Kepler, who believed that the Earth itself is an ensouled body , and of myriad native cosmogonies that regard other animals as sources of more-than-human wisdom and emissaries of the numinous.) Kowalski — a parish minister by vocation, who spends his days praying with the dying, blessing bonds of love, and helping people navigate moral quandaries — celebrates the soul as “the magic of life,” as that which “gives life its sublimity and grandeur,” and reflects: For ancient peoples, the soul was located in the breath or the blood. For me, soul resides at the point where our lives intersect with the timeless, in our love of goodness, our passion for beauty, our quest for meaning and truth. In asking whether animals have souls, we are inquiring whether they share in the qualities that make life more than a mere struggle for survival, endowing existence with dignity and élan. […] Many people think of soul as the element of personality that survives bodily death, but for me it refers to something much more down-to-earth. Soul is the marrow of our existence as sentient, sensitive beings. It’s soul that’s revealed in great works of art, and soul that’s lifted up in awe when we stand in silence under a night sky burning with billions of stars. When we speak of a soulful piece of music, we mean one that comes out of infinite depths of feeling. When we speak of the soul of a nation, we mean its capacity for valor and visionary change… Soul is present wherever our lives intersect the dimension of the holy: in moments of intimacy, in flights of fancy, and in rituals that hallow the evanescent events of our lives with enduring significance. Soul is what makes each of our lives a microcosm — not merely a meaningless fragment of the universe, but at some level a reflection of the whole. Half a century after Henry Beston insisted that “we need another and a wiser and perhaps a more mystical concept of animals,” for they are “gifted with extensions of the senses we have lost or never attained, living by voices we shall never hear,” Kowalski writes: Without anthropomorphizing our nonhuman relations we can acknowledge that animals share many human characteristics. They have individual likes and dislikes, moods and mannerisms, and possess their own integrity, which suffers when not respected. They play and are curious about their world. They develop friendships and sometimes risk their own lives to help others. They have “animal faith,” a spontaneity and directness that can be most refreshing… all the traits indicative of soul. For soul is not something we can see or measure. We can observe only its outward manifestations: in tears and laughter, in courage and heroism, in generosity and forgiveness. Soul is what’s behind-the-scenes in the tough and tender moments when we are most intensely and grippingly alive. By investigating the inner lives of other creatures, Kowalski argues, we are invariably deepening our own: As [modern] shamans, we are allowed to examine enigmas like “What makes us human?” and “What makes life sacred?” We can ask not only about the mating behavior and survival strategies of other animals but whether they have souls and spirits like our own. The danger here is that we are often in over our heads. But at least we are swimming in deep water and out of the shallows. In searching for answers to such queries, I have found, we not only enrich our understanding of other creatures, we also gain insight into ourselves. […] There is an inwardness in other living beings that awakens what is innermost in ourselves. I have often marveled, for instance, watching a flock of shore birds. On an invisible cue, they simultaneously rise off the beach and into the air, then turn an

articles.snippet: There’s a lot of dispute to yesterday’s title story on “ Weight Space Programming ” — and we agree that some of the claims are presented in overly favorable light and overall took away from the impact of the paper’s more substantial discoveries. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Instead today we’re featuring AI Engineer Shanghai and also sharing an exclusive interview on the history of Latent Space ! AI News for 11/02/2026-11/03/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Weight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network Weights Core claim and replications : Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication : Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline ( summary ). Hugging Face reproduction : Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo ( NielsRogge ). Hand-written classifier : A user had Fable hand-write a 100K-parameter network that classifies real versus fake legal citations, reportedly outperforming a trained version ( jacsebl ). Legora's CTO highlighted the result ( mstockton ). Astra's Qwen edit, reconstructed : GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B without backprop, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. A Zhihu reconstruction from the logs shows the gain is narrower than the headline ( ZhihuFrontier ): Failure mode : 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K-token limit because of looping. Method : Astra derived a "repetition direction" from contrastive looping/productive contexts, located it mainly in the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted 6× the projection from the top 64 aligned neurons per layer. Held-out result : Accuracy rose from 10.6% to 60.4% on 1,152 held-out problems. Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish. Laptop reproduction : Simon Willison reports that Qwen 3.8 27B achieved the same weight-interpretation feat on his laptop after 45+ minutes ( simonw ). Skeptical readings : Baselines : Critics say the big claims lack competent baselines, the Qwen result is bug-fixing rather than recursive self-improvement, and the thread overclaims ( paul_cal ). Benchmark overfitting : Fitting weights directly against a benchmark is "essentially meaningless," as the nesformer Mario example shows ( dbreunig ). Mechanism : One thread asks whether models mainly read the first and last layers, which map to known inputs and outputs ( ravfogel ). Interpretability takeaway : Another view is that the real lesson is how effectively coding agents use mechanistic-interpretability tools ( jbhuang0604 ). Optimistic framing : Supporters frame the work as meta-learning finally working and treat weight optimization as structured-text optimization. They suggest hybrids that interleave backprop with direct edits ( yoonholeee ). Model Releases and Independent Evals Tencent Hy4 : Tencent reports 75.2 on APEX-Agents versus 72.1/72.9 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, though the two trade wins on other benchmarks ( summary ). Pricing and weights : The API costs $0.834/$2.501 per million input/output tokens, and Tencent plans to release weights. Agent Arena : Hy4 ranks #14 overall across 8.5K+ sessions, at $0.55/task versus $1.46 for Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max). The two scores are within 1 point ( arena ). Sarvam Prism : This "System One" decision model is built on Sarvam 105B. It scores 71.8 with a 44 ms median response time, which Sarvam says is the best average among sub-100 ms decision models ( SarvamAI ). Open-weight releases : Kimi K3.1 Pro : Weights are due Wednesday ( Together ). P-H3-Image : Pruna's open model, distilled from MiniMax-H3, runs in 8 steps instead of 50, is 7× smaller and produces a 4 MP image in 2.6 s ( PrunaAI ). LongCat-2.5 : The model has 1.6T total and ~48B active parameters and is priced at $0.30/$1.20. It built a browser game for $0.28 versus $0.82 for Qwen3.8-Max in one user's test ( omarsar0 ). Other releases : EmbeddingGemma 2 : The paper is out ( osanseviero ). Krea 3 : The technical report covers a model built by a research team of under 10 ( krea_ai ). Crouton Alpha : A free stealth reasoning model on OpenRouter offers 1M context ( OpenRouter ). articles.title: Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor?
articles.snippet: Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones. Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries. Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet )). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower. The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone. Delivery Drone Concerns Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility : “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.” As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies—including Alphabet’s Wing Aviation , Amazon Prime Air , Doordash Air , JD Logistics , Manna Aero , Matternet , Meituan , Zipline , and more, say their flying robots are quiet , safe , and unobtrusive . Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai , while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China . In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027 . And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026. A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot. Wing Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison , a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation, who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.” Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa . Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors . The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone. Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States, including suburban Detroit ; Richardson, Texas ; Glendale, Ariz .; East Cobb, Ga .; Maplewood, Mo .; and Westborough, Mass . The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely. An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia, shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament . In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped [its] engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms, and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens. Communities Take Action Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there. In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “ overwhe

Nobody Knows Anything, 2026 Midterms Edition
articles.snippet: 250 House seats, ~55 Senate seats. The past few months have been fascinating, watching pundits wrestle with what would become a historic election. All presidents lose Congressional seats in the midterms (with only 4 exceptions). Given how close the margins had been, a shift in at least the House was likely. But this particular president has been uniquely polarizing. He won in 2024 by broadening traditional Republican demographics, adding a coalition that included young males, the uneducated, and Hispanics. That left the GOP coalition vulnerable in a normal midterm. How did that it turn out? ~~~ Everywhere I looked – stock futures, prediction markets, polls – turned out to be a panoply of errors. Stock futures were in a deep selloff by 6 p.m.; prediction markets underpriced Democratic candidates; and the Polls , which got the general direction of the race right, had significant errors in the magnitude of the changes and wildly misread Democratic wins in traditionally GOP strongholds. The S&P sold off about 100 points; now it’s up 150 points from those lows. At ~noon today we are +3% on the Dow and +2% on the SPX and NDX; that’s quite a swing. maybe double-check your math…? About those Prediction Markets : The FT reported that “ Polymarket’s gamblers had a bad night of forecasting, undermining the reputation of prediction markets. ” (I have been criticizing their inaccuracy forever). And the Polls! The margins were far wider than even the final polls suggested; polling missed the “Texas Shock” where Talarico won a Senate seat by ~10 points and over a million votes; Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor’s race by 7% and 750k votes; traditional red states like Kansas and South Carolina elected Democratic senators for the first time in nearly a century. The so-called “Shy Trump” voter vanished; exit polls said 43% of voters cast ballots to oppose Trump vs 16% who supported him. Turnout Models missed intense motivation among Dem-leaning voters. Some right-wing politicians imagined the MAGA coalition would last, but it showed signs of fraying almost immediately after the 2024 election. Each of the president’s three signature policies was a factor in the coalition pieces I mentioned to start: 1) ICE ‘s aggressive immigration enforcement; 2) War , and a muscular foreign policy supporting multiple wars; 3) Inflation , driven partly by a silly tariff policy. ~~~ Whenever I channel William Goldman to emphasize how little we know about the future, I feel I am cheating, taking advantage of a flaw in the human condition that most either don’t know or don’t care about. We evolved in a very specific environment to deal with threats very different from the ones we face today. Tribalism, a bad information diet, and an inability to accurately assess our own skill sets are a poor tool set when analyzing social events and politics. It is an utterly fatal combination when putting capital to work in markets… UPDATE: Nov 6, 2026 These folks were right that the polls were wrong — but it was a matter of magnitude, not direction: Previously : Why Polls Fail: Attitude, Intention, Behavior (November 3, 2026) Bad Polling is a Behavioral Problem (October 6, 2024) Finding Investing Lessons in 2020 Election Fails (December 10, 2020) Polls Were Wrong (again). They Often Are (November 4, 2020) What Models Don’t Know (May 6, 2020) Nobody Knows Anything archive The post Nobody Knows Anything, 2026 Midterms Edition appeared first on The Big Picture .

articles.title: How big is the open model economy today?
articles.snippet: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports. articles.title: Robotics Startup Radar 2026
articles.snippet: The Robot Report tracks startups throughout the year, and our second annual Startup Radar spotlights some of the most interesting new companies developing commercial robotics and related technologies. From industrial automation and drones to humanoid robots, 2026 has been a year of innovation in the face of persistent labor shortages and geopolitical challenges. To qualify, organizations must be no more than five years old and must be working on enabling technologies, new full systems, or novel business approaches. The free download notes their application, headcount, and total funding raised to date. This year, we received a significant number of submissions around software, which is no surprise given the recent wave of interest and investment in data, simulation, and next-generation AI models. They promise to make robots more autonomous, combining the ability to perceive, understand, act, and improve. The 2026 Robotics Startup Radar features 60 companies working to serve a range of industries, from manufacturing and supply chain/warehousing to agriculture, defense, healthcare, and more. They are based in more than a dozen countries, and several have already successfully raised millions of dollars. What makes a successful robotics, automation, and AI startup? Such companies offer a strong technical foundation, teams with vision and experience, some business savvy, and key partnerships with industry stakeholders. While not every startup will scale or have an exit or an acquisition, understanding the target market is a key first step. The Robot Report will continue to cover and share financial news and success stories from this competitive space. As startups look to incubators and grants for support, investors and analysts are always looking for the next big thing and the right mix of technologies to continue expanding automation worldwide. Note that the call for The Robot Report (TRR) 50 Robotics Innovation Awards, to be presented at the Robotics Summit & Expo in Boston on June 2 and 3, 2027, is already open . articles.title: How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot
articles.snippet: GlobalLogic developed the UV disinfection robot with Haystack Robotics. | Source: GlobalLogic In hospitals, hygiene is critical. But the cleaning process, which is time-intensive and difficult to scale, remains manual work. This often means the process is also inconsistent. Healthcare facilities are under pressure to care for more patients with fewer resources. These challenges are why the Silicon & Embedded division at GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics engineer a mobile robot to handle disinfection. The project started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when disinfection became a critical use case for robots. “Obviously, this was a big use case at that point of time, in terms of being able to sanitize hospitals and care facilities,” Kunaal Mahanti, physical AI lead at GlobalLogic, told The Robot Report . “So [ Haystack ] came up with this concept of being able to do disinfection better.” “While there were disinfections which are happening manually, it wasn’t really good coverage,” he added. “We were really the engineering and collaboration partner there to see how we can take this concept and make it.” The result is an autonomous mobile robot ( AMR ) that combines real-time perception, edge-based intelligence, and navigation to deliver hospital-grade UV disinfection with minimal human intervention. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company said it can operate safety alongside people, interpret its surroundings, and adapt to changes in its environment. GlobalLogic aims to create a scalable platform When designing its robot, Mahanti said GlobalLogic didn’t want to just quickly design a system for one use case or environment. “We wanted to make it an expandable platform,” he explained. “The idea was that you can look at, for example, the track part of it, which is the thing that is carrying the robot, independent of what it is carrying, which is the UV. Architecturally, you keep them separated so that we can mount other things at a later date.” “It went from a concept to what would be an architectural foundation, so that it’s not just that one product,” said Mahanti. “It actually becomes a class of solutions that we can build for the same industry segment.” While GlobalLogic hasn’t done many other deployments in hospitals , Mahanti did say the company used some of the base components of the UV robot for other projects. “When you look at the platform that moves, there are things that have come out from there in terms of the control of the motors,” he said. “Then we use ROS to do the programming and the sensor fusion part, that is reusable, and we’ve used that. So, if not necessarily the same device, but that architecture broadly.” Navigating the challenges that come with hospitals Healthcare facilities are crowded, chaotic, and involve many closed-off spaces, making them difficult for robots to work in. “The known part was that, obviously, you have to interact with humans. The unknown part is that there are doors, there are things that need to be opened, and you can’t always just barge in,” Mahanti said. This is different from more common use cases for mobile robots in warehousing or manufacturing, which typically involve open-spaces that are easy to navigate “There are two modes that we ended up building for [the robots],” noted Mahanti. “Essentially, one was this autonomous mode, where it would navigate and find the right room. The other was a ‘follow me’ mode, in which case it would follow a caregiver or a nurse.” This means the caregiver can open doors and ensure spaces are ready for the robot to enter. It also means a patient wouldn’t be blindsided by a robot entering their room, for example. However, designing an AMR that can work in these complex spaces has created benefits in other parts of GlobalLogic’s business. With a much higher bar for safety, the company could apply the platform to other industries. “The other learning is just being able to be in an environment where you cannot be loud, for example, when we are designing the motors or looking at what we need to put in [the robot],” said Mahanti. “Those things are specific to this industry, but then dealing with that has helped us build machines with higher fidelity elsewhere, where it is not necessarily a given, but it’s a good thing to have. Why wouldn’t you want to have a nice quiet thing that doesn’t interfere with the rest of the environment?” What’s holding back robotic adoption in hospitals? While more robots are making their way into hospitals, most people cannot yet walk into their local hospitals and find robots roaming the halls. This is still an emerging area for robotics, so what challenges still exist? Mahanti said three things come to mind. The first is cost. “There needs to be an ROI,” he replied. “For example, if you look at this use case during COVID, at that point of time, you needed less people in the hospitals. You needed to be safe. It was a big issue. So that ROI was justifiable.” Second is compliance with medical standards , which becomes much trickier when deploying robots that will interact with the public and patients. Third is the perception of robots. Mahanti acknowledged that hospital staffers don’t want a big, bulky robot taking up space in busy corridors and elevators. Prem Balasubramanian, chief technology officer of GlobalLogic, said that safely integrating into hospital workflows is also challenging. “There are clearly safety concerns, from multiple angles. Navigating in a very human-crowded situation is not easy,” he said. “For a disinfectant use case, if a robot waits for people to keep moving and then slowly moves, you’re okay. But if you’re using it for anything else, like if a doctor calls and you have to get something fast to help a patient or bring some stuff, a robot could get stuck because it sees people moving and it can’t move.” The hospital is difficult on its own, and it’s made even more difficult when you consider how made-for-humans they are, said Balasubramanian. articles.title: LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action
articles.snippet: LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation. In an evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6, it achieved 36.0% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those target tasks. The model combines large-scale human video, glove-recorded hand motion and embodiment alignment to transfer human manipulation experience to robots. Liber-0 achieves 36.0% overall success in a zero-shot evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6. LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a world action model (WAM) pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. The Beijing-based startup said the model combines human video with glove-recorded motion and embodiment-conditioned learning to transfer human manipulation experience to robots. A central test of Liber-0’s generalization is whether it can perform target tasks without robot demonstrations collected specifically for them. LiberAI evaluated the model on a separate suite of 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks, distinct from its internal scaling benchmarks: 20 pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, 20 non-PnP manipulation tasks, and 20 challenging non-PnP and long-horizon tasks. Examples from the suite include placing a pen in a pencil case, pushing a drawer closed, and a longer sequence in which a pen is placed in a pouch and the pouch is stored in a drawer. LiberAI reported task success rates of 63.5% on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on non-pick-and-place manipulation tasks and 10.5% on challenging non-pick-and-place and long-horizon tasks, with an overall success rate of 36.0% across 600 trials. Here, zero-shot means the evaluated checkpoint was not trained on robot demonstrations collected specifically for these target tasks; pretraining still included robot data. Why learn from people? Robot manipulation has traditionally relied heavily on demonstrations recorded on a specific robot for a specific task, usually by a human operator teleoperating the machine. That data closely matches deployment, but collecting it can be slow and expensive, particularly when new tasks or robot platforms require additional demonstrations. Human activity is far more abundant, and much of it is already on video. The obstacle, according to LiberAI, is that human video does not translate directly into robot commands. Cameras sit in different places, hand poses estimated from video are noisy, and human bodies move differently from robots. Liber-0 connects human experience with robot action in three ways. First, LiberSense Glove, LiberAI’s data-collection system, directly records hand movements, helping link human video to the motions behind it. Second, LiberAI’s robot platform uses camera views and hand, wrist and waist movements that more closely match those of humans, making skills easier to transfer. Third, a Unified Embodiment Representation gives the model information about body shape and joint movement, so it can adapt actions to the body performing them. Liber-0 jointly predicts future video frames and actions. This lets it learn from ordinary videos without action labels alongside glove and robot recordings that include measured motion. Human-to-robot transfer. Conceptual illustration of how action-grounded human recordings and visual and kinematic alignment support transfer to LEO. Learning actions that robot data lacked Glove data can also introduce behaviors missing from a policy’s robot data. LiberAI trained policies whose robot demonstrations covered only pick-and-place, while glove demonstrations included actions such as folding, pressing and opening. Performance was measured as a progress score, a 0 to 100 measure that credits partial completion, across four pick-and-place and six non-PnP tasks. With robot data alone, the non-PnP progress score was 2.2. Adding glove recordings of those actions raised it to 47.5, and to 54.6 when the glove set also included pick-and-place, close to the 56.3 scored by a policy trained on robot demonstrations of every action. This controlled experiment is separate from the 60-task suite: the actions appeared in the glove demonstrations but not in the policies’ robot demonstrations. A quarter of the robot data A separate experiment examines whether glove recordings can reduce the need for robot demonstrations. In an eight-task evaluation on LiberAI’s robot platform, where the full robot and glove pools contained equal numbers of demonstrations, a policy trained on 25% of the robot pool plus 100% of the glove pool reached a progress score of 75.6. A policy trained on 100% of the robot pool scored 72.8. In that setting, glove recordings delivered comparable performance with 75% fewer robot demonstrations. The saving applies to robot demonstrations specifically, as the mixed policy still drew on the full glove pool. Because glove collection does not require a robot at each site, LiberAI says experience can be gathered from more people, in more places, and potentially at lower cost. Evaluating the pretrained model directly On LiberAI’s internal benchmarks, the pretrained checkpoint achieved progress scores of 81.4 on pick-and-place and 72.3 on non-PnP tasks when evaluated directly. Robot post-training added 2.2 and 1.5 points, to 83.6 and 73.8. LiberAI said the small gain indicates the pretrained model already captures much of the capability needed for the evaluated tasks. LiberAI has developed an interactive simulation in which users can upload their own objects and watch Liber-0 manipulate them in a virtual environment. The simulation demonstrates object-level generalization: that version of the model was post-trained on 100 hours of simulated teleoperation data and receives no further object-specific training. “Human video shows what people do, but not exactly how their hands move or how that movement fits a different body,” said Songming Liu, founder and CEO of LiberAI. “Grounding that experience in measured motion and aligning
