articles.title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
articles.snippet: At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. For this reason, Arca has developed an internal memory system . “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.” In other words, there are certain tools and tasks the agent can execute by itself — but not ones that involve risk to the client. Arca also runs verification checks on known AI security issues, such as prompt injections. Arca’s agent isn’t itself sandboxed, but it does use sandboxes for computation. Singh explained they’ve gone even further, with extra security measures for handling sensitive data. “We've built systems to make it safe for code inside of that sandbox to access our data,” he said. “So we have this thing which translates the code it [the agent] wrote into a strict format that we expect, throw away the code, and you install guardrails on that format before it reaches your back end. So we allow the agents to use code to query our data, which means that they can aggregate it, they can munge it, they can work with it as they see fit to produce [things] like a financial plan.” Another interesting process Arca has implemented is using feedback from human advisors, along with traces from the agents, to improve the harness. A “meta-agent” is used to analyze all this data and suggest changes to the harness. articles.title: The Hallmark dilemma
articles.snippet: The slogan is “when you care enough to send the very best.” But more accurately, it’s “when you don’t care enough to be on the hook.” For a low-stakes social interaction, the Hallmark card is a convenient and safe solution. Low-risk, it gets the job done. People don’t blame you for letting someone from Kansas say a nice thing on your behalf. Now, it’s happening at scale. If you want to be left off the hook, AI is a convenient excuse. Do what it says. Ask it what to dress up as for this Halloween, or what to write in your marketing copy. Let it design your website or write your resume. Perhaps you could have it write your wedding vows as well. Our culture prizes convenience ahead of just about everything else, and AI slop is convenient. It saves us time but it also saves us emotional labor. The dilemma is obvious. Unlike a Hallmark card, AI is available to do just about everything. And when we’ve streamlined our life to a convenient nub of its former self, then what? There’s a different path. Insist that AI ask you questions. Challenge it to challenge you. Then choose. Sign your work. AI isn’t the cause of slop, and it’s not a good excuse for slop either.

articles.title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
articles.snippet: Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and a long-standing GitLab bug, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this transition. The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid. A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand. Share Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine? When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. It seems like this was wrong. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure. Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers. To start the reflection, I wanted to do more due diligence and track down some receipts on the claim that the AI safety community was reacting as if open-weight Mythos would be an actual disaster, and not just a painful headache. This was distinctly my impression having lived through the online discourse. I’ve gotten criticism that the frontier AI community never said it would be a “true disaster,” but regardless of exactly what they said, it is always about how people hear and internalize your information. Here are some examples of the sort of language that I felt was too exaggerated and from prominent people, which spilled into the public and more importantly federal government perspective that this was a cyber weapon include: Rob Wiblin, host of the 80,000 hours podcast, on his own podcast (April 10, 2026): “If it fell into the hands of criminals or hostile state cyber actors, it would be an actual disaster.” Anthropic, in the Project Glasswing announcement blog (April 7, 2026): “Given the rate of AI progress, it will not be long before such capabilities proliferate, potentially beyond actors who are committed to deploying them safely. The fallout—for economies, public safety, and national security—could be severe.” For one that is actually more reasonable, to illustrate the fine lines between correct and exaggerated, from Zvi Mowshowitz (who I don’t agree with a ton of things on) on April 9, 2026: “Claude Mythos would give attackers a cornucopia of zero-day exploits for essentially all the software on Earth … It would be chaos.” To date, this chaos has been confined to those running large-scale digital products, which is good, but could change. I largely still stand by my above writing a few weeks ago, but I’m nervous about it. I’m not a cyber expert, I’m working hard to make the most educated predictions I can. It’s a fine line between “all of our tech companies need to work extra hard to keep us secure” and “public infrastructure is actually going down.” It is very clear as of writing this that there are way more critical vulnerabilities which are being found in popular tools and fixes are being built. For example, Epoch AI recently published a nice post on their internal work using GLM-5.3 to try and find vulnerabilities and chain them into what could be an attack. The actual exploit they found in Firefox is a good example of why cyber risks need multiple things to align for harm to be done: We used GLM 5.3 to create a website that, simply when visited by a Firefox user and without further interaction, gave the attacker the ability to exfiltrate files from the user’s computer. Here, the exploit is in Firefox, and a would-be hacker needs to plant a website that is looking for this exploit. This is doable, and could have serious consequences, but just finding the exploit is only one step in a multi-stage process. In the previous post, I should’ve been more specific on what “fine” is for a future of cybersecurity, and in this case it means giving more credit to some of the AI safety community that discussed this reasonably as a new era in cyber instability. Reflecting on it, I’m not sure fine is the right word to describe what is inevitably coming – a forced industry update to a new way of working with software, which will clearly be expensive and accompanied by some hard work. articles.title: Confidence isn’t about having more, it’s about calibrating the right amount
articles.snippet: Joe Burrow is once again among the NFL’s elite quarterbacks. Through five weeks of the 2026 season, he ranks fourth in touchdown passes, sixth in passing yards, and leads the league in completion percentage at over 70%. Yet, what sets him apart isn’t physical. It’s mental. Burrow has a nearly perfect level of confidence, which has been calibrated over time. Calibrated? Yes, calibrated. Let me explain. When Burrow was just nine years old, his AAU basketball team was trailing by eight points with thirty seconds left. His coach thought the game was over. Burrow didn’t. He scored nine straight points, including several consecutive free throws, and somehow won the game. Afterward, Burrow’s coach, a sociology professor at Ohio University, pulled his parents aside and told them their son possessed an unusual quality. His blood pressure, he said, appeared to be the same whether he was shooting a basketball, cutting the lawn, or pulling someone out of a burning building. He was unfazed, regardless of the task. Then the coach paused before telling them he was thankful their son was using his talents for good. Otherwise, he could be the next Dexter, the fictional serial killer. Thankfully for Burrow, his parents, and Cincinnati Bengals and LSU Tigers fans alike, that confidence was channeled in the right direction. Over the past decade he has won a national championship and a Heisman Trophy, earned multiple trips to the NFL Pro Bowl, and came within minutes of winning the Super Bowl in 2022. The older I get, the more I appreciate how much confidence matters. In fact, I am now convinced it might be the most significant differentiator in many walks of life. But here’s the critical nuance: it’s not about having “a lot” or “a little”. It’s about calibrating whatever amount of confidence you have. For some people, confidence needs to be unlocked. For others, it needs to be reined in. And for people like Joe Burrow, the challenge is channeling it in the right direction. Too little confidence can prevent someone from taking risks, facing challenges, or even engaging at all. Meanwhile, too much can morph into arrogance. Taken too far, it convinces someone that the rules, the odds, or even reality itself doesn’t apply to them. The key is finding the right balance. I witness this every day with my two sons. My younger son, who is about to turn eight, thinks he can rule the world. There is absolutely no reason for him to possess this much confidence. He hasn’t earned it. He hasn’t justified it. He just has it. And, in many ways, it’s wonderful. Very few things scare him. He’s adventurous. He jumps into nearly everything he does with reckless abandon. This extreme level of confidence might be his greatest strength. Yet, it has the potential to become a material weakness if he doesn’t learn to keep it in check. My older son has confidence too, but his is more like a flame that needs oxygen. It often requires encouragement before it begins to grow. Yet when it does, you can see it. He consistently surprises me with what he is willing and capable of doing. Neither is better. They’re just different and in need of different levels of calibration. But how is someone supposed to find the right level? First, calibrating confidence starts with the people who surround you or you surround yourself with. To this point, while Burrow’s coach may have sounded like he was complimenting his star player, I actually think he was directing his comments at his parents. Burrow’s confidence was the easy part. He simply had it. The challenge was channeling it into productive use, which, as Michael Moritz of Sequoia Capital said on The Outsider podcast, is the essence of parenting. That said, we obviously can only control this to a point. Our parents are ours whether we like it or not. The same is often true of our teachers, coaches, and bosses. However, what we can do is identify those who bring out the best in us, determine what makes them unique, and seek out more people like them. Personally, I’ve had countless teachers, coaches, and bosses. Unsurprisingly, I had a lot of good, or even very good ones, but only a few were truly great. So, what made them different? For one, they didn’t treat everyone with a broad brush. Knowing that people are wired differently, they took the time to figure out what made people tick and adjusted accordingly. In many ways, it’s the same lesson I’m learning from my sons. One needs to be encouraged to take more risks. The other occasionally needs to be reminded that he isn’t invincible. Treating them the same way wouldn’t necessarily bring out the best in either of them. The best teachers, coaches, bosses, and parents understand this. In doing so, they become what are often called force multipliers. Latch on to these people. Study them. Work for them. Hire them. Second, confidence is calibrated by pursuing hard things and experiencing difficult moments. Even Joe Burrow needed this. Burrow arrived at Ohio State as a highly recruited quarterback with every expectation of becoming the starter. Instead, he spent three years as a backup, largely watching games from the sideline. In doing so, it humbled him and he said as much after being drafted by the Bengals, admitting that his confidence was really shaken as a result of his experience in Columbus and that he didn’t know if he had what it takes. Ironically, his two teammates who started over him — J.T. Barrett and Dwayne Haskins — had little-to-no success in the NFL. Yet Burrow didn’t transfer when things got difficult. He stuck it out, graduated, and then looked for a fresh start. And when he did, he didn’t seek out a lesser program where starting might be easier. He chose LSU. Two years later, he produced one of the greatest seasons in college football history, winning the national championship and Heisman Trophy. articles.snippet: (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. Finally, Some Anthropic Numbers. Monday morning brought us Anthropic’s S-1, and not a moment too soon. After four years of arguments about the economics at frontier labs, we now have some real numbers to sink our teeth into, and Ben did just that with his Update on Tuesday . Come for that analysis, and then head over to this week’s Sharp Tech where we talked in depth about what Anthropic is telling investors, questions that remain unanswered, plus why the SEC forced Anthropic to help us understand Meta’s Muse bet . — Andrew Sharp The End of the Internet as We Know It (and I Feel Fine) . Arriving on the heels of a handful of ominous cybersecurity incidents and with continued upheaval guaranteed, Monday’s Article made two distinct predictions . First, the pressure applied by AI will eventually (or imminently?) rupture the global internet that we’ve come to know for the past 25 years. But second, as society moves to more localized solutions and products, that may in fact be a welcome development for all of us who have come to accept degraded experiences throughout our technological lives. As an avid group chatter who’s more or less abandoned public social media, I can certainly get behind the second take! — AS Autocracies Then and Now. On Sharp China this week, we began with an extended look at the climate of fear across the Chinese bureaucracy as Xi Jinping continues an anti-corruption crackdown that was absolutely necessary but may be going further than Xi’s earlier proponents ever expected. Then, we turn to a glorious mess surrounding Mao Zedong and international soccer star Kylian Mbappé. On both that episode and in this week’s Sharp Text , I make the point that connipitions like this one, anchored in a bizarre debate over Mao’s governing history, are evidence that rumors of a Chinese century have been greatly exaggerated. — AS Presented by When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery. Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms. Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it. AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves. No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try. articles.snippet: The Robert Caro interview. Watch on YouTube ; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . Sponsors Antithesis lets you run thorough simulation tests on every PR your coding agents ship. Every minute your software spends in Antithesis is one of the unluckiest hours it will ever experience. Learn more at antithesis.com/dwarkesh WorkOS ’s Airlock is a judgment layer that sits between your agents and your most important tools. When an agent makes a request, Airlock evaluates it against your company’s policies and decides whether to allow it, block it, or escalate it to a human. If it allows it, Airlock takes action on behalf of the agent, which means your agents never see your API keys or other credentials. Airlock is in early access. If you’re interested, go to workos.com/airlock Jane Street ’s mystery ASIC puzzle is over, and they’ve published a blog post that reveals the chip’s purpose. You can read it here: blog.janestreet.com/asic-puzzle-results/ . More importantly, there’s another challenge live now! For this one, you have to design a protocol-emulator ASIC that can be used to test chips outside of a live system. Jane Street will pay to fabricate their favorite submissions. The competition is open until January 18th. Get started at janestreet.com/dwarkesh Timestamps (00:00:00) – How Caro gets people to talk (00:05:03) – Does America need a little more Moses today? (00:12:42) – Moses the young idealist (00:17:57) – Watching Moses lose power (00:24:01) – Did Moses realize he was changing? (00:27:53) – Building during the Great Depression (00:32:51) – The threats and promises of Lyndon Johnson (00:36:08) – Could Kennedy have passed Johnson’s laws? (00:41:00) – Getting a book down to one sentence (00:46:21) – All the material that never made it into the books (00:52:59) – Loneliness Transcript 00:00:00 – How Caro gets people to talk Dwarkesh Patel “If you do everything, you will win.” That is the maxim by which Lyndon Johnson lived his life. My guest today is Robert Caro . Over the 50 years that he has spent writing about Lyndon Johnson , he has lived in the edges of the Texas Hill Country to understand the poverty and loneliness of Johnson’s youth. He has sifted through millions of documents in the Senate and presidential libraries of the entire nation. He has chased down for interviews everyone, from the former goon who helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur who drove him on his first desperate campaign . In other words, my guest today is a man who understands Johnson’s aphorism: “If you do everything, you’ll win.” Mr. Caro, it is such a huge honor to have you on the show. Robert Caro It’s great to be here. Dwarkesh Patel My first question is what I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself represented in Johnson or in Moses ? Is part of the reason you’re able to write so compellingly about them that you share some of their qualities? Robert Caro Let me say first, I think, I hope, there are qualities of both these guys that I don’t share. Among other things they’re so, I’ll use the word, ruthless. You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness. I remember when I started learning about Robert Moses, I went to the La Guardia papers, which were kept in the Boat Basin. They were stored by the Municipal Archives , literally in the 79th Street Boat Basin on the Hudson River, three levels down. There was this row of file cabinets against the wall. I’m sitting there day after day going through these documents. Occasionally I’d come across a note that Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually. Dwarkesh Patel Obviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to here is that just like Johnson or just like Moses, you refuse to take no for an answer. If somebody says, “I won’t give you an interview,” you don’t stop there. You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that you share with these subjects. Robert Caro I’m going to take that as a compliment. Yes. You feel there are certain people that you have to interview. If they don’t want to give you an interview, you can’t, I feel, say no. Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one who rode in the car with him on the campaigns. I said, “There’s no other human being on earth who knows what Lyndon Johnson is doing all these hours driving back and forth across Texas. I don’t know what I have to do, but I have to get him to tell me honestly about this thing.” Dwarkesh Patel This raises another question that I wanted to ask you. You’re interviewing all these people, and in many cases, they must know that it’s not good for them to tell you what you want to know. In many cases, they tell you anyway. How do you get people to tell you things that they know they shouldn’t tell you? Robert Caro You ask terrific questions. Sometimes you’re sitting there and you know this person doesn’t want to talk to you about what you want to get out of them, like John Connally on how Johnson used money to get political power. I’m thinking, “But I’ve been through the notes. Connally collected the money and gave it out at Johnson’s instructions, so he’s the only guy who can tell me how Johnson did this, how he judged who to give money to.” Sometimes Johnson would write on a request for money. If the guy asked for $1,500, Johnson would write, “Okay, 1,500.” Sometimes he’d write 500, sometimes he’d write no, but sometimes he’d write, “No, never.” I asked Connally what that meant, and he said, “This guy was never going to get money from Lyndon Johnson.” Then when you ask why he felt this way about this particular congressman, that’s when the really fascinating stories emerge. 00:05:03 – Does America need a little more Moses today? Dwarkesh Patel

Developed by bluZenit, monkeyBot 2.0 is an innovative robotic platform designed to navigate complex industrial piping systems. [ bluZenit ] Thanks, Trevor! articles.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
articles.snippet: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument. Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours. Science Fact, Not Fiction The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula. Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon. Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science .

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #217
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome back to our 217th Weekly Dose of Optimism. And what a week it’s been! Per New York Metro Weather , we’re in the midst of the longest streak of 8/10 or higher days since the account started in 2021, and here at the Dose, we’re in the middle of a string of 9/10 or higher weeks so long that I’ve lost count. Have a great Halloween tomorrow. For now, all treats no tricks. Let’s get to it. This Week’s Weekly Dose is Brought to You By… Reducto The Document Editor Built for AI Products AI products need more than file generation. They need a fast, accurate document editor that agents can also use. Reducto Editor brings full-fidelity DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX editing into your product through an SDK and embeddable UI. Lightweight and browser-based, it gives agents the tools to revise contracts, update presentations, and edit spreadsheets while preserving formatting and all the functionality you’re used to. Users collaborate in the same file, review native Word tracked changes and comments, and make their own edits without leaving your application. Files retain their full formatting when opened in Microsoft Office. From the team behind the document infrastructure trusted by Harvey, Scale AI, Toast, and Vanta, Editor runs in the browser or on your own servers. Build with Reducto Editor → (1) Anduril Unveils American-Made BlueChip Computer Another week, another extension of Anduril’s capabilities 1 . Last week, we wrote about Warhound , Ben Lamm’s effort to (humanely) genetically engineer dogs to be used in police and military work. Anduril is providing “software and hardware enhancement for items such as dog protection vests and eye goggles.” This week, Palmer Luckey announced that Anduril would be making its very own Made in America computer, BlueChip: designed here, with components from here, with metals America can mine, refine, process, and mill at scale and at reasonable price. American batteries, too. This is cool because as Palmer says in the video, “If you don’t control your technology, you can’t control your future.” But it’s also cool because it seems as if Anduril has gotten to the point where it’s built a machine that can make machines. Assemble enough engineers, capital, manufacturing capacity, distribution, etc… and you can build almost anything. It’s very Elon Companies-esque. And as we wrote in The Electric Slide , making products that can sell a ton of units, like laptops, can create the pull to bring more of the supply chain here, too. (2) OpenAI Says Its Models Disproved the ETH (and more) Video created with Runway The race to solve everything solvable continues apace. This week, OpenAI announced “three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.” In math, OpenAI’s models produced a proof of Christopher Sogge’s 1991 local smoothing conjecture in every dimension, which would also settle the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture (of course). For context, Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved Kakeya in three dimensions just last year, and it was one of the biggest math stories of 2025. In computer science, a model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), the widely held belief that problems like 3-SAT can’t be solved meaningfully faster than brute force. If that makes no sense to you, check out the explainer video I made with Runway , which breaks it down in claymation well enough that I could actually understand it. In physics, the models produced a rigorous proof that interacting quantum field theories, including QCD and pure Yang–Mills, exist in four dimensions. That’s half of a Millennium Prize problem. Whereas before OpenAI has just dropped a bunch of solutions on the internet’s head and walked away, leading to quasi-embarrassing situations like when they said GPT-5 had solved ten open Erdős problems but it turned out the model had mostly found solutions that were already sitting in the literature, this time, OpenAI is sharing the outputs as research data with experts they call “shepherds” in each field, who will choose what to do with the data and where/when to publish. Shepherds don’t have to sign NDAs, don’t get paid, and do get the credit for explaining the work. Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who proposed ETH, are leading the review of its disproof with MIT’s Ryan Williams. Nobel laureate David Gross is leading the physics group, which chose to withhold the AI material and write it up themselves. The math proof and the ETH disproof are on GitHub with Lean formalizations. Lean, a checking software, guarantees the proof proves the formal statement, but human shepherds still have to confirm that the formal statement is the right one. Big week for Lean, by the way. On Tuesday, Axiom announced a complete Lean auto-formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, the “periodic table of symmetry.” The proof runs about 15,000 pages and was written by more than 100 mathematicians over several decades. It’s so big that no single person has ever checked all of it. For a sense of scale, it took Georges Gonthier’s team six years to formalize just one piece of the classification, the Feit–Thompson theorem, back in 2012. But Axiom’s machines can do a lot of human-years quickly, and they’re going to need to to keep up with all of the math and physics coming out of the labs. Because not only did OpenAI announce those results this week, a physics neolab, Physical Superintelligence (which we covered in Dose #209 ) released results on five problems from IQOQI Vienna’s list of open quantum problems , each with a paper, a Lean formalization, and open source verification code on GitHub. articles.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
articles.snippet: Thanks to Max Farrens , who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay. I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written. They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro. I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters. I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday. In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power. Robert Moses Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money. For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power? Exploits in law Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting. The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence. At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses. Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off. And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use. And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it. All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America. But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that no state shall make “any … Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts” entered into by a government entity. A bond issued by a public authority is such a contract. Moses snuck a clause into the law that allowed him to add into those bond contracts “any other matters, of like or different character, which in any way affect the security or protection of the bonds”. These “matters” included whether Triborough could charge tolls for however long they wanted, and whether they would get to keep the surplus thus generated. That is to say, Moses could now entrench his powers simply by writing them into the bonds he issued. From the moment the bonds were sold, those powers could no longer be revoked by the Legislature, the governor, or the mayor - by anything, in fact, short of a Constitutional Convention. The powers that Moses now had were guaranteed for the bonds’ entire lifetime - a lifetime which could always be extended simply by refinancing. So, with just a few minor tweaks

articles.title: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War
articles.snippet: Listen to this post: Good morning, Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar . Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize , an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023 . That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI. To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government. This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion Background Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery. SS: Ben, thanks for having me back. Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey , the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally . But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India? SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos. And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast , seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “ nature always finds a way “, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started. Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World? SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun. What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus , and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take? SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream. I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things? SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages. After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir. SS: Xoom with an X. Xoom with an X, that’s right. Not the Zoom with a Z — which maybe I shouldn’t be talking to, since you’re now an executive at Palantir using Zoom with a Z, but that’s another discussion. You worked on Xoom and remittances, then Palantir, working on national security, arguing for building our homegrown industrial base. There’s an argument there that — to take a paradox that’s maybe unfair — how do you go from a career focused on sending money out of America to being an advocate for money here in America, rebuilding our capital bas

The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
articles.snippet: I am a dabbler, by nature, moving on from topic to topic, but this year, I have spent more time than usual on AI, but that is because it seems to be part of almost every business or economy related story. I tried to value SpaceX ahead of and after the filing of the prospectus for its initial public offering before moving on to the question of whether it and OpenAI and Anthropic should be part of the S&P 500 index . I started my analysis of how AI would affect the rest of us , from doomsday to do-nothing scenarios, largely in response to Citrini and Citadel reports on the topic. in August 2026, I took my first big picture look at AI as a business, which I titled its bar mitzvah moment, with a look at its potential market, business economics and moats. That look was a prelude to the initial public offerings in the works (then) for Anthropic and OpenAI, and I provided a simple way to reverse engineer how much investors would need in revenues from these companies to justify their sky-high pricing. In early October, I looked at how the massive investments in AI are playing out in the aggregate earnings , cashflows and invested capital at US companies, and why it is contributing to holding the market intact, in the face of rising rates. Just last week, I argued that both Anthropic and OpenAI would be priced , rather than valued, for their initial public offerings, using what I called buzzy metrics (like annualized run rates) and promised that I would try to value the company, when it filed its prospectus. On October 26, Anthropic filed its prospectus , and at the risk of being called hopelessly wrong by both bulls and bears, I will try to value the company, using what I see as its most likely pathway, while also leaving the door open for you to disagree with me, and pick your own pathways to valuing the company. The Prospectus Before I delve into the details of the S-1 filed by Anthropic, it is worth noting that at 416 pages, it is long and filled with distractions, as has become the case with almost every initial public offering in the last two decades. (I chronicled this trend in my post on the d isclosure dilemma , arguing that while filings have become longer, they have become less informative). The Anthropic IPO has useful information that both bulls and bears will spin to justify their priors, and in the section below, I look at key disclosures, broken down by valuation input into revenue growth, profitability, risk and reinvestment categories, from both an optimist (glass half full) and pessimist (glass half empty) perspective: Revenue Growth and Composition : The good news in the revenue story is that the company has grown exponentially over the last year, with revenues in the first two quarters of this year about fourteen times as high as the revenues in the first two quarters of the last year, but the sobering news is that revenue growth slowed down in the third quarter of 2026, as OpenAI increased market share, compute capacity acted as a constraint and some enterprises moved to cheaper open source models. The good news on customer composition is that the number of enterprises that spend more than $1 million a year on Claude increased to 1900 , from less than a hundred a year ago, but the bad news is that the company still has concentrated revenues , with its top five customers accounting for 25% of revenues. Operating and Net Profitability : In bad news, Anthropic reported an operating loss, corrected for non-cash and one-time charges, of over $ 8 billion, for the first six months of the year. The actual loss reported was $80 billion, but $72 billion represented a non-cash charge, expensing the conversion option of the convertible bond. The good news, though, is that not only are the trend lines working in their favor, with the company claiming that it had an operating profit in the most recent quarter. The company is also delivering its revenues more efficiently over time, with all of its expenses decreasing as a percent of revenues across the quarters, with compute costs, its biggest cost,, decreasing from more than 250% of revenues to 48% of revenues, on a quarterly basis. Reinvestment for growth : AI agents are computing power hogs, and AI companies invest immense amounts in compute power. The financial statements in Anthropic's prospectus actually do not show this investment at the moment, with neither the cap ex in the statement of cash flow nor the debt (and invested capital) in the balance sheet showing substantial investment in compute power. Before you accuse Anthropic of hiding the truth (or worse), the company is open about its future compute power commitments, reporting hundreds of billions in compute commitments in future years. The good news is that Anthropic is now catching up with OpenAI, which had the lead on compute power, but the bad news is that this catching up has not been cheap, in terms of cost commitments in future years. It i s also worth noting that compute power will need to be renewed and reinvested in, and while chip costs (a key component) may come down, data centers, facing opposition from communities, may become more expensive. Operating and Regulatory risk : Anthropic's argument is that its customers, once they adopt Claude models within their enterprises, will find that they become so integral to operations that they will not abandon them (making revenues sticky and the business less risky). That has not been fully tested yet, and it is entirely possible that spending on AI agents is cyclical and that companies will pull back in bad times. On the financing front, committing to hundreds of billons in compute, purchase and lease commitments exposes the firm to default risk (with a bond rating of BB+), but in response the company will argue that its access to new capital, as a publicly traded large market-cap company, will make this risk recede. In addition, its cash balance, already at $114 billion, and likely to be bulked up with another $100 bill

articles.title: Thin, Light and Built for Everything: NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows Laptops Gain New Models, Agent Tools and Games
articles.snippet: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere. New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark. The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support. Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents. Phantom Blade Zero , S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5. Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark. Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages. Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to: “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.” “Translate this audio into English.” “List what decisions were made in this meeting.” Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware. It’s available today on Hugging Face . Quantized versions are coming soon, so developers can run Transcribe locally onNVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices or scale up on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs. NVFP4 versions will be deployable through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM. Learn more in the NVIDIA technical blog . Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment. With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App , users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings. Liquid AI : One Model Family, Many Ways to Work Liquid AI’s LFM3 provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model. These models support local workflows such as agents running in Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw to triage inboxes and manage calendars, read documents and app screens, transcribe and translate speech, answer spoken questions about handwritten math, and route support tickets or voice requests. Developers can run LFM3 models on RTX Spark with native support through llama.cpp and vLLM, and fine-tune the models locally. ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches With DLSS 4.5 S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches tonight, Oct. 28, at 7 p.m. PT on Steam and the Epic Games Store . Players can take on the role of Soul, a swordsman framed for his master’s murder, as he travels the martial world to uncover a conspiracy. NVIDIA worked with S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing to add ray-traced effects to the title. On RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX GPU-powered PCs, ray tracing adds more accurate bounced lighting, detailed reflections and realistic shadows on foliage and terrain. The NVIDIA DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation feature boosts frame rates with up to 6x frame generation, or adjusts the multiplier on the fly to hit a player’s target frame rate. Read more on GeForce.com . RTX Remix Breathes New Life Into Classics NVIDIA RTX Remix , the modding platform for remastering classic games with path tracing and DLSS, released version 1.6 last week. This update brought RTX Remix to the world’s largest gaming community: Minecraft . Both creators and players can render Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1 through RTX Remix with DLSS-accelerated path tracing and take full advantage of realistic lighting and materials in their future creations. The update also adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, up to 6x Multi Frame Generation, native RTX Spark support and agent-assisted workflows. Starting today, those upgrades come to Portal with RTX and the Half-Life 2 RTX demo. Both now support RTX Spark, with DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering for more lifelike lighting and materials, a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation and new options that speed up

articles.title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
articles.snippet: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregation metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. Language models are capable of so much today, and this scope of capabilities is growing quickly. Our era of singular intelligence indices should be phased out soon, but it will take a long time. A summary of AAv5 is below, from their blog post, where they describe it as “reflecting real-world usage today:” Intelligence Index v5 weights: ➤ Knowledge Work (25%): AA-Briefcase (15%), AutomationBench-AA (5%), and GDP.pdf (5%) ➤ Coding (25%): FrontierCode 2.0 (15%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (10%) ➤ Science (25%): Terminal-Bench-Science (15%) and CritPt v2 hard subset (10%) ➤ General (25%): AA-Omniscience v1.1 15% (10% accuracy, 5% non-hallucination) and HLE-Diamond (10%) Here’s the new ranking of models: The problem with trying to benchmark real-world usage today is that it is extremely jagged, just like the models. The most proven use-case is coding, where open models are far more competitive and likely to keep up. In knowledge work, I’m less confident in open models. At first glance, in aggregate, their model ranking definitely looks reasonable. Still, it shows signs of strain and confusion, as any benchmark will, with GPT 6.1 Terra beating Claude Fable 5.1 on AAv5. Today, some benchmarks measure the absolute frontier of capabilities, playing nicely in open-ended tasks through your favorite harness, which often does take a large model. Some other benchmarks measure certain skills that will be needed of a model in repetitive agentic tasks. I get the feeling that AA is tuning their benchmark more towards the former, a general agentic collaborator, but all of these behaviors overlap. This takes us to the plot going around that prompted me to write this, where they showed the balance of open vs. closed models on the new benchmark. This plot shows 8 closed models beating the best to-be open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro (which isn’t colored blue). This benchmark is taking the opinion of trying to measure where frontier models are moving into, which grows the gap to open models. This is an okay decision to take, but over time as existing workflows of open models become key factors of the economy, it could become a benchmark that misses where the core economic engine of the industry is. Open models’ demise from this seems greatly exaggerated, but I do think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly. Consider this plot from the Kimi K3.1 Pro launch — yes, the open models are strong and useful in some cases, but the best OpenAI and Anthropic models have been a major step ahead in their flexibility and reliability. Some of the evaluations in AAv5 that open models are most behind on are “science” evals like terminal-bench-science and CritPT v2 . Open models are behind, but the value proposition was never to compete truly at the frontier. The open model economy will be about Reducing domains with high market demand for inference to a commodity price of hardware. Allowing ownership of intelligence, specializing it to internal data, and controlling internal agents across many companies in the economy. Both of these will take a very long time to materialize and are partially represented in benchmarks. The supply of compute is currently so low that open model providers also are raking in solid margins – when this shrinks, we will know the system is starting to work. The same goes for diffusion into enterprises, it’s not clear what the exact ceiling on it is because of the difficult ML expertise that is needed to build evaluations and do post-training today. Share At the next major model cycle, say in 2-3 months with GLM 6 or Kimi 3.5, I expect the leading open model labs to make substantial steps on this index, again surprising many observers. This is a cycle we have been on for years now. I’ve written many times about how open models keep up with the frontier, and a summary is that: The best open models do benchmax a little. The worst open models benchmax a lot (but don’t get a ton of attention anyways). The best open mo

articles.title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
articles.snippet: This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions. Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models , a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did. In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack. VicOne Safety-related decisions have inputs too An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated? At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved. A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall. Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information. Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm. VicOne Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed. Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research , a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once. Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated. Security testing strengthens robot safety evidence Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated. That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation , which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team. VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community , VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. articles.title: How AI Is Changing the Pace of Discovery for Millions Living With Dementia
articles.snippet: There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease. The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that. Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet. The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published. C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and a consortium of 18 member institutions across academic, philanthropic, pharma and research organizations, launched in November 2025 to help scientists make better, faster discoveries by accelerating the research that makes new treatments possible. “We have a window of opportunity with artificial intelligence to do research fundamentally different than we’ve ever done before, in a way that accelerates discoveries to help patients,” said Bateman, founder and director of C-BRAIN and the Charles F. and Joanne Knight Distinguished Professor of Neurology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He described their work as “AI tools built by scientists, for scientists.” The consortium is building a system that harnesses previously untapped Alzheimer’s research data to support scientists’ work. Speeding Research From Weeks to Hours Essential assets in Alzheimer’s research are datasets that have never been publicly accessible to AI tools or human researchers. This includes unpublished findings, negative results and governed proprietary data from member institutions. “A lot of life sciences data doesn’t make its way into the frontier models,” said Dr. Ade Ojewole, chief technology officer of C-BRAIN. “The consequence of that is we’re leaving a lot of intelligence on the table.” C-BRAIN refers to this as “dark data,” which slows down Alzheimer’s research. Some dark data is directly deposited into secure computer systems for AI tools to access. To use this data without compromising patient privacy or institutional governance, C-BRAIN uses a hybrid centralized and federated approach — where AI models learn from data at each institution without that data ever having to leave its walls. This kind of infrastructure is technically demanding to build and scale, which is part of what NVIDIA brings to the collaboration. C-BRAIN currently runs 64 NVIDIA data center GPUs on premises alongside cloud-based nodes on Microsoft Azure, with additional NVIDIA GPU capacity, including NVIDIA Blackwell systems , on the horizon as the consortium’s ambitions scale. To explore how AI and accelerated computing can advance Alzheimer’s research while navigating its technical demands, C-BRAIN is working with NVIDIA to incorporate technologies including the NVIDIA BioNeMo open developer platform and the MONAI framework for C-BRAIN’s research pipelines. “The C-BRAIN collaboration with NVIDIA aims to unlock those models in a way that they can deliver something quite impactful and important,” said Bateman. “A great deal of optimization is going to be needed as we push the boundaries of what today’s spatial omics machine learning architectures can model,” Ojewole said. “NVIDIA software is definitely going to come into play there.” Researchers at C-BRAIN have already built two tools: OpenScientist — built with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in an effort led by research scientist Justin Reese — and InsightEngine , built with 387 Labs. OpenScientist is an open source agentic AI co-scientist that takes a scientist’s research question and dataset, then semi-autonomously generates hypotheses, runs analyses and produces verifiable, auditable insights. InsightEngine is an open source research platform that uses agentic AI to test hypotheses against the scientific literature, analyzing user-supplied datasets, exploring a biomedical knowledge graph and checking every claim against evidence to catch hallucinations before researchers commit to costly experiments. In published case studies, OpenScientist completed analyses in minutes that domain scientists estimated would take weeks to months, at a cost of under $10 per run. At C-BRAIN’s current reach of over 200 research groups, this capability could release substantial research capacity, potentially exceeding one million hours annually at scale. From Correlation to Cause Looking ahead, C-BRAIN aims to build a multimodal biological foundation model trained on the full breadth of its data — neuroimaging, multi-omics, fluid biomarkers and longitudinal clinical measures. By year three, it aims to discover new causal mechanisms of brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease, moving to testable scientific principles using the full scope of available research and data. Bateman said, “ AI that can think and reason has the potential to accelerate discoveries that will lead to powerful and implementable preventions and treatments for the entire population.”
