articles.title: A Field Guide to Getting Lost - by Rebecca Solnit
articles.snippet: summary: Really beautiful writing. Wonderful semi-poetic words around the subject of exploring, venturing into the unknown, and identity. Only downside is the subjects became just memoir for the second half of the book, instead of sticking to the theme. recommend: 6/10 my notes: Transformative, extending the boundaries of the self into unknown territory, about becoming someone else. Capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. To be lost is to be fully present. It is a conscious choice, a chosen surrender, a psychic state. Being at home in the unknown, so that being in its midst isn’t cause for panic or suffering. “Lost” comes from the Old Norse los, meaning the disbanding of an army. Explorers were always lost, because they’d never been to these places before. They never expected to know exactly where they were. A Hawaiian biologist discovers new species by getting intentionally lost in the rainforest. She need not think about anybody. She could be herself, by herself. To be silent; to be alone. A need to become no one and anyone, to shake off the shackles that remind you who you are, who others think you are. Some questions are more significant than their answers. Art: Does the work mean what the artist intended it to mean, or is it larger than they intended? We treat desire as a problem to be solved. Rather than on the nature and the sensation of desire, cherished as a sensation on its own. Look across the distance without wanting to close it up. Love this distance. Distance ceases when we arrive in it. The far becomes the near, and they are not the same place. Adults scan the landscape for picturesque panoramas. Kids on their hands and knees, engaged with what was immediately before them. Adults travel by abstraction. There is no distance in childhood. Distance comes with time, with the discovery of melancholy, of loss, the texture of longing, A desire to be lost, to be far away, a desire for that melancholy wonder that is the blue of distance. Yiddish insults can describe defects of character with the precision that Inuit describes ice. The place they were exiled from no longer existed, and they were no longer the people who had left it. A man galloping by a monk who asks, “Where are you going?” “Ask my horse”, says the man. The ethnic past was regarded as unnecessary baggage. The old longings had become little more than habit. Some people receive as birthright a sense of self that those who set out to reinvent themselves, for survival or for satisfaction, travel far. Some people inherit values and practices as a house they inhabit. Some of us have to burn down that house, and build from scratch. Vacant lots like missing teeth gave a rough grin to the streets. Places gave punk part of its aesthetic. Like most aesthetics this one contained an ethic, a worldview with a mandate on how to act, how to live. Nature is allowed to take over when maintenance is withdrawn. Solitude in the city is about the distance of other people. But in remote places solitude seems natural. Writing is an opening statement in a conversation that takes place long afterward without the author. Male hermit crabs often drag a female around by her claw, fighting off rival suitors, until she molts. Only when she is between shells can they mate. Nonfiction seems photographic, finding form and pattern in the stuff already out there. Fiction lets you start with a blank canvas. Romance once meant heroic, adventurous, or mysterious. A poet so perfectly describes the emperor’s vast and intricate palace. The palace disappears when the poem replaces it. To destroy false notions, without even going any further, is one of the ways to advance knowledge.

articles.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . *** Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . *** OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. articles.title: Podcast: Kimi K3.1 Pro, the new cyber reality, and Muse musings
articles.snippet: We — Nathan and Florian — wanted to discuss all the messy trade-offs of a busy week in AI and ask all the pressing questions like: Why did Kimi K3.1 Pro have a mixed reaction with such incredible benchmarks? Will it be adopted? Were we wrong about the risks of open-weight models and cybersecurity? Why do cyber experts discuss recent events so differently than AI experts? What comes next in the few months? What will change our minds? We will write more about this subject, but wanted to bring you behind the curtain as we aspire to quickly learn more about the cybersecurity industry and trends across the last few years that have been leading us today. We conclude the podcast with some lighter topics, from Muse-maxing to excitement in still hiring junior technical talent. Please send us questions and topics, as we plan to record more of these podcasts going forward. Share Listen on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and wherever you get your podcasts . For other Interconnects podcasts, go here . YouTube ↓ Chapters 00:00 Kimi K3.1 Reaction 08:15 Kimi’s open-weight cyber principles 11:23 You can hack everything era 15:54 PHP2Shell, LiteLLM, and the new internet 24:00 Abliterated APIs, safeguards, and trusted access 31:41 Anthropic not hiring juniors employees 36:16 Florian’s Muse addiction 45:30 Wrap-up Links we discuss My thread with Dean Ball about the “boy who cried wolf” story of the frontier labs Kimi K3.1 Pro announcement blog Kimi K3.1 Pro on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index Kimi K3.1 on Artificial Analysis defensive cyber benchmarks Program Bench Open-weight Mythos would’ve been fine take PHP “hasn’t caused a disaster yet” update Abliteration.ai serving abliterated models API Morph serving abliterated DeepSeek via API Joshua Saxe’s Substack on AI and cybersecurity Azeem Azhar, “The internet’s Wuhan moment” Anthropic, “How employment is changing at Anthropic” LiteLLM security incident report Transcript 00:00:00 Nathan Lambert: We are back with another Interconnects podcast. We are with Florian, eval guy, recently moved to SF. Florian, is Kimi K3.1 Pro , name is a mouthful, going to live up to the benchmark scores, for example on Artificial Analysis , or where is it going to land? 00:00:17 Florian Brand: In the past, the Kimi models always lived up to the expectations, but this release is kind of weird compared to the others. I think it is also partially because they are becoming more professional, and the previous model drops were kind of out of nowhere. This time, which also got some criticism, they launched a bigger social media campaign, which allegedly also involved paying people to post about the model without disclosing. 00:00:56 Nathan Lambert: I think a lot of companies do this and tell you not to mention it, but it’s a mess. It’s bad form. No company should do it. Essentially, one person tweeted a screenshot of the press instructions for Kimi that said, “Don’t say this is a paid promotion.” And to my knowledge, no one has corroborated it after that. 00:01:15 Florian Brand: Yeah, and there are right now a few of these model launches, including by American companies, that are just very obviously astroturfed. We have seen launches where it’s thousands of retweets and a few hundred likes, because it works so well to get the attention. Some of them disclose that it is a paid ad while others don’t. But in general, we have seen the professionalization of model launches over time, and pretty quickly. A year ago, everyone just dropped the model, then patched vLLM afterwards, so no one was actually able to run any of the open models for a while. Now you get all the inference frameworks on day one, you get all the inference providers on day one. Or, which is also what we see more and more, the model creator has a few weeks of exclusive access before they release the weights. And that’s also what’s happening with K3.1 Pro. I think it’s two weeks of exclusive access before they release the model weights. 00:02:38 Nathan Lambert: They said the weights would come out by November 4th. And the headline things... I don’t know if I’m going to be able to share screen. I don’t have this set up on this computer. But the headline is this Artificial Analysis number where it’s ahead of GPT-6 Astra. And then if you look at the Kimi K3.1 blog, they have their headline numbers, which are really strong, and then they also have some numbers later on which seem a bit more jagged. I think it was Terminal-Bench Science , which is 20 points behind GPT-6 Astra. I think there were a few others, like ProgramBench . Do you know Terminal-Bench Science and ProgramBench? Are any of these things that people think are important benchmarks for frontier models? Or how do you explain the fact that on Artificial Analysis the model is top, what, three, four? It’s the two latest Claude 5.5 models, Muse Wonder Full, and then Kimi K3.1, which looks crazy. It just looks like totally crazy scores, and I think everybody is still surprised by it. But then there’s this long tail of details that you use to evaluate a model now. I had posted a thread on Twitter of, “What are people’s impressions?” And there’s a lot of people that are like, “This seems not great,” and then some people that are like, “Yeah, it’s fine.” I don’t know, there’s a mixed bag. Relative to K3, which I think was pretty unanimously, this feels like a big model and the post-training seemed a little bit undercooked for that. Maybe this is just a tiny bit RL fried. We’ll see where we land. 00:04:26 Florian Brand: For the benchmarks, one of the things is that the benchmarks that are right now used by Artificial Analysis, they will post their new version probably very soon after we release this podcast. 00:04:43 Nathan Lambert: We can’t tell you the exact date, but both of us know. 00:04:48 Florian Brand: In general, the Artificial Analysis benchmarks are rather short in terms of time horizon, whereas something like ProgramBench is really long and also very explorative.

articles.title: Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course
articles.snippet: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. articles.title: Video Friday: Quadruped Robot Solves Giant Rubik’s Cube by Itself
articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! A quadruped robot autonomously solves a giant Rubik’s Cube using only its feet. [ ETH Zurich Robotics Systems Lab ] Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. [ Reflex ] Thanks, Weikai! I have long advocated for exactly this in the context of robotic laundry folding , or more broadly, other robot recognition and manipulation tasks. Why not make it easy when we can make it easy? [ ACM SIGCHI ] We first wrote about Parallel Systems in 2022 . Nice to see them still rolling. [ Parallel Systems ] I’ll be honest with you: The end of this video is freaking me out a little bit for some reason. This video showcases the whole-body loco-manipulation capabilities of KAIST Humanoid v0.9, developed at the DRCD Lab in collaboration with RAILAB, which developed the robot’s arms. Using onboard visual feedback, the humanoid demonstrates pushing objects weighing up to 35 kilograms and lifting objects up to 20 kg to arrange the letters “KAIST.” [ KAIST DRCD Lab ] When you don’t spend any money on sensors for your robots, you can afford much bigger wheels. [ RaiLab Kaist ] Those robots with wires have gotten somewhat weirder. [ JSK Robotics Laboratory ] The AthenaZero has two, three-fingered robot hands driven by tendons. This design allows the fingers to interdigitate to hold objects of different sizes, such as an egg or a hammer. Each finger is powered by a motor located in the robot’s torso to keep the hand light, transmitting force through flexible cables. This hand is both fast (closing in about 80 milliseconds) and strong. With the addition of highly accurate barometric pressure sensors, it can also be gentle. [ Robotics and AI Institute ] via [ Science Robotics ] A biohybrid robot combines living tissue with engineered materials—here, lab-grown skeletal muscle paired with a soft, 3D-printed scaffold that turns the muscle’s contraction into movement. What if you designed the living muscle and the soft scaffold together, instead of growing the muscle and then building a skeleton around it? In this work from the Soft Robotics Lab at ETH Zurich, we adapted a soft-body simulation framework to co-optimize both at once—and the resulting centimeter-scale bioactuators achieve up to 11x more range of motion than previous systems of comparable tissue volume. Strong enough to jump, swim, walk, and grasp. [ ETH Zurich Soft Robotics Lab ] Oh yes, this is definitely the use case that will scale humanoid robots. [ Unitree ] Here are a couple more teasers from the upcoming ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST). [ ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology ] In three hours, on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for seven days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than 1,000× and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. [ Hybrid Robotics ] This is getting out of hand! Now there are two of them! Introducing the Grain Weevil dual robot attachment. Two robots linked into one larger machine, run by a single operator, doing the work of up to three robots. [ Grain Weevil ] Today [21 October 2026] at CES Unveiled Milan, Generative Bionics announced its plan to build Europe’s largest Physical AI Data Factory, with AMD as its AI infrastructure partner. [ Generative Bionics ] From robotic rovers exploring the rugged lunar landscape to lunar terrain vehicles carrying Artemis astronauts across the surface, mobility will play a crucial role in establishing an enduring human presence on the moon. During the early phases of Moon Base development, these vehicles will help NASA investigate the lunar South Pole region, conduct scientific research, test new technologies, and gather the information that will inform future missions. In this Moon Base update, get a closer look at some of the lunar terrain vehicles and robotic rovers helping to pave the way for humanity’s first lunar outpost. [ NASA ] I appreciate the designer of this single motor drone crediting previous research, which included some cool drones from UPenn that we wrote about in 2014. [ Joshua Bird ] Why choose a bipedal, human-form robot over specialized wheels, gantry arms, or quadruped platforms? Speaking at the Humanoids Summit Seoul 2026, Michael Perry from Persona AI tackles the single most debated question in the industry and delivers the definitive business and engineering justification for the humanoid form factor. [ Humanoids Summit ]

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #216
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome to the 216th Weekly Dose of Optimism! It looks like the hacks this week broke a lot of the internet, but over here in our little corner of it, things are looking good. We have everything from cancer to plant communications to genetically engineered war dogs to basically alchemy. Once again, the week was so jam packed that we have more in the Extra Dose (7 Extras!) than we do up top. Let’s get to it. This week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Reducto The Only Document Parsing Product You’ll Need Reducto is the document ingestion layer trusted by AI teams at Scale AI, Harvey, Toast, and Vanta to reliably turn complex files into structured, grounded data for production AI systems at scale. Processing more than a billion pages per month, Reducto has built its reputation on the long tail of difficult documents that break conventional OCR: dense tables, unusual layouts, handwriting, low-quality scans, strikethroughs, and formatting-dependent information. Its new frontier parsing model, r-1 , combines layout detection, reading order, tables, formatting, grounding, and granular citations in a single request. It reduces parsing errors by up to 20%, improves latency at high volumes, and costs 1¢ per page all-in. Already using another parser? Apply for up to $5,000 in migration credits and hands-on support to benchmark r-1 against your current stack on the documents that matter most. Apply at Reducto.ai/migrate (1) FDA Approves Rectal Cancer Immunotherapy (+ more) U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Jeff Tang, Coherence Neuro; video created with Runway We hate cancer here at the Dose, and we’re not afraid to say it. It’s probably why not a single cancer reads the Dose. We’re willing to sacrifice our numbers for our belief. Consequently, we love when humans come up with new ways to kill cancer, and they’ve done it once again (and again, and again) this week. In June 2022, in a small trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering, twelve patients with locally advanced rectal cancer took six months of an immunotherapy called dostarlimab. In all twelve, the cancer disappeared without chemo, radiation, or surgery. On Monday, the FDA granted dostarlimab (GSK's Jemperli) accelerated approval as a standalone first treatment for stage II and III rectal cancers that are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR). These tumors basically have a broken DNA spell-checker, so mutations pile up until the cancer looks foreign to the immune system. Dostarlimab blocks PD-1, the off switch tumors use to keep T cells at bay, which lets the immune system clear the cancer (explained in the video above). In GSK’s 154-patient trial, after a median of 26 months, cancer hadn’t progressed in 71% of patients treated with dostarlimab alone. In MSK’s expanded 50-patient study, every patient responded, and 93% stayed cancer-free for at least a year. Only about 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers are dMMR, per the FDA, so this isn’t a cure for all rectal cancers, let alone all cancer, but we’re getting into a pretty consistent, almost weekly, pattern of new therapies working against specific cancers, which seems like the way we’ll beat cancer overall. In some cases, individuals are even figuring out how to cure their own, n-of-1 specific cancer. In #177 we led with Elliot’s story on one of those people, GitLab founder Sid Sijbrandij, going founder mode on his osteosarcoma after running out of standard options. articles.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
articles.snippet: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs), rather than with total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. Young Companies in a Corporate Life Cycle All businesses, no matter how large and established they might be today, started as young businesses and matured. With that perspective in mind, I will start this discussion by placing young businesses in a corporate life cycle in the figure below: One of the first steps in analyzing a company is placing it in the right stage of the life cycle, and there are three choices that you can use in making this placement: Chronological age : The first and simplest choice is to look at the age of a business, putting companies that have been in operation for short periods into the young company grouping and classifying those that have been in operation for longer as mature. While this approach is easy to use, and for the most part, effective, it can be misleading in businesses like infrastructure, where it can take decades to get established, and in technology, where the lack of capital intensity can allow a company can go from start-up to mature in a few years. Industry grouping : Another choice is categorizing industry groups into life cycle stages and assuming that any company that belongs to a specific industry group shares its life cycle characteristics. For decades, investors have viewed technology as a shorthand for growth and put technology companies into the earlier stages of the life cycle and utilities as mature or even declining and put all utility companies into the mature to declining company grouping. The limitation of this approach is that there will be divergence within each group, where some companies separate themselves from their industry group; there are mature and even declining companies that are in the technology grouping, and there are power companies that have taken advantage of the data center boom to become growth companies. With technology in particular, where companies age in dog years, I talked about how companies can get mis-categorized and sometimes mismanaged as growth companies , even though their best days are behind them. Operating metrics : Ultimately, life cycle effects show up in the operating metrics of companies, and there are common characteristics that young companies share, and they include the following: High revenue growth : Young companies usually have high revenue growth, and while this is usually off a small revenue base, there are exceptions, where companies with scaled up revenues are still able to show high growth. Operating losses : As young companies scale up, they usually struggle with unformed business models, and at low scale, their fixed costs overwhelm their revenues, resulting in negative or very low operating profit margins. Negative free cash flows : Free cash flows are after reinvestment, and as young companies invest to deliver on their potential growth, that reinvestment will generate negative free cash flows. Failure risk : The confluence of small revenues, losses and negative free cashflows, which must be funded with external capital (equity or debt) exposes young firms to significant risk of failure. The figure below captures the shifts in operating metrics, as companies move through the life cycle: Put simply, if a company has revenue growth in single digits, stable margins and positive free cash flows to the firm, it is a mature company, no matter how it views itself. Conversely, a firm with high revenue growth, negative or very low profit margins and large negative free cashflows to the firms is a young growth firm, no matter what its scale. Recognizing those characteristics is critical in understanding why so many give up on valuing young companies, and why pricing will often be based on unfamiliar metrics. How do Anthropic and OpenAI measure up in the life cycle? articles.title: What will computer chips look like in 2045?
articles.snippet: I spent two days touring Intel’s most advanced fab and talking to its technical leadership to understand what the chips of the future will look like. A lot of what’s coming next – gate-all-around transistors, backside power, CFET, hybrid bonding – is hard to follow without actually seeing it, so we made all the awesome animated explainers that I wish I had while I was prepping. I also asked Intel’s leadership how the semiconductor industry will cope with the enormous shock in demand from AI. AI compute has grown 3x a year for the last decade, but according to Intel’s CTO, Intel could only double leading-edge wafer production with today’s global stock of chipmaking tools. What kinds of tricks can foundries pull to extend this crossover point where demand surges way ahead of supply? This was a totally new format for us - hope you enjoy! I also made flashcards for the concepts I had to learn to prep for this episode here . Watch on YouTube , Apple Podcasts or Spotify . Sponsors WorkOS helps you do business with enterprises. It gives you access to all the features most commonly required by enterprises: SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and more. It’s easy to plug these features in — it only takes a few lines of code — and WorkOS is releasing new functionality all the time, including things like auth for agents. If you want to join the 3,000+ companies that rely on WorkOS, go to workos.com Jane Street built a powerful tool called magic-trace to help analyze and debug their trading systems. It only exists because one engineer noticed a feature on Intel chips called Processor Trace and thought it’d be valuable to build on top of. Now, traders and developers across Jane Street use magic-trace every single day! If you want to be trusted to pursue the ideas you think matter most, Jane Street is hiring. Go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh Antithesis ’ testing platform lets you perfectly reproduce every single bug you find. That’s because it runs on a fully deterministic computer, which strips out all the unpredictability that can make certain bugs flaky and hard to pin down. To build it, Antithesis found every source of non-determinism in Intel’s x86 architecture and either sealed it off or replaced it with a controlled simulation. articles.title: Latest open artifacts (#25): DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, American-made models, and new regulatory controls in the US & China
articles.snippet: The geopolitics of open-weight AI are accelerating again this fall, as we would expect with the risks of all AI systems (open and closed) rising rapidly. We’ve seen many news items in the last week showing both the U.S. and Chinese governments positioning themselves for some controls on open models. MOFCOM, the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, released a policy proposal (it’s not yet a law) that would require frontier AI models and some other technologies to get pre-approval from the government before they can be shared internationally. We found the reaction to this to be overblown – as the document states that open-source technologies will be set up for automatic approvals – but many in geopolitical circles say this is a big deal because it proposes a regulatory framework that could be used in the future to regulate China’s AI industry. Others we trust on this issue say this proposal could be more about preventing issues like the sale of Chinese startup Manus to Western companies, rather than being about frontier AI models. Either way, the wheels of control are moving around AI, and open-weight models are not free from any influence. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released an order on DeepSeek , which restricts DeepSeek itself, as a company, and DeepSeek’s models, as a technology platform, from being a vendor in federal civilian procurement. It is not clear how this will relate to finetuned models or models trained on the outputs of DeepSeek (e.g., Nvidia’s Nemotron models have long relied heavily on DeepSeek models in their training recipes – will they be banned?), but this is an expected action and reinforces the need for a domestic open model ecosystem. Other model makers in China, such as Zhipu AI, makers of GLM, are already on the Entity List under Commerce/BIS, which restricts their access to American technology. DeepSeek followed the above news up by releasing their internal inference stack publicly, DeepInfer , which is likely far more efficient than existing open-source tools like vLLM/SGLang for their models. Estimates point to DeepSeek making up to 90% gross margin when selling tokens on this inference stack. It is well-known that the top AI labs have much more inference-efficient tools internally, and this is the first time we’ve seen a leading lab share them. Inference companies will be quick to adopt these tools, which will drive prices for DeepSeek’s models down across the ecosystem (or margins up). While not an open model or dataset, we consider this release to be one of the bigger open-source AI artifacts in the last few months. Share As of writing this, Kimi K3.1 is rumored to be released very soon, with metadata associated with it starting to appear in public libraries . Exciting times! You can view the models in this email, and all previous issues, on our Artifacts Hub. It includes commentary and other ecosystem metadata. Browse the Artifacts Hub Our Picks MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL by XiaomiMiMo : an update for Mimo, which reuses the same bases as MiMo V2.5, but used a lot more resources on RL training. They also release an in-depth tech report , as well as some of the used environments, which is rare at this scale. The final model from this recipe, V2.6-Pro, is the top open model on Artificial Analysis’s ranking today, and the scaled RL runs came with a fun live dashboard of training. We’ve been fans of Xiaomi for months now, and their efforts are bearing fruit. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 by deepseek-ai : Since the latest Artifacts, the whale has not released one, but two new model iterations with a new size (552B-A16B) which also support image inputs. The model has gained a lot of (well-deserved) attention for its performance at a small price. It also carries the MIT license, continuing the trend established by DeepSeek themselves. This is notable in times where licenses seem to become more bespoke and exclusionary. Below is the Pareto of performance vs price on DeepSWE, a favorite agentic software engineering benchmark today, which DeepSeek dominates. clef by Cloudflare : Decision models are all the rage after being introduced by the startup Typesafe . In short, they are general classification models that output few tokens with their probabilities. Its usefulness has led to quick adoption and also a lot of open model finetunes such as Clef. NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 by nvidia : The mid-sized model of the Nemotron family got its long awaited update. It is strong for its size and can be run at home (given you own a beefy laptop or RTX Spark). As usual, NVIDIA releases the vast majority of the data and an in-depth tech report . Beam-1.0-501B-A23B by reflection : The long awaited open model by Reflection, making it the strongest open American model released under a permissive license (Apache 2.0). While not the smartest open model available, Beam is very impressively token efficient (second to only GPT-6-Astra below). This is a sign of a well-developed post-training stack. Models General Purpose Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf by prism-ml : A ternary version of Qwen3.8-27B for on-device deployments. Ornith-1.5-397B by ornith-ai : A series of Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 finetunes that gained attention in the local AI community for its strong performance over the respective (strong) baselines. Ling-3.0-flash-VL-fp4 by inclusionAI : A 124B-A5.5B model by Ant Ling (within Ant Group), which continues to churn out models consistently. Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B by meta-models : META has released their open version of Muse, which we have written about in more detail ! Read more

articles.title: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)
articles.snippet: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. From the release of GPT-4 to the end of the METR measure, the amount of work AI could do doubled eight times. In 2024, an AI could do a four minute task. At the moment I turned in my draft of Co-Existence in April of 2026, an AI could do 17 hours of human work. And then the benchmark ran out. METR said they could no longer accurately measure the amount of work an AI could do using their current methods. Other studies suggest that number might be 17 weeks of work, or more. And, even as ability has increased, prices have dropped. My old favorite AI benchmark, the Google Proof Question and Answer Exam, which gives the AI problems that regularly stump graduate students, used to cost 30 cents in AI usage to get a single correct answer. Now, it costs four hundredths of a cent to get the same result. How humans work with AI is changing Despite all the progress, the frontier of AI ability is still jagged, just as it was 30 months ago. Some areas have stayed stubbornly weak (AI is still quite a bad long-form writer), while others, like solving math problems, went from terrible to superhuman in the same period. And, as I discuss in the book, even where AI is excellent, small gaps create large needs for humans, at least for now. But AI’s gains have been so large that how we work with it has to change. In Co-Intelligence , I wrote about centaur work (divided between AI and humans) and cyborg work (blended between AI and humans). Both keep you in the loop… but you can only be in so many loops at once. Now that we have real agents, I added a third way to work with AI: the conjurer. Conjurers summon agents when needed, assign them work, and evaluates what comes back. The charts in this post were made that way: I summoned agents, gave some general guidance, and I said “make it better” a lot. It is the most powerful way to use AI, and it carries new risks as we lose control over what, exactly, the AI is doing to get us those results. The Otter Test has fallen Regular readers will know that I have been testing AI image generation and movie tools with the prompt “Otter on an Airplane Using Wifi” for the past few years. This is what the best image generator, Midjourney, produced 30 months ago. So today I asked Opus 5.5 the following (typos and all, prompting has become much less important as AIs get better): “I have a post showing the what happened over the past 30 months of AI in honor of my new book (published 30 months after the origina). i want you to make the ultimate otter on an airplane using wifi video. just something fantastic, i know you are creative, give it a go.” Using my subscriptions to various online services from Google and ElevenLabs, it produced the following. (Turn the sound on) The video has a few flaws. But the AI figured out how to make it, from the script to the images to the concept to the music to the technical aspects of creating all of this, without any help from me. That is what has changed. This is the least we will ever talk about AI As a result of all of these gains, AI is only becoming a bigger issue in the world. articles.title: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
articles.snippet: By Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, and Arvind Narayanan. See the full author list and affiliations here . There are growing calls for independent and embedded AI evaluation, especially of AI agents. But much remains unclear: what constitutes a “good” evaluation, what needs to be evaluated in the first place, and how best to coordinate and support the influx of people entering the burgeoning evaluation ecosystem. Our group at Princeton has been working to improve the state of AI agent evaluation for about three years . We teamed up with people who’ve done foundational work on evaluation at Stanford, the UK AI Security Institute, and Brookings. Our paper is titled Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation. We synthesized the trends we see across three dimensions—the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem—with the goal to help those who are upskilling for this new paradigm. We also aim to equip evaluators, funders, and the public with a set of questions to ask, and provide actionable recommendations. Thirty-three emerging trends in AI agent evaluation. (Figure from the paper .) Challenges for agents, new and old AI developers have long made claims about the real-world performance of their systems based on benchmark scores. It is harder now to assess whether the evidence gathered supports claims made about agents. The evaluator must scrutinize the entire trajectory, not just the final outcome. It is important, for example, to know if agents took shortcuts, particularly since they have access to tools and environments. And when agents perform better or worse, it is harder to attribute these changes to different components of the agent. Addressing these concerns requires significant engineering effort, and the work is getting increasingly expensive—for example, several agents on the ExploitBench benchmark cost tens of thousands of dollars in credits to evaluate. These numbers also don’t factor in the significant engineering effort needed to set up and maintain the evaluation infrastructure itself. Agent evaluation is much more complex than model evaluation. (Figure from the paper .) Faced with the massive volume of traces that agents generate, evaluators are also struggling to inspect and monitor these agents at scale. The tools evaluators rely on today to do this work are not foolproof—and themselves require evaluation. To investigate the recent OpenAI-HuggingFace incident after the fact, evaluators relied upon other agents to look for and identify instances of harmful action, an approach they acknowledged carried its own limitations and biases. Because agents are deployed in dynamic settings (and increasingly together with other agents), it is harder to design good metrics to capture the underlying concepts of interest, and create valid conditions to implement them. Addressing these challenges will require better tools, more rigorous benchmarks, and experimentation with different approaches and formats, such as through open-world evaluations and growing observational data on real-world usage. The scope of evaluation needs is growing Evidence about agents is needed to understand their effects at different layers, but does not always translate across layers. (Figure from the paper .) Crucially, the results of evaluation at one level of scope are not guaranteed to translate to another. An agent might demonstrate capability in the lab, but face limits when placed in a specific use case. Consider METR’s randomized controlled trial which found that, despite expectations, usage of agent tools toward software development actually increased overall completion time on the tasks at hand. Agents may be able to perform certain tasks, but how that capability translates for humans in the real world requires evaluation in context. An expanded research agenda is therefore needed to understand agents at each level: their capabilities, their interactions with humans, and their impact on institutions and incentive structures. This work requires both technical and sociotechnical evaluation to study not just the agent itself but the agent(s) in context. Across these different layers, evaluators have a choice in framing the questions they ask and the findings they generate. Can an agent automate a task or process? Or, can an agent augment the work of a human? These are two complementary lenses. If evaluation largely focuses on how agents automate certain tasks, we will better understand where and how human work can be replaced. But it won’t tell us how humans can better collaborate using agents, or how agents can improve human work. Who gets to evaluate and how? This expanded research agenda will require an expanded set of evaluators from a mix of disciplines. It will also require that evaluators have the freedom to choose which questions to pursue and how. When evaluators with different approaches agree, we might gain greater confidence in those results. And when they conflict, evaluators can identify vague definitions and limitations to their findings. Who gets to participate, and with what independence, will shape the questions evaluators ask and the methods they use. Meaningful independence is influenced by several factors. As the costs of frontier evaluation keep increasing, the ability of independent evaluators to participate will be increasingly determined by their access to increased funding. Whether independent evaluators have sufficient access to models also impacts their ability to measure and assess the true frontier. Questions of access now also extend to Chain of Thought traces for agents, since frontier labs now release summarized versions instead of raw traces. Alongside these challenges, evaluators also need to navigate whether they can conduct work without fear of retaliation, and how they can transparently share their findings. Where do we go from here? There is a clear window now to bring in new participants, methods, and ideas for agent evaluations, an

articles.title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
articles.snippet: Agility Robotics , the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5 . It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined. From ATRIAS to Digit My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals. We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS —short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait. With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones , and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie . Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year. Agility Robotics Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash. Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1 , which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers. Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins . Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. articles.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later. My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves. Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world – as we’ve heard in so many sessions here – and is contributing to its own development. Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work. What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why. For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up. They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun. The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities — on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” The singularity is here . The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril. Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development. I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly – ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find. But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. As a consequence, the field of software development is changing – A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans. We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life. But new AI capabilities bring new challenges – the coding improvements have meant AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these p
