articles.title: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
articles.snippet: This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open , which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4 , with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too! In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant. This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively? That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs. Share Why Muse Spark Open should take off — and why it may not One thing we see again and again at Interconnects through our open model analysis is that Western open-weight models get astonishingly more adoption than Chinese models with the same performance-to-size footprint (even though the Chinese models usually come out first)! Muse Spark Open is landing into this environment, at the same time as when open-ended LLM agents are finally real (~ GLM 5.2 capabilities and on ). Riding off a rapid increase in performance of Chinese models, the open ecosystem has been living through an acceleration in demand. The inference providers are rapidly scaling, the open post-training economy is forming, and countless enterprises are looking to own their intelligence. Muse Spark Open’s performance falls somewhere above GLM 5.2, near DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and behind GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3. It should be squarely “good enough” to slot right into this. For some background, from the Muse Spark Open model card on Hugging Face: Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter open weights model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal. This open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. We recommend deploying Muse Spark Open as part of a broader AI system, with additional guardrails suited to the specific use case. Here’s the distribution of the various Muse models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. This is included to loop back to the original model card snippet. It was shared that this open-weight model underwent additional safety training to prepare for this open release. Many observers saw this release as potentially a model that was “broken” during the safety training, as it came out after Muse Spark 1.3. In reality, this was much more likely a safety tune of Muse Spark 1.2, which would only be a 1 point drop on Artificial Analysis to shore up safety behaviors. When Meta released Muse Glimmer , the 30B agentic model, Alex Wang said that they were preparing to release the Muse Spark 1.2 model as open weights, which fits with the above. If anything will hold Muse Spark Open back, it’ll be the specific license they designed for it. In summary, this custom license has pretty much all of the restrictive license behaviors we’ve seen (and criticized here) in the last few years of building with open models. They are as follows: Users of the models in products must display “Built with Muse” on their products. Meta did this with Llama, and Kimi has tried it, but almost no one complies. There is a revenue-gating factor, where companies that make more than $20M per month across their entire business deploying the model need a separate license with Meta. Other prominent open model providers are doing this too, in order to set up revenue share agreements for re-selling inference. Muse Spark Open makes you agree to an acceptable use policy, which in the true “open source software” corner of the world makes this model extremely not open-source. All of the above applies to outputs from the model as well, and derivatives, so there is legal ambiguity if you can safely use the model for synthetic data. The license does permit using Muse Spark Open for internal research and applications. We’re at a weird equilibrium where this license is complex and unproven in court, but many players will likely ignore it. Many, many people will build on this model from various inference providers, and Meta will only likely go after egregious violations. For now, licenses haven’t been the determining factor of AI adoption, but this could change in the future. This is why we think it’s an unnecessary strategic risk for labs trying to compete and regain adoption to have complex, non-standard open licenses for their models. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. Is Meta a tier 1 (OpenAI/Anthropic) or tier 2 (Gemini/xAI) frontier lab? Just a few days before Muse Spark Open, Meta unveiled their closed frontier models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full . 1 On traditional benchmarks, these are very strong models only behind Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 and similar to Open

articles.title: Video Friday: When Two Robots Become One
articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! When one robot loves another robot very much, and they’re connected by a wire, they can get together and make a brand new robot! SFW. [ JSK Lab ] What happens when Microducks meet? They start to sing together. Each Microduck syncs with its neighbors over Bluetooth, then they compose a song on the fly, in harmony and in perfect time. There’s no score and no conductor. Two, three, or four ducks are enough for a choir to break out. If Pollen isn’t selling Microducks in four packs for this exact reason, WHAT ARE THEY EVEN DOING!? [ Pollen ] In an internal test, Google DeepMind robotics researchers instructed Gemini 4 Argon to watch a video of a human playing cornhole. Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI. [ Google DeepMind ] As of 11 October 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), becoming the new off-world record-holder for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. The previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) was held by NASA’s Opportunity rover. Perseverance reached that mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15. [ JPL ] Let’s not argue about whether these are robots or not and just agree that they’re cool. [ OATs ] If one cute little robot can clean up one block, how many blocks can 40 cute little robots clean up? Science has the answers! [ Paper ] Thanks, Keisuke! Before Rosalind Franklin can explore Mars, it has to get off its lander. Engineers are rehearsing that first journey on Earth, using a full-size rover model and Mars-like terrain. The test recreates some of the challenges Rosalind Franklin will face on the Red Planet, from reduced gravity and a 20-degree incline to uneven ground and obstacles beneath its ramps. [ European Space Agency ] From custom part to running robot, the Atlas shop floor is built on precision, rapid assembly, and real-time collaboration. By machining parts in-house and streamlining assembly and repair under one roof, we are driving the manufacturing velocity needed to turn complex designs into walking hardware at scale. [ Boston Dynamics ] What can a quadruped robot do beyond the lab? Deep in China’s Ailao Mountains, DEEP Robotics Lynx M20S joined a team of researchers on a biodiversity field expedition—navigating rugged terrain, scouting routes ahead, carrying research equipment, and capturing wildlife in areas that are difficult to access on foot. [ DEEP Robotics ] The Kamino simulation software is a GPU-accelerated physics solver designed for accurate simulation of complex mechanical systems with kinematic loops, such as parallel manipulators, planar and spatial linkages, and multi-limbed robots with coupled joints, without requiring simplified approximations. [ Disney Research ] The original Kawasaki UNIMATE robot as featured in (remember this show?) The MacNeil/Lehrer Report in 1982. [ Kawasaki Robotics ] WildOS enables autonomous robots to perform long-range, open-vocabulary object search in previously unmapped and unstructured outdoor environments by unifying geometric safety with semantic visual reasoning. Through a vision-scored navigation graph and beyond-horizon target localization, the system demonstrates more efficient and robust exploration than conventional geometric or purely vision-based approaches in extensive field experiments. [ ETH Zurich Robotics Systems Lab ] Who needs an AI-generated person when you can have an actual robot that looks exactly like an AI-generated person instead? [ UBTECH Robotics ] The recovery behaviors here are impressive, but the robot is far slower than a human would be, suggesting that the value it generates is primarily in novelty. Which is fine for now, but novelty wears off, and then what? [ Sharpa ] Here are a couple of good panels from ICRA 2026 in Vienna, including one on “Impact and Return on Investment on Humanoid Robots” and a second on “Advancing Sustainability in Robotics.” [ ICRA 2026 ]

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #215
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome back to our 215th Weekly Dose of Optimism! Welcome to the flying flipping car era. As bad as things have been for my Philadelphia Eagles, that’s how good they’ve been for humanity. Let’s get to it. This week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Reducto The Only Document Parsing Product You’ll Need Reducto is the document ingestion layer trusted by AI teams at Scale AI, Harvey, Toast, and Vanta to reliably turn complex files into structured, grounded data for production AI systems at scale. Processing more than a billion pages per month, Reducto has built its reputation on the long tail of difficult documents that break conventional OCR: dense tables, unusual layouts, handwriting, low-quality scans, strikethroughs, and formatting-dependent information. Its new frontier parsing model, r-1 , combines layout detection, reading order, tables, formatting, grounding, and granular citations in a single request. It reduces parsing errors by up to 20%, improves latency at high volumes, and costs 1¢ per page all-in. Already using another parser? Apply for up to $5,000 in migration credits and hands-on support to benchmark r-1 against your current stack on the documents that matter most. Apply at Reducto.ai/migrate (1) Neural Networks Are Already Clean Nick Cammarata · Goodfire Good news - AI is probably way less likely to kill us all now because humans rock and one of us just kind of figured out how to learn to read their minds. It is beautiful that a person I became aware of and started following because of his understanding of his own mind—I discovered Nick Cammarata through his tweets on meditation and the jhanas—seems to be the person who’s figured out how LLMs’ brains work. In the “The Short Version” section, he writes: I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean. Basically, he thinks that we can understand what’s going on inside of models’ brains - “interpretability” - which means that alignment is probably solveble. As he explains, “interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don’t think we can solve alignment if we don’t know what we’re building.” Cammarata used to work on interpretability at OpenAI, and he himself “came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots.” Now, he tweeted: the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works. If he’s right, not only did the p(doom) from runaway AI just tank, but it’s also another win for using technology to solve problems that previously seemed unsolvable. Chalk one up for the optimists. (2) Tesla Introduces Flying Roadster Thank god we’re going to live, because it seems like the future is going to be as cool as advertised. Last night, nine years and a number of delays after Tesla first teased the second-gen Roadster, Elon took the wraps off at a SpaceX test site near Waco. It was worth the wait. The car went 0–60 in about a second, which would have been the coolest thing at any car reveal in history, except this one. Next, using 10 nozzles fed by a 600-liter compressed-air tank, plus some very large fans, it drove up an upside-down ramp, spun around, and set itself down on the pavement. Then it hopped over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while moving. Tesla said the car would go half the speed of sound (?!?!) at 380 MPH? Musk said production starts in 2028 (for real) and joked, I think, that they’d try to jump the Snake River Canyon, the ramp where daredevil Evel Knievel attempted to cross the canyon on a steam-powered rocket. Just… watch the video if you haven’t. (3) Arrowhead Shot Cuts Tau in the Brain by 73% Arrowhead Pharma, video created with Runway Speaking of brains… As I’ve written before, my grandmother had Alzheimer’s, and me or someone I love getting Alzheimer’s is one of my biggest fears in life. So whenever there’s a potential development on the Alzheimer’s front, we cover it, even if they’ve historically ended in disappointment. The hard part of treating brain disease like Alzheimer’s is getting drugs to the brain. The blood-brain barrier is very good at its job, which is why RNAi drugs, which silence a gene before it can make a protein, have been ineffective against brain disease. They’ve mostly been effective in targeting the liver (which filters everything). On Wednesday, Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals reported interim Phase 1/2a data on ARO-MAPT, which silences the gene that produces tau, the protein that tangles up in Alzheimer’s, frontotemporal dementia, and progressive supranuclear palsy. Healthy volunteers who got two subcutaneous doses at 12.8 mg/kg saw mean total tau in their spinal fluid fall 73% by Day 105, with one participant down 85%. Day 105 was 90 days after the last shot, which means the effect held for three months and the eventual dosing schedule could end up be quarter

articles.title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
articles.snippet: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. But we think AI can also augment human workers in many interesting ways, that some of the maximalist attempts to completely automate all human labor are deeply unpromising on both technical and economic grounds, and that right now too much of AI research is devoted to the latter at the expense of the former. The bias toward the automation agenda is partly because of economic incentives, but partly because of some deeper intellectual and cultural aspects of computer science as a field. The alternative view has deep intellectual roots in the history of computer science, especially the subfield of human-computer interaction. Moreover, there are compelling technical and economic reasons to pursue it now. A small but growing number of businesses are now coming around to it, after witnessing the economic disappointments of attempting to implement the first program. Despite this, it remains a minority position today, poorly understood, and disorganized. Above all, computer science as a field today lacks a clear articulation of a systematic program for the architecture of AI that would further this agenda. In this essay, we briefly discuss what is at stake here, the history of this debate in CS, the status of this debate today in economics and elsewhere, and the automation agenda in the culture and curricula of CS in the university. Above all, we sketch in Section 1 a few research directions for AI that push in the direction of human-AI collaboration. Designing AI for true collaboration requires solving a very different set of technical problems than today’s models and agents, problems that are often ignored, or not even understood to be problems. The specific directions we sketch are intended to be tentative and experimental. But the point is to explicitly conceive of a project for AI that differs from the dominant Silicon Valley one, and moves beyond criticism to the positive articulation of an alternative direction. Our hope is that this can serve as a seed for a much broader, sustained, experimental, and collective research program. In Section 2, we discuss the high level motivation for our project, and in Section 3, we give a brief history of some of these ideas. In Section 4, we put this all into the context of the debates today about AI and automation in economics and in policy, and in Section 5, we outline a bottom-up, market-driven approach to steering the direction of AI development and deployment. 1. A Research Agenda for Collaborative Agents A serious research program for human-AI collaboration elevates novel technical problems that the automation agenda for AI is more likely to ignore or treat as relatively unimportant. We present four such illustrative directions. Problem #1: Can we produce white-box agents for various domains of human labor? The dominant paradigm for AI models and agents is “black box”: the system is evaluated based on the final output it produces. The intermediate steps are generally not revealed to the user, may be mysterious even if revealed because they depart greatly from how people approach the task, and are not treated and optimized as an aspect of task performance. One reason for the black box paradigm is the absence of process traces in model training. If we train a new AI model on a thousand paintings from the Renaissance, but we have no data on any of the many intermediate steps and revisions involved in the creation of any given painting, we can’t expect anything other than a black box model. Maybe it can generate the image of a new painting in a similar style, but it will not be able to actively talk us through the steps involved in creating such a painting. What we instead call “white box agents” are AI systems that are epistemically more legible to their human users, and explicitly reveal their intermediate processes (sources, assumptions, methods, uncertainties, process artifacts). White box agents could open the door to all kinds of more direct forms of human-AI collaborations: if humans can see the intermediate processes, they can directly interact with them. The successful development of white box agents will require tackling many technical sub-problems. Chiefly among them: capturing process traces for a much broader range of human labor. The past few years of AI model training and deployment have had a disproportionate focus on software coding. There are many reasons for this, but a big one is that we benefit from the very public availability of a massive number of coding repositories, which include traces of every step of the process of software development. But for so many of the other important professional occupations in the economy today — l

articles.title: Collaborative Fund Conversations: Matt Sonsini
articles.snippet: The limits of good intentions: Matt Sonsini on philanthropy’s feedback problem, startup term sheets, and learning to be an optimist. 🎙️ Listen on Spotify , Apple , or wherever you get your podcasts. Matt Sonsini is Managing Partner and co-founder of Ravello Impact, and the former CEO of The Sobrato Organization. Before moving into investing and philanthropy, he spent almost two decades as a corporate lawyer in Silicon Valley, working with startups, venture capitalists, and public companies. In this conversation, he explains why waiting to give can become its own excuse, why measuring philanthropic impact is harder than measuring investment returns, and what founders sacrifice when they chase the highest valuation. He also revisits the boardroom moment when a CEO quit on the spot and the unlikely IPO that still stands out decades later. “Well, I guess if you’re Warren Buffett, you have a reasonable shot at compounding capital at a greater rate than the world’s problems are compounding. But for mere mortal investors, I’m personally doubtful that’s the case.” Key Takeaways: Giving has its own risk-return spectrum : Local food banks offer immediate, measurable results. Systemic change demands more time, more resources, and a willingness to accept uncertain outcomes. Sonsini approaches those choices as a portfolio, allocating across both. Good intentions need honest feedback : A business with a bad product hears from the market. A donor can still get a gala and a name on a building without knowing how much good the money did. He also argues that funders, nonprofits, and government need to collaborate more to make their resources count. A higher valuation can hide a worse deal : Senior liquidation preferences and separate investor approval rights can create conflicts when growth stalls. He urges founders to resist trading away important terms to reach a headline valuation. Venture’s failures are part of the process : Funding booms draw talent and ideas into new markets. Many companies fail in the correction, but investors cannot know the eventual winners in advance. He sees that experimentation as necessary. Optimism takes practice : Legal training taught Sonsini to look for downside. Investing taught him that optimism is essential. The best advisers, he says, tell clients which risks matter and which they can stop worrying about. Timestamps / Table of contents 00:00 – Introduction to Matt Sonsini 01:03 – Give Now or Compound for the Future? 05:01 – Measuring Impact and the Risk of Virtue Signaling 07:52 – Building a Philanthropic Portfolio 09:20 – Government, Philanthropy, and the Need to Collaborate 12:43 – The Term-Sheet Rights Sonsini Would Remove 16:31 – Why He Dislikes Pay-to-Play Provisions 17:00 – Don’t Chase the Valuation 19:18 – Why More Venture Capital Doesn’t Eliminate Failure 24:25 – A Boardroom Takeover and an Unlikely IPO 29:17 – Learning to Be an Optimist 31:49 – Closing Remarks

articles.title: Q&A: Mars Perseverance Rover Sets a Distance Record
articles.snippet: On 11 October , the Perseverance rover completed a drive that brought its total distance traveled on Mars to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers). This is a new record for Mars rovers, enabled in large part by Perseverance ’s ability to drive with much more autonomy than its predecessors. Over the past five years, Perseverance ’s autonomy software has been steadily upgraded, and to learn more about how the record was broken and what the future holds for the rover, we spoke with Mark Maimone , the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who designed and developed the self-driving software for Mars rovers Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance. Before we talk about Perseverance, let’s pour one out for the previous record holder, Opportunity , which landed on Mars in January 2004 for a three-month mission and ended its epic journey 15 years later in February 2019. This NASA video compresses Opportunity ’s entire mission into four minutes and gives a poignant sense of the incredible distance that this little rover traveled over its 15-year life on Mars, doing science as it went: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory/YouTube Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers until a planetary-scale dust storm stopped it in its tracks, appropriately enough, in Perseverance Valley. On 18 February 2021, Perseverance joined NASA’s Curiosity rover on the red planet, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter tucked under its belly. Curiosity and Perseverance both ditched Opportunity’ s solar panels for a radioisotope thermoelectric generator . Curiosity has been active on Mars since 2012 . Despite Curiosity’ s nearly 10-year head start, Perseverance is the rover to first break Opportunity ’s record. There are several reasons for Perseverance overtaking Opportunity — ruggedized wheels for one —but the biggest contributor is that Perseverance was built for autonomy . Maimone shares how JPL added enough autonomy for its Mars rover to drive itself from 225 million km away without crashing . This animation shows Perseverance’s point of view during a drive of 807 feet (246 meters) along the rim of Jezero Crater on 10 December 2025, the 1,709th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Captured over 2 hours and 35 minutes, 53 Navigation Camera (Navcam) image pairs were combined with rover data on orientation, wheel speed, and steering angle, as well as data from Perseverance’s Inertial Measurement Unit, and placed into a 3D virtual environment. The result is this reconstruction with virtual frames inserted about every 4 inches (0.1 meters) of drive progress. JPL-Caltech/NASA Let’s talk about rover autonomy on Mars. Even before Perseverance, rovers were driving themselves, right? Mark Maimone: Yes! Sojourner [in 1997] had an early kind of autonomous behavior—for sensing, it used four laser stripes projected onto the surface, which it used to measure the height of 20 points in the terrain in front of it. It could steer around big obstacles, or even thread the needle between two things. It was a real autonomy system, which is very impressive considering its CPU was less than one megahertz. With Spirit and Opportunity, I developed the autonomy for those rovers. Every time they drove, they would use 256 x 256 pixel stereo pairs to map the geometry of the terrain and find a safe route forward. Spirit actually ended up driving itself 23 percent of the time, which I was frankly shocked by, since it drove much more slowly in that mode. But using autonomy helped Spirit travel 50 percent faster than it otherwise could have . Opportunity and Curiosity both only used autonomous driving about 5 percent of the time. Perseverance is the first Mars rover that drives itself 90 percent of the time, with its enhanced autonomy system that includes a second processor with an FPGA to speed up extra image processing operations. What was it like to let Perseverance drive itself for the first time? Maimone: Perseverance is the culmination of decades of work on Mars rover autonomy, so seeing Perseverance use its AutoNav system to drive itself basically at full speed, up to 120 meters an hour, was incredible. These two images taken by Perseverance’s hazard avoidance and navigation cameras show (at left) the very first AutoNav drive on Mars where the rover autonomously stopped before running into a rock pile, and (at right) the second AutoNav drive where the rover successfully steered around a rock. JPL-Caltech/NASA Where are the humans in this process? Maimone: The plan of where to go is specified by the science team, and then on the engineering side, the strategic route planning team develops a path to get us to that goal by guessing, based on lower-resolution maps from orbit, what the terrain is going to look like for the rover. Each day, a tactical operations team combines the strategic overall route with that day’s science goals to pick the actual route the rover will follow. We want humans to keep doing long-range planning because that avoids wasting time. For example, we’ve learned that if we see sandy areas with intersecting waves or crests—not just ripples blown in one direction, but cross-ripples going in multiple directions—the rover tends to sink into terrain like that, so we tell the rover to keep out of those areas. The onboard autonomy only measures terrain shape, not terrain type, so it benefits from those location-based annotations. We now have years of experience correlating images taken from orbit with images taken by the rover, and understanding how different kinds of terrain affect the drive. With the current orbiters at Mars, we sometimes get 25 centimeters resolution on orbital images. That’s still not quite enough to see all obstacles; there could be a big rock that doesn’t really show up on a scale of more than one or two pixels, making it very hard to notice. That is why you want to have autonomy on the rover, but the greater help we can give it at a high level, the faster we can reach our goa

articles.title: Runway: Learning From Watching the World
articles.snippet: Welcome to the 1,825 newly Not Boring people who have joined us since our last essay ! Join 281,011 smart, curious folks by subscribing here: Subscribe now Hi friends 👋, Happy Tuesday! A couple of weeks ago, I mentioned that I was partnering with Runway this quarter as our presenting sponsor to bring some of my writing to life in the form of video. It took us a while to land on the right partner to form a deeper relationship with — it has to be a company I want to talk about a bunch — but when Runway reached out, it was a clear perfect fit. For one thing, I’ve had a lot of fun playing around with their video models. But for two others: 1. I’m fascinated by World Models (and quoted Runway co-CEO Anastasis Germanidis in the essay Pim DeWitte and I wrote ) and 2. Runway has been on a tear with new product releases. I wanted to understand how, so to kick off the partnership, I asked to write an essay with me explaining how video, interfaces, operating systems, and robotics all fit together, why video was the right starting point for World Models, where the world is heading if Runway’s bets are right, and whether or not, as someone who simulates worlds, he believes we’re living in a simulation. Let’s get to it. Runway: Learning From Watching the World A Co-Written Essay with Runway Co-CEO Anastasis Germanidis Cover image generated by Runway From time to time, a certain company catches fire. You can tell when it’s happening by the pace and breadth of their product releases. One day, a new capability. Cool. The next day, another. Woah. Next day, another still. Runway , the world model company best known for releasing the first commercial video generation model, is on such a run. Over the past six weeks, it has shipped a real-time interface model, a new interactive world model, an open-weight robotics model, an AI agent for performance marketers, a research preview of an operating system, and it bought a robotics lab in Paris along the way. Meanwhile, the business is growing faster than at any point in its history, adding more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue in the last quarter alone. From the outside, it looks like a company that suddenly figured something out. From the inside, the view is much more interesting. Runway has been pursuing a particular set of bets for eight years, and that near-decade of research and iterative deployment is now yielding a seemingly disparate but actually related set of new models and products. On September 1st, Runway introduced Solaris, the “first Interface World Model,” which allows users to generate interfaces in real-time, through prompts or actions on screen, like this one where a guy takes a selfie and tries on glasses and tweaks his hair and smile with the drag of a mouse. On September 8th, Runway announced it had acquired Kinetix , a Paris-based research lab, which specializes in… robotics? From the video company? Then at their September 30th AI Summit, the team shared Praxis-1, “an open-weight World Action Model that turns our video pre-training expertise into real world control for robots.” The thesis is that while robotics data is limited, video data is practically infinite. So Runway pre-trains on video data and then uses that as a policy model for robotics developers who can train it on their specific embodiments. Standard Bots , whose co-founder Evan Beard and I co-wrote an essay on robotics , is working with Runway to deploy Praxis-1 on its arms. And then the very next day, on October 1st, Runway previewed Project Continuum, “a new operating system research application built around real-time video interfaces.” A video model. An interface model. A robotics model. An operating system. Are you getting it? These are not separate pretrains. They’re different applications, built around the same General World Model backbone, with different post-training on top. Made with Runway All of them are examples of what you can do when you can simulate any pixel. An operating system ends up as pixels on a screen, like video and interfaces do, and like the world does through a robot’s eyes. If you can simulate every pixel at high enough fidelity and speed, then you can make almost anything that shows up to the world as pixels. This is the future Runway is building towards. Runway is making a few different bets, on a research direction, the Bitter Lesson, and a business strategy. It is betting that world models can learn, like humans do, from third-person observation. It is betting that letting models watch a ton of video will lead to models that understand how the world works better than they could by reading about how the world works or from any other human-mediated data source. And it is betting that it can build a massive business in content creation in order to both help fund the large investment into better and better models, and to become the rare company that is both a frontier lab and a distribution layer. Runway’s commercial success and product prolificness points to a surprisingly wide set of applications for World Models; surprising, that is, unless you read the essay Pim DeWitte and I co-wrote explaining why World Models have the potential to eat everything. In it, we wrote: World models — these systems that learn from watching the world and the actions taken in it — are a fundamentally new kind of foundation model. They can compute what was previously uncomputable. There are a number of different types of models whose makers call them World Models, although many don’t fit our definition; they don’t predict the next state based on intervention. We categorized Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs, which AMD recently agreed to acquire for $8.2 billion, as building “3D Reconstruction and Generation Models.” Runway, we wrote: Is blurring the lines between video generation and world generation, as mentioned in the Video Model section. articles.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters – HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) . Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) . *** The AI race is going to space – and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger – of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) . *** AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”. The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental comp

articles.title: I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence
articles.snippet: I’ve often been surprised when I hear from top researchers in industry that they think AI will be better than them at their job in a few years, and I didn’t really know why I doubted it. The explanation I arrived at is that researchers are seeing this massive acceleration in the infra and engineering capabilities of the models. I fully agree that the models will be superhuman distributed GPU engineers in a few years. This will make experimentation and tinkering with the formulation of the models far easier, but it will not make our models dramatically different in nature. In some ways, Ilya was early in his declaration of AI being in the era of research . Research is much easier today now that we have coding agents. This ease is through a different form of work that is flexible and engaging, which signals the start of an era where good ideas can be much more valuable than good execution in software. Subscribe now We’re very early on this path. It’s also not the first transition the field has seen across the balance in if AI is more “research” or “engineering.” Before deep learning took off, AI was also far more of a research endeavor. Today, the best researchers are well-known to be judged by their ability to implement and scale their ideas in complex infrastructure. We’re about to go through a massive acceleration over a few years where the bottleneck is less and less engineering again. Some call this RSI, but a more grounded form is simply “parallelized, AI-assisted language modeling.” You don’t need to buy into takeoff scenarios to see just how much infrastructure improvements are coming, and how this’ll change the nature of working in AI. The goal of this piece is to give an overview on why this engineering acceleration will happen, and touch on what it won’t quite fix. This’ll be a massive boon for diffusion of the technology into the economy, even if we don’t get economically valuable superhuman traits outside of math and coding. A lot of this near-term progress comes from scaling the inference-time compute we have with current tools, rather than dramatic step-changes in how good the models are at research. Share Many pieces of the AI training and inference stack are very verifiable. Training metrics like tokens per second per GPU, which is just training speed. Inference metrics look like tokens per prompt, FLOPs per token, or really just cost per answer. Both of these are very optimizable, especially as there are established sub-problems and architecture trade-offs which can improve them. I expect AI agents to help optimize this process end-to-end in a few years, where our inference capabilities get very close to the underlying maximum compute possible on our accelerators like GPUs. Over the previous few years, the gains companies can make on inference efficiency were already giant, e.g. saving like 10-30% on cost to serve a model after announcing it at a certain price point. This entire stack will compound, and I expect the effective cost of model intelligence to decline near-exponentially over the coming years (potentially faster than recent trends). This low-hanging fruit of efficiency should take only a few years to capture. The longer term will be co-design of accelerators and models on longer timelines, which give extra orders of magnitude in efficiency on top of the flexible GPU platform. During this time of rapid efficiency gains, the flexibility of the GPU should be king, as the exploration space in architecture feels important and like a major lever of automated research. A prediction of pretraining research, at least in architecture and data selection to serve our current class of models, being automated in 2-3 years feels reasonable to me. All of this will be a massive trigger of Jevons paradox for agentic models. I expect demand to only increase, as the industry is largely bottlenecked on figuring out better ways to orient and deliver the agents. Meta’s Muse agent is an early indicator of this and we should expect more Muse-like experiences for different audiences and target use-cases. It’s value created by understanding how agents work, rather than pushing the frontier of performance. The equivalent phase in the broader scientific literature like biology and chemistry will be an era defined by models finding numerous cross-sub-field findings. The AI models are superhuman at crawling literature and making connections across sparse networks which are currently stewarded by small communities of scientists who rarely interacted. There will be a fine line between this heralding a new era of scientific discovery, e.g. with cures of most cancers, or an acceleration of the arc science was already on. Another industrial-scale piece of low-hanging fruit is improving the general quality of RL environments. You don’t have to look far to see another new RL data company that’s crossed $100M or $1B in revenue. There are way more than I expected. The average outputs from this sector are remarkably low-quality. Countless researchers agree that lots of what they buy is frankly crap. At the same time, the leading labs see clear return on investment from buying the data. The way that many RL environments are cruddy is clearly fixable. Read more

articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! It’s possible that I wasn’t the only one who thought that Figure’s recent stunt was somewhat ridiculous. Devanthro is, in fact, selling these plastic balls for $1,000 each, and they’ll arrive in time for Christmas. [ Devanthro ] Not that anyone uses ringtones anymore, but if we did, this would be absolutely everywhere, and I’d be loving it. [ Pollen ] Let’s not get too excited, but this threadlike linear motor is pretty sweet. [ Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne LMTS ] What is this robot for? It’s for doing exactly what you see here, that’s what it’s for. [ RAI Institute ] Humanoid robots still struggle to plan contact-rich whole-body manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception. Workhorse learns such manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations. On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse sorts boxes with its hands and a kick, catches a thrown box, and topples and climbs a suitcase. Yeah that happens to me too when I have a communication failure. [ Hybrid Robotics ] A car wash that models your vehicle, then cleans it with robot arms? Interesting idea. The recent reviews from this location suggest that the robots aren’t quite up to snuff yet, but it really seems like there’s potential here. [ KUKA ] So this is not the worst idea I’ve ever seen for what to do with humanoid robots. [ DEEP Robotics ] Some lovely manipulation with a deceptively simple gripper. [ Generalist ] I am genuinely embarrassed to say that this robot dances better than I do. [ General Robotics Lab ] MIT researchers developed SANDO, a new navigation system that helps robots safely navigate unfamiliar environments while avoiding moving obstacles. The system can rapidly plan and adjust a collision-free path using onboard sensors and computing, with safety backed by mathematical guarantees. [ MIT News ] Can you spot the part of this video that I’m side-eyeing? Yep, it’s where the middle clip starts after the hand already has a good grip on that peelable strip. [ Sanctuary AI ] Inspired by feather stars, the NC State researchers report a soft underwater swimming robot capable of achieving three distinct swimming modes—jellyfishlike vertical swimming, fishlike directional steering, and rotorlike 3D reorientation—using only two pneumatic inputs. [ NC State University ] Here’s a series of mini-keynotes from ICRA earlier this year on manipulation, humanoids, and embodied design. [ ICRA 2026 ]

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #214
articles.snippet: Cover image generated by Runway . Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome back to our 214th Weekly Dose of Optimism! I took Dev to watch LeBron James’ first preseason game as a Sixer last night, the good guys gave us too many great stories to fit into one Dose (check the extras), and it’s beautiful here in NYC. Life is good. Let’s get to it. Today’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Guru Your company’s knowledge is one of its most valuable assets—but only if your AI can trust it. Guru helps organizations create a verified, current knowledge layer that people and AI can rely on. You’ve probably experienced the frustration of giving AI access to a mountain of company information, only to see it struggle to distinguish an approved policy from an outdated document or an old Slack conversation. Guru helps companies structure, govern, and continuously improve the knowledge behind their AI. The Knowledge Accuracy Gap guide explains how leading organizations are closing the gap between what AI can do and whether it has accurate company context to work with. The guide covers how to: Correct an AI answer once and apply that correction across connected agents and AI experiences Keep people involved where judgment and approval matter, while AI handles routine knowledge work Build a trusted knowledge layer that supports both employees and AI Improve knowledge quality and governance as AI adoption grows Your company is already using AI. Make sure it is using the right knowledge—with Guru . Build AI Your Company Can Trust (BONUS) KILO: a not boring film on Airbound Last week, I wrote a Deep Dive on Airbound . In the Before Times, that would have been that. Hit send. On to the next. But we are in the Now Times. In the last Dose, I told you about our new partnership with Runway, and over the weekend, I decided to see what would happen if I gave my essay, a few references, and some creative direction to Claude/ChatGPT and asked them orchestrate the production of a short film using Runway. The result is KILO, the story of a package that was batched and pushed around until a kid in India figured out how to let it fly solo. Again, I’m not great at this yet, but I find it incredibly magical that I can take all of the work that I pour into writing and turn it into a film in just a few prompts. It’s a good time to be a storyteller. (1) Nobel Prize Picks 2026 Laureates This week, the Nobel Prize committee began handing out the most coveted prizes in science, starting with The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were awarded Prize for their “discoveries leading to optogenetics, which makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain.” Optogenetics is a wild field - by shining light at cells, you can turn them on and off, make them do different things. I had a non-meat burger made using a process that involved optogenetics once and it was delicious. This video of Diesseroth telling his kids he won has racked up 4.5M views. It’s awesome. Other winners announced so far are: Francis Halzen in Physics “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin” Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai in Chemistry “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis” Anne Carson in Literature “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature” Now, I need to figure out what any of this actually means, but I, for one, am happy that we take some time out of every year to celebrate the world’s geniuses, and to let them celebrate their great achievements to humanity. (2) Atomic Machines Comes Out of Stealth with Matter Compiler Just in case you thought we might not be living in the future, we are living in the future. Yesterday, a startup called Atomic Machines came out of six years in stealth with a product called the Matter Compiler: “an AI-native manufacturing system that builds working micro-machines from code alone. No per-product tooling. No process development. Different code, different machine.” If the name sounds familiar, it’s because a matter compiler is a long-held sci-fi dream. In one of my all-time favorites, Neal Stephenson’s The Diamond Age , he literally calls the machines they use to make everything up to and including entire islands “matter compilers.” The idea goes back further. In 1959, Richard Feynman gave "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom" and offered $1,000 for a working motor that fit in a 1/64th-inch cube. He expected it to take a whole new approach to engineering. William McLellan won it in 1960 with a microscope, a watchmaker's lathe, and a toothpick. In 1986, Eric Drexler's Engines of Creation imagined molecular "assemblers" that could "build almost anything that the laws of nature allow to exist." A year later, Star Trek: The Next Generation upgraded the old food synthesizer into the replicator . Biology got here long before humans did: founder & CEO Jeff Holden's essay compares the Matter Compiler to the ribosome, which builds every protein in your body from code. Now, anyone can say they’re building a matter compiler. But Holden was Amazon's tenth engineer, built Prime, and became Uber's first Chief Product Officer . He's also been watching Star Trek since he was five. He has both the skills and the childhood dream necessary to pull this off. The first product AM is building with the Matter Compiler is the PrimeSwitch PS-150 , a 9.5 mm relay that carries 150 amps and opens in 50 microseconds, ~1,000x faster than a contactor, for the 800-volt DC data centers that AI is pushing the industry towards. No existing chip fab can process its materials or assemble its moving parts, but AM says it can, and is beginning to ship to early customers now. articles.title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Cashflows: The AI Effect plays through!
articles.snippet: In a post at the end of August 2026, I talked about interest rates in 2026 and marveled at the capacity of equities to keep rising in the face of rising rates. I argued that the resilience of stocks during the year could be traced to higher-than-expected earnings being reported by companies in 2026, and a concurrent increase in expected earnings in 2027 and 2028. Now that September 2026 is one for the record books, it is time to take stock and dig a little deeper, especially since the month brought about one of the largest increase in treasury yield rates in recent memory, and stock prices still held their own. In particular, I want to examine the earnings at US companies, in the aggregate and by sector, trying to trace out where the earnings increase is coming from, and how that increased earnings is playing out on corporate balance sheets and cash flows. Stock Prices and Rates In my earlier post on interest rates, I had looked at treasury rates by day through the end of August, and I will begin this section by updating that chart to include a tumultuous September: I had described the rise in rates between January and August as gradual, but the rise in rates in September was anything but, as the ten-year rate rose from 4.75% at the start of the month to 5.29% at the end. In fact, to put the 54 basis point rise in the ten-year rate in context, take a look at the distribution of monthly rate changes in the ten-year treasury in the chart below: The September rise in rates would put in the top ten percent of 770 monthly rate changes that we have seen between 1962 and 2026. In the face of the mark up in rates, stocks held their own in September, at least in the aggregate, and you can see that in the chart below, where I look at aggregate market values, by month, and by sector: = The market added $2.5 trillion in market capitalization across all stocks in September 2026, but almost $1.5 trillion of that came from technology As you look across the entire year, broken down by quarters, here is what you see in the aggregate market caps: Only companies listed at the start of 2026 included I excluded firms that were not listed at the start of 2026 from the list since including them will give a misleading sense of returns to investors; adding SpaceX, for instance, which was listed in June 2026, will increase the value of communication service companies by more than $2 trillion, but it was listed at roughly that value. There are many who have pointed to the fact that US equities, while up for the year, have seen divergence in performance, and you can see that phenomenon play out in two statistics. The first is that three sectors - technology, energy and materials have carried the market, with technology being the biggest contributor to market gains. The second is that the percent of companies within each sector that are up for the year is about 50% across the market, and in the third quarter, about 65% of all listed stocks saw dropping stock prices. It is often difficult to make sense of what is moving stock prices because there are so many factors from growth to interest rates to cash payout that are pulling in different directions. It is to counter this confusion that I have resorted to estimating an i mplied equity risk premium , where I estimate the internal rate of return you can earn by buying equities, given how they are priced, and their expected earnings growth and cash flows, as well as interest rates. That calculation, which I have done at the start of each month since September 2008, yields an expected return of 8.99% for equities and an equity risk premium of 3.70% (3.92%) over the ten-year treasury rate (dollar riskfree rate) of 5.29% (5.07%) at the start of October 2026: Note that this estimation is model-agnostic and is an internal rate of return for investing in stocks, given expectations of the cash flows from investing in equities. If you are a market timer, and I am not one, you could use this implied equity risk premium as a barometer of market priciness, with a lower number indicating overpricing and a higher number indicating underpricing. Download spreadsheet The jump in US treasury rates in September 2026 has had an effect, with the equity risk premium dropping below 4% for the first time this year. In fact, even as the ten-year treasury rate has climbed this year from 4.18% to 5.29%, the expected return on stocks has also gone up from 8.41% at the start of 2026 to 8.99% on September 30, 2026. The AI Cap Ex Boom: Accounting and Corporate Finance Consequences The focus on stock prices and interest rates can sometimes distract us from paying attention to corporate investing, financing and cash return policies that drive value. It should not surprise you, given the times we live in, that AI is at the heart of the business story that is driving corporate behavior, and in the process, providing the fodder for market resistance to higher rates. I will begin with an assessment of how the trillions of dollars in AI cap ex will show up in financial statements: As you can see, the AI cap ex story is a complicated one, if you are looking at market aggregates, because the market includes both the companies that are spending the money building the AI architecture, which includes data centers and other infrastructure, as well as the companies that are supplying the ingredients for that infrastructure. The builders of the architecture are the hyperscalers (Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft et al.), and the money they spend on cap ex will cause lower earnings, at least until the cap ex starts paying off, in the form of amortization of the AI cap ex, as well as a hit to their free cash flows, which are after cap ex. The money spent on AI cap ex though becomes revenues to the chip makers (Nvidia and TSMC leading the way), network equipment manufacturers (Broadcom, Micron and Marvel, to name just three), power plant builders (Constellation Energy et al.) and even real estate developers focused

articles.title: This Disembodied Hand Is All the Robot You Need
articles.snippet: A hand attached to the end of an arm is a given for most humans, but what if robots didn’t have to play by the same rules as we do? Researchers from ETH Zurich have turned an off-the-shelf robotic hand into a completely self-contained robot that walks on its fingertips while using those same fingers to manipulate its environment. Besides making the perfect Halloween accessory for anyone planning to dress up as a member of the Addams Family—who were famously accompanied by a disembodied walking hand called Thing —this robotic hand could make it possible to operate controls and handle objects in places a traditional robot arm can’t reach, the researchers say. Soft Robotics Lab, ETH Zurich/YouTube Amirhossein Kazemipour , a Ph.D. candidate in the Soft Robotics Lab at ETH Zurich who led the project, believes this hand could prove useful in contexts like fiddly maintenance tasks in industrial settings, or in search and rescue, where a robot could detach its hand to explore confined spaces too tight for the rest of its body. More broadly, he says, the work is a step toward a new approach to robotics in which body parts are not confined to a single role. “I wanted to see how much a robotic hand could do without the rest of the robot,” Kazemipour told IEEE Spectrum . “Instead of having this traditional view of robotic parts, what if we could use those parts to do other tasks that they are not designed to do?” This is not the first attempt to get a robot hand to walk , but previous work has typically relied on specially designed hands. The ETH team instead decided to use off-the-shelf hardware from Wuji Technology , augmented with an 80-gram backpack containing a battery, an inertial measurement unit (IMU), and a Raspberry Pi Zero. Kazemipour says they decided to go with a commercial robot hand because they didn’t want to compromise on the hand’s manipulation capabilities. This introduced significant challenges, he adds, because a hand’s shape is optimized for grasping rather than crawling. How to Walk With Fingers To teach the hand to walk, the researchers trained a model in simulation using reinforcement learning—an approach in which models learn skills through many rounds of trial and error, receiving rewards for getting closer to the desired behavior along with penalties when they diverge from it. But Kazemipour says the unusual geometry of a hand meant they couldn’t just reuse methods used to train other kinds of legged robots. Standard quadrupeds or bipeds tend to be symmetrical on their left and right sides, which simplifies walking and balance, he says. Hands, in contrast, are not at all symmetrical, with fingers of different lengths and an opposable thumb. In addition to rewards for moving at the right speed and in the right direction and penalties for things like wobbling or jerky movement, the team introduced a novel way to keep the hand in a crawling stance during the simulated training. To account for unequal digit length, they gave each finger its own target position relative to the palm, based on where it naturally sits when in the crawling posture. They then penalized the fingers for straying too far from that reference point, creating what they describe as “virtual springs” that pull the fingers back to the crawling stance. Crucially, the penalties for fingers moving forward and backward are significantly less than those for moving side to side, so taking steps in that way costs the hand very little compared with the rewards it receives for moving. The team also trained separate models for skills like righting the hand when it falls over, pressing keys on a keyboard, and pushing objects to a target. All four models fit on the onboard computer, says Kazemipour, and the controller can switch between them as necessary. In real-world tests, the hand crawled across 14 different surfaces including smooth floors, metal grates, grass, and gravel. Other experiments confirmed that it could make both right and left turns, and hit an average speed of 9 centimeters per second. The hand was able to right itself in 21 of 25 trials. When given a video feed from an overhead camera, it even managed to autonomously push a 41-gram cube to targets up to 40 cm away 15 times in a row. “What interests me most about this work is that the same fingers can move the hand, support its weight, and interact with its surroundings,” says Masahiko Inami , a professor at the University of Tokyo whose group has developed hand-shaped walking robots . He agrees that a mobile hand could be useful for reaching confined spaces and operating controls that an entire arm could not easily access, though he says practical deployment would require onboard perception and more robust navigation. Hideki Shimobayashi , a Ph.D. student in Inami’s lab, also points out that walking puts very different loads on a hand compared to grasping, so durability may be a challenge. However, Matei Ciocarlie , an associate professor of mechanical engineering at Columbia University, says it’s a “cool result” that suggests robot hands don’t have to be restricted to the same capabilities as their human counterparts. “One can imagine an entirely new class of mobile manipulators that are simultaneously dexterous, able to traverse complex terrain, and able to manipulate payloads comparable in size to themselves,” he says. Kazemipour sees his work as part of a longer-term vision for robots made up of parts that are not tied to a single job or even a single body plan, something he calls “autonomous modular embodiments.” “Robotic body parts should not be permanently assigned to a single function,” he says. “They can dynamically transition between roles, between being components of one embodiment system and autonomous agents, according to the task.”

articles.title: HiPHI: A Large-Scale Benchmark for High-Precision Human Motion and Object Interaction
articles.snippet: This White Paper gives robotics researchers and engineers an overview of a new large-scale motion capture dataset built to close the data gap limiting humanoid robot learning. It also shows how policies trained on the dataset transfer to a real humanoid robot. What you will learn about: Why humanoid robot learning, a central problem in embodied AI and Physical AI, needs data that internet video and existing motion capture datasets cannot provide. How FrameNet , a linguistic framework for human action, can guide motion capture collection to systematically cover a broad range of whole-body motion. Why synchronized object trajectories and meshes make human-object interaction data useful for teaching robots real-world tasks such as carrying, pushing, and pulling. How reinforcement learning policies trained on this motion capture data improve with scale, and how sim-to-real transfer carries them onto a physical humanoid robot.
